description: Every theory listed on the Landscape of Consciousness (loc.closertotruth.com), pulled verbatim from the structured data on each theory page: name, category, subcategory, summary, the page's key takeaways (its claims), theorists, and LOC verification status. No quiz content and no categorisation of our own — see README.md.

theories.name: Anomalous & Altered States—Overview
theories.summary: Can nonphysical consciousness (or realms) be revealed or accessed via anomalous, psi, or paranormal phenomena—extrasensory perception (ESP), out-of-body experiences (OBEs), near-death experiences (NDEs), and the like? Psychical research beginning in the late 19th century and parapsychology in the mid-20th century sought to study the phenomena scientifically. In addition, some claim that meditation and psychedelics can reveal hidden realities of consciousness.

claims.title: Core Concepts
claims.text: Explores claims that psi, NDEs, OBEs, and altered states reveal nonphysical aspects of consciousness.

claims.title: Scientific Context
claims.text: Parapsychology and psychical research study anomalous phenomena; debates over validity, replicability, and interpretation remain fierce.

claims.title: Why Meaningful
claims.text: If any phenomena defy physics, non-materialist consciousness theories gain serious empirical motivation.

claims.title: Major Challenges
claims.text: Strong skepticism, anecdotal bias, poor replicability, and lack of accepted mechanisms limit mainstream acceptance.

theories.name: Anomalous and Altered States Additional Theories
theories.summary: Additional theories of anomalous or altered states.

theories.name: Barušs’s Meaning Fields
theories.summary: Imants Barušs proposes a transcendent theory of consciousness that takes into account anomalous phenomena, altered states, and quantum field theories, and in which “meaning fields” play a special role.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness emerges from a transcendent, pre-physical substrate structured by nonlocal “meaning fields” containing layered meanings.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Meaning fields organize events, define boundaries, and are tunable or alterable through human intention.

claims.title: Distinguishing Ideas
claims.text: Nested, overlapping, temporally nonlocal fields integrate influences from past and future into present events.

claims.title: Notable Implication
claims.text: Meaning exists beyond humans, with fields capable of selectively shaping reality without physical intermediaries.

theories.name: Bitbol’s Phenomenological Ontology
theories.summary: Philosopher of science Michel Bitbol suggests that a radical view of neurophenomenology amplifies “the available range of interpretations of altered states of consciousness, from OBEs and NDEs to meditation and psychedelics, and which may suggest a new ontological category.” There are generally three such interpretations, he says: “two objectivist-realist and one non-committal (mild) phenomenological interpretation.”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Radical phenomenology reframes altered states as revealing a hidden, self-manifesting mode of being.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Rejects both naturalist and supernaturalist views, focusing on embodied, lived experience as primary.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Proposes “endo-ontology,” an inner perspective arising from the process of being itself.

claims.title: Transformative Role
claims.text: Altered states disclose a continuously present yet usually overlooked nature of mind and being.

claims.title: Philosophical Roots
claims.text: Draws on Merleau-Ponty, Heidegger, Sartre, and Tibetan Dzogchen nondualism for ontological insight.

theories.name: Broad’s Emergent Mind and Psychic/Psi Factors
theories.summary: Broad argued that phenomenal consciousness is real and irreducible: even complete microphysical knowledge of a brain could not reveal what an experience—such as smelling ammonia—feels like. His strong emergentism therefore held that consciousness may arise lawfully from complex physical organization while possessing genuinely novel qualitative properties. Broad systematically compared 17 possible mind-matter theories, favoring “Emergent Materialism” on ordinary evidence. However, taking psychical research seriously led him toward a Compound Theory in which consciousness might emerge from the conjunction of brain and a further “psychic factor.” Telepathy, precognition, mediumship, and survival evidence were therefore potentially crucial tests of whether consciousness exceeds normal neural constraints—possibilities Broad investigated rigorously but conditionally, without claiming paranormal phenomena established.

theories.name: Combs’s Chaotic Attractor and Autopoietic Systems
theories.summary: Consciousness researcher and systems theorist Allan Combs uses nonlinear dynamics, and more specifically chaos theory, to understand how all the elements of conscious experience “cling together to form the many states and structures of consciousness that characterize the onflow of our experiential lives.”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness is a self-generating, chaotic-like attractor that produces ever-changing yet recognizable experiential patterns.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Uses nonlinear dynamics and autopoiesis to explain how thoughts, emotions, and perceptions sustain and evolve.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Each person’s onflow of experience is a unique, self-organizing pattern—dynamic, never identical, yet individually distinctive.

theories.name: DOPS’s Consciousness Research and Theory
theories.summary: The Division of Perceptual Studies (DOPS), a research unit within the Department of Psychiatry and Neurobehavioral Sciences at the University of Virginia, has contributed both empirically and conceptually to emerging nonphysical theories of consciousness, which picture mind as irreducible and grounded in some sort of highest consciousness that forms the ontological foundation of reality as a whole.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Mind is irreducible, grounded in a highest consciousness forming the foundation of reality.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Brain functions as a filter or transmitter, shaping but not producing fundamental consciousness.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Rigorous research on reincarnation, NDEs, and psi directly challenges physicalist mind-brain models.

claims.title: Key Evidence
claims.text: Large databases document verified CORT cases, transformative NDEs, and anomalous cognition under extreme conditions.

claims.title: Theoretical Scope
claims.text: Integrates Myers/James model, idealism, and alternative metaphysics compatible with modern physics.

theories.name: Ferrer’s Participatory Enactive Realism
theories.summary: A Participatory Theory of Consciousness shifts the ontological focus from a search for foundational substances—whether matter or consciousness—to the co-creative, enactive relationship between the human and the mystery of the Real. Thus, phenomenal consciousness is an embodied and relational event. Subjective experience is not an isolated “inner light” but is inextricably linked to the relational field—between persons, between the body and the environment, and between the human and the Real.

claims.title: Core Problem
claims.text: Overcomes materialism’s qualia gap and idealism’s closure by refusing premature metaphysical conclusions.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Consciousness arises through embodied, co-creative engagement with a dynamic, evolving cosmic reality.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Neither mind nor matter is primary; participatory events enact reality through relational interaction.

claims.title: Key Implication
claims.text: Reality is pluralistic and emergent, allowing for diverse ontologies and post-mortem possibilities.

claims.title: Philosophical Payoff
claims.text: Reframes consciousness as a mystery best approached through awe, openness, and epistemological humility.

theories.name: Gebser's Ever-Present Origin: How Space, Time, and Self Change Shape Across Mutations of Consciousness
theories.summary: Human consciousness is not a fixed faculty observing an independently constituted world, but a historically mutable structure through which self, world, space, time, causality, and meaning become phenomenally manifest. His five structures—archaic, magic, mythical, mental, and integral—are discontinuous mutations rather than rungs in a linear ladder; each remains operative within contemporary consciousness and may function efficiently or deteriorate into a deficient form.

theorists.name: Jean Gebser
theorists.role: Cultural philosopher and historian of consciousness

theories.name: Graboi’s Three-Aspect Model
theories.summary: Cognitive neuroscientist Daniel Graboi, motivated by telepathy and clairvoyance being real and nonphysical, proposes a “three-aspect model of consciousness”: matter, mind (nonphysical), and pure awareness (an “absolute”). In his model, “pure awareness energy” interacts with a brain to produce consciousness in the mind, which exists in a nonphysical dimension of reality.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness arises from interaction between matter, nonphysical mind, and absolute pure awareness.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Neural patterns convert to universal “pure information” accessible nonlocally to receptive mind-brains.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Mind exists in a nonphysical realm, enabling telepathy and clairvoyance as real phenomena.

theories.name: Grinberg’s Syntergic/Neuronal Field Theory
theories.summary: Iconoclastic neurophysiologist Jacobo Grinberg-Zylberbaum presents a psychophysiological theory of consciousness—“The syntergic theory”—which postulates that “the human brain is able to create a hypercomplex field of interactions that are the result of the activation of all its neuronal elements.” He calls this interaction matrix the “neuronal field,” and “one of the effects of its activation is the unification of neuronal activity.”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness arises from the brain’s “neuronal field,” a hypercomplex interaction matrix unifying neuronal activity and distorting space-time to create experience.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: The neuronal field interacts with an undifferentiated energetic matrix, transforming it into perceptual experience and enabling nonlocal brain-to-brain communication.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Proposes that gravitational and communicative phenomena can stem from alterations in the space-matter continuum caused by neuronal field interactions.

theories.name: Harp’s Universal or God Consciousness
theories.summary: Physicist and “spiritual scholar” Dennis Harp, who seeks to unify theoretical physics and spiritual teachings, claims that “each of us exists as consciousness attached to a mind and body, making sense of the universe by experiencing individual states in a causal sequence.”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness is the union of Universal or God Consciousness with mind and body.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Through detachment from body and mind, one experiences the universe beyond space and time.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: In pure consciousness, all quantum states exist simultaneously without causal interaction.

theories.name: Hiller’s Eternal Discarnate Consciousness
theories.summary: Maverick physicist Jack Hiller posits an “eternal discarnate consciousness” or, as he says, in common parlance, the “soul”—which, “when freed from its hard attachment to the body, functions in a Universal Field of Consciousness (UFC), which may also be characterized as the mind of God.” The soul brings to the body the moral values that exist in the UFC, and these values may often conflict with, in Hiller's Freudian terms, “the Id and the Ego's pleasure-seeking functions.”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness is an eternal “soul” functioning in a Universal Field of Consciousness (UFC).

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: The soul exists before, during, and after life, bringing UFC moral values into bodily life.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: OBEs reveal a nonphysical reality with timeless perception, multidimensional travel, and universal telepathy.

claims.title: Possible Mechanism
claims.text: UFC phenomena may relate to quantum entanglement enabling instantaneous, nonlocal connections.

theories.name: Hobson’s Dreaming Protoconsciousness
theories.summary: Hobson proposes that rapid-eye-movement (REM) sleep constitutes a protoconscious state: a genetically programmed, brain-generated virtual reality that models a world and a body, and serves to develop and maintain waking consciousness. Dreaming is thus not a degraded form of waking experience but the evolutionary-prior, pure expression of primary consciousness—perception and emotion generated without external input—while the waking state adds the secondary but content-rich features of language, abstraction, self-reflective awareness, and volition.

theories.name: Huxley’s Mind-At-Large Filter Theory
theories.summary: Huxley’s theory of consciousness is a modern mystical-filter theory: ordinary phenomenal consciousness is a biologically narrowed fragment of a wider “Mind at Large,” constrained by the brain, nervous system, language, ego, and practical survival. Psychedelics, contemplative disciplines, hypnosis, aesthetic absorption, and spontaneous visionary states may partially loosen this constriction, disclosing intensified perception, diminished ego-boundaries, altered temporality, and sometimes unitary awareness.

theories.name: James's Plural Consciousness, Brain as Filter of a Wider Consciousness
theories.summary: James’s theory of consciousness holds that normal waking rational consciousness is only one form of mind among many, bordered by subliminal, mystical, dissociative, trance, mediumistic, drug-induced, and religious forms of experience. He calls for pluralism: consciousness studies must take marginal and exceptional cases seriously because they reveal hidden dimensions of mind. He proposed that the dependence of consciousness on the brain, though empirically undeniable, does not settle whether the brain produces consciousness or merely transmits it. The distinction is foundational.

theories.name: Johnson and Debold’s Urantia Theocosmic Cosmopsychism
theories.summary: The Urantia Book (UB) presents consciousness within a “theocosmic cosmopsychism” and frames it as participation in a personal, Deity-originated mindal architecture (Urantia Book, 1955). In this model, consciousness originates in an infinite personal source and flows through a hierarchical, top-down, mindal architecture that manifests through progressively complex levels of mind.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness is personal participation in a divine mindal architecture flowing from an infinite Deity-originated source.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: A cosmic mind mediates between spirit and matter, with personality unifying mindal states across levels of existence.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Unlike impersonal cosmopsychism, this model centers consciousness in a purposeful, personal Deity.

claims.title: Integrative Framework
claims.text: Coordinates scientific, philosophical, and spiritual knowledge as facets of a unified Deity-centered causation.

claims.title: Unique Contribution
claims.text: Personality functions as the integrator of consciousness, preserving identity while aligning finite minds with universal mind.

theories.name: Josephson’s Psi-Informed Models
theories.summary: Nobel laureate physicist Brian Josephson approaches consciousness from the dual perspectives of fundamental science and psi phenomena. He posits understanding the brain by “implementing the demands of an appropriate collection of models, each concerned with some aspect of brain and behaviour”—in particular, explaining “higher-level properties [e.g., phenomenology] in terms of lower-level ones by means of a series of inferences based on these models.”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness and psi phenomena may reflect biological and physical principles beyond current science, possibly requiring new dimensions of reality.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Multiple specialized models integrate brain, behavior, and anomalous effects, with quantum and biological fields as possible mechanisms.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Goal-directed, observer-influenced processes could shape reality itself, contrasting with physics’ conventional view of a meaningless universe.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Accepting psi would transform science, expanding cosmology, biology, and consciousness research into a unified, purpose-driven framework.

theorists.name: Brian Josephson
theorists.role: Theoretical Condensed Matter Physicist & Nobel Laureate

theories.name: Jung’s Collective Unconscious and Synchronicity
theories.summary: Psychiatrist/psychoanalyst Carl Jung famously posits a “collective unconscious,” a hidden, quasi-nonphysical aspect of reality with which each individual human subconsciousness is in some sense connected. Prime features of the collective unconscious, according to Jung, are “archetypes” and “synchronicity.” Archetypes are ancient primal symbols, themes, and images that are apparently universal and recurring and can impact individual psyches; and synchronicity describes putative connections between physical and/or mental events that are acausal and seemingly random but appear to be meaningfully related.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: A shared collective unconscious connects all minds, containing universal archetypes and enabling acausal, meaningful coincidences called synchronicities.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Archetypes shape both mental and physical events, while synchronicity links them through meaning rather than causality.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Collaborating with physicist Wolfgang Pauli, Jung tied synchronicity to a psychophysically neutral reality paralleling quantum entanglement.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: If true, synchronicity and the collective unconscious challenge materialism and support nonphysical theories like idealism or dualism.

theories.name: Khasho’s NDE-Enabled Field-Substrate Translation Model
theories.summary: A translation model in which a unified field-level state and a biological substrate are linked, with consciousness as an organized mode of awareness embedded in the field-level state and rendered or filtered through the brain’s biological substrate as localized experience. The model is called “I Think Therefore, 'I AM'” (ITTIA) because it proposes that the irreducible nature of a single human thought within conscious awareness, together with the unique features of NDEs, reflects participation in a deeper organizing field rather than being generated by the brain. The claimed veridical nature of NDEs forms the foundation of the theory.

theories.name: Meditation and the Brain
theories.summary: The scientific consciousness community generally recognizes that meditation can provide insights into consciousness, at least enriching descriptions.

claims.title: Core Claims
claims.text: Meditation alters consciousness and brain activity, offering therapeutic benefits and insights into mind–brain relations.

claims.title: How it Works
claims.text: Alpha wave regulation during mindfulness enhances focus by suppressing irrelevant sensory information.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Extreme meditative states can desynchronize brain activity, resembling anesthesia but not sleep.

claims.title: Theoretical Implications
claims.text: Findings align with materialist models like Global Workspace and Integrated Information Theory, yet remain consistent with nonphysical views.

theories.name: Mishlove’s Beyond-The-Brain Filtered, Survival Consciousness
theories.summary: Mishlove’s theory of consciousness is an evidence-based, parapsychologically grounded, survival-oriented account in which phenomenal consciousness is not produced by the brain, but is filtered, localized, expressed, or constrained by brain-body systems within a wider field of universal mind.

theories.name: Mossbridge’s Informational Substrate as Collective Unconscious
theories.summary: Julia Mossbridge’s Informational Substrate as Collective Unconscious (IS/CU) model has several motivations for a theory of consciousness. One is the recognition that the collective unconscious is an ontological reality (but is rarely included in theories of consciousness). Another is the recognition that consciousness theories rarely separate consciousness per se (i.e., pure awareness) from its contents.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: A quantum-level informational substrate underlies reality, equivalent to Jung’s collective unconscious.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Individual unconscious minds read from the IS/CU, filtering content into conscious awareness.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Consciousness uniquely “writes” intentions to the IS/CU, influencing future spacetime events.

claims.title: Purpose of Consciousness
claims.text: Enable direct interaction with the IS/CU, granting shared free will with all contributors.

claims.title: Testable Implication
claims.text: Universal love may enhance efficiency of IS/CU read/write, potentially measurable via psi tests.

theories.name: Near-Death Experiences, Survival, Past Lives
theories.summary: Near-death experiences (NDEs) command great popular interest but receive only modest discussion here on the Landscape. Obviously, if even a minuscule fraction of this vast ocean of anecdotes were actually true, it would instantly falsify every materialist theory and support (but not confirm) a host of nonphysical theories. I [RLK] am open-minded—and obviously something is going on here—but as to the core claim, I still skew skeptical.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Genuine NDEs or past-life cases would seriously challenge materialist theories of consciousness.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Reports suggest consciousness can function when brain activity is absent or severely compromised.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Multiple independent survival evidence categories converge on the possibility of post-mortem awareness.

claims.title: Skeptical View
claims.text: Physiological, biochemical, and psychological mechanisms, like REM intrusion and neurochemical rushes, can explain NDE features without survival.

claims.title: Research Status
claims.text: Scientific interest is growing, but no dispositive evidence confirming consciousness survives death.

theories.name: Noël’s Nested Field Theory
theories.summary: “Nested Field Theory” has consciousness as a ubiquitous quantum-like field, an information field that is “nested” within quantum fields and operates at a higher frequency than the rest, such that it cannot be directly detected. Nested Field Theory is founded on the purported reality of paranormal phenomena, events, and experiences, and their tangible signs and symptoms, and it claims to account for such paranormal phenomena more naturally than any other theory of consciousness.

theories.name: Psychedelic Theories of Consciousness
theories.summary: Throughout human history, psychedelics have been used for spiritual purposes by inducing altered conscious experiences dramatically different from the norm. Colors explode. Time slows, speeds up, stops. Self-shatters, dissolves. The body dissipates, melts away. Magical creatures emerge. Spirit Beings appear. All things vibrate, resonate. All is alive. All is connected. All is One. Some attribute the advent of religion to the use of psychotomimetic or hallucinogenic substances in rituals. In each culture or condition, interpretations of psychedelic experiences were made. Mystics conjoined with cosmic consciousness.

claims.title: Historical Context
claims.text: Psychedelics have long induced profound altered states, influencing spirituality, religion, and cultural worldviews.

claims.title: Scientific Insights
claims.text: Neuroimaging links psychedelic effects to synchronized brain activity and altered high-level priors, informing brain models.

claims.title: Philosophical Debates
claims.text: Some argue psychedelics may reveal metaphysical truths; skeptics see them as phenomenological but not ontological.

claims.title: Current Consensus
claims.text: Useful for studying “easy problems” of consciousness, but unlikely to solve the “hard problem” directly.

theories.name: Radin’s Challenge to Materialism
theories.summary: Coming at consciousness from an empirical point of view, parapsychologist Dean Radin calls on what he believes to be the overwhelming evidence for psi phenomena in order to infer that “intention affects the physical world.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Psi phenomena show that consciousness can affect the physical world, challenging the view that mind is brain-bound.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Nonlocal mind interacts across space and time, enabling telepathy, clairvoyance, precognition, and psychokinesis.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Radin links empirical psi evidence to a fundamental “ocean of consciousness” underlying matter and energy.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: If verified, psi would require post-materialist models of mind, reshaping science’s view of reality and causation.

theories.name: Schlitz’s Theory of Mind
theories.summary: Anthropologist and social scientist Marilyn Schlitz proposes a Theory of Mind (ToM) that views consciousness as an interconnected blend of inner and outer realms of existence. Essentially, ToM is the link between subjective consciousness (what it feels like to be someone) and objective phenomena (how someone behaves or reacts). This interface is a potential explanatory model for psi phenomena and other transpersonal experiences.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness is an interface linking inner subjective experience with observable outer behavior and events.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Fluid boundaries between inner and outer realms may allow minds to tap shared, possibly non-local, informational fields.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Psi and transpersonal experiences could be heightened expressions of this mind-world interface.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Such a model could explain veridical after-death encounters and offer therapeutic benefits through altered-state engagement.

theories.name: Schooler’s General Resonance Theory and Subjective Time
theories.summary: Experimental psychologist Jonathan Schooler outlines a theory of consciousness that combines two novel ideas: “General Resonance Theory” (co-developed with Tam Hunt), where multiple levels of consciousness interact, and “subjective time,” where consciousness arises with an observer's movement through objective time relative to a currently unacknowledged dimension of subjective time.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness emerges from nested, resonating levels of awareness and a hidden subjective dimension of time.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Multiple “observer windows” synchronize via shared resonance; movement through subjective time shapes experience.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Suggests a “Cartesian Multiplex” and extra temporal dimension that could explain psi and anomalous cognition.

theories.name: Sheldrake’s Morphic Fields
theories.summary: Biologist Rupert Sheldrake proposes “morphic fields” as a field of form or shape or organization, “such that every entity has its own field: each ant colony, each termite nest, a flock of birds, a pack of wolves and a herd of animals.”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: All self-organizing systems—from cells to societies—are shaped and connected by “morphic fields” containing collective memory, influencing both form and behavior.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Each entity’s morphic field organizes patterns of activity, retains habits via “morphic resonance,” and maintains nonlocal connections among members of a group.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Suggests telepathy and other psi effects arise naturally from extended mental morphic fields that link minds beyond the brain.

theories.name: Shiah’s Contentless Consciousness Theory
theories.summary: Contentless Consciousness Theory posits that true consciousness is an eternal, non-dual state devoid of independent mental phenomena, a "contentless" reality that is obscured by our ordinary "delusional" consciousness, which erroneously perceives the self and the external world as permanent and separate. Drawing heavily from Buddhist wisdom, Shiah argues that what we commonly call “consciousness”—the stream of perceptions, desires, and ego-driven thoughts—is actually a transient, dependent illusion.

claims.title: Core Claims
claims.text: True consciousness is a timeless, contentless state obscured by delusional, ego-driven mental activity.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Delusional consciousness, driven by desire and false identity, can be dismantled through compassion, meditation, and detachment.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Consciousness is not produced by the brain but is an eternal, independent reality revealed by dissolving the self.

claims.title: Empirical Support
claims.text: Near-death experiences, mediumship, and reincarnation studies suggest consciousness exists beyond bodily death.

theories.name: Swimme’s Cosmogenesis
theories.summary: Mathematician and integral studies professor Brian Swimme presents the cosmology of a creative universe—cosmogenesis—in which human consciousness plays an essential role. He views the evolution of the universe toward greater complexity and consciousness as “the ultimate aim of the universe.”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: The universe evolves toward greater complexity and consciousness as its ultimate aim.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Matter inherently generates life; human awareness is part of the universe’s creative process.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Consciousness is woven into the universe, which “faces us” as we awaken to it.

theories.name: T. Campbell’s Theory of Everything
theories.summary: Consciousness researcher (and former nuclear physicist) Thomas Campbell presents “My Big TOE,” his theory of everything: “Consciousness is the fundamental reality. The physical world is an illusion, a virtual reality that only exists in our minds. We are Individuated Units of Consciousness: immortal, interconnected parts of a Larger Consciousness System. We choose to be players in the virtual reality game called life on Earth, set in a virtual universe computed by the system to aid our consciousness evolution.”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness is fundamental reality; our physical universe is a computed virtual reality.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: A Larger Consciousness System simulates universes to foster individual and collective consciousness evolution.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: The Absolute Unbounded Oneness split into many units, birthing creative, autonomous consciousnesses.

claims.title: Practical Goal
claims.text: Life’s purpose is to reduce fear, increase love, and evolve the quality of consciousness.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Paranormal and quantum phenomena are natural effects of a simulated, consciousness-based reality.

theories.name: Tart’s Emergent Interactionism
theories.summary: Consciousness explorer Charles Tart proposes “Emergent Interactionism” as a dualistic theory of consciousness, based on his long work on altered states of consciousness, transpersonal psychology, and multiple forms of parapsychology.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness emerges from continuous interaction between brain/body systems and separate mental/life systems.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Auto-psi processes read and influence one’s own body, while allo-psi extends these effects beyond the self.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Psi phenomena show mind can operate beyond normal space and time, challenging materialist brain-only models.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Survival after death may occur, but personal identity could change or dissolve without the body’s patterning role.

theories.name: Wilber’s Integral Theory
theories.summary: Charismatic, iconoclastic philosopher Ken Wilber puts forth “Integral Theory” as an overarching metatheory that seeks to harmonize numerous (100+), diverse philosophical and spiritual theories—including consciousness studies, meditative traditions, religious traditions, psychology, transpersonal psychology, parapsychology, and sociology—into a single, coherent framework that accounts for the human condition, broadly conceived.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Seeks to unify 100+ philosophical, scientific, and spiritual systems into a single metatheory of human development.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Uses the AQAL model (All Quadrants, All Levels) to integrate individual/collective and interior/exterior dimensions of reality.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Consciousness evolves from matter to life, mind, soul, and finally Spirit, reuniting with transcendental reality.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Offers a framework that could reconcile science and spirituality, challenging materialist limits on consciousness theories.

theories.name: Akselrud's Explanatory Faculty: Consciousness as Internalized Explanation
theories.summary: Akselrud's explanatory-faculty theory holds that phenomenal consciousness is constituted by the mind's innate, ungrounded capacity to generate and recognize explanations, turned reflexively upon its own states—"self-consciousness is internalized explanation." On this account, the hard problem is neither solved nor dissolved but denied: it is not a property of nature but a structural collision between two mutually exclusive explanatory forms: impersonal physical lawfulness and first-person givenness, each coherent alone and paradoxical when fused.

theories.name: Challenge Additional Theories
theories.summary: Additional Challenge theories

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Some leading scientists doubt humanity’s ability to ever fully explain consciousness.

claims.title: Notable Voices
claims.text: Martin Rees and Edward Witten both question whether science can bridge brain function to subjective experience.

claims.title: Key Contrast
claims.text: Witten finds the Big Bang easier to imagine explaining than the nature of consciousness itself.

theories.name: Champagne’s Semiotic Account
theories.summary: A semiotic account of consciousness that pivots on C. S. Peirce’s demonstration that qualities can be extricated from causal and inferential relations only in thought, not in fact. By expanding the standard type/token framework to include tone, and by foregrounding similarity-based reference, Champagne claims to construct a new conceptual toolbox that prevents experiential qualities from being explanatorily anomalous. The task, he says, is not to solve the hard problem but to dissolve it, by not reifying the warranted distinction that generates it.

theories.name: Cohen’s Ultra-Fine-Tuned Personal Consciousness
theories.summary: An “ultra-fine-tuned personal consciousness” means that absolutely all indispensable a priori events and conditions, bar none, of physics, chemistry, stellar and planetary development, biology and evolution, physiology and human brain structure, world history and personal family history, in all needed sequences and interrelationships, occurred unerringly as required for you, the reader of these words, to now be experiencing the immediate, first-person qualia of being conscious.

theorists.name: Jundo Cohen
theorists.role: Zen Buddhist priest, teacher, and writer

theories.name: Conway Morris's Convergent Sentience Beyond Materialism
theories.summary: Conway Morris argues that phenomenal consciousness is real, irreducible, and not generated by matter. Convergent evolution, his overarching theory, repeatedly generates sensory systems, brains, cognition, and, he argues, sentience; reflective human consciousness then crosses a qualitative threshold through abstraction, language, counterfactual thought, technology, and imagination. His mature position is explicitly anti-materialist: Brains, he proposes, facilitate, filter, access, and encounter a mind belonging to a wider, orthogonal reality. The theory therefore links consciousness to evolutionary directionality while leaving qualia, subjecthood, and the causal mind–brain relation unresolved, contending that biological evolution stalls at phenomenality. The account is avowedly speculative, offers no mechanism, and rests on a theistic metaphysics.

theories.name: CROW’s Funhouse of Consciousness
theories.summary: CROW’s Funhouse of Consciousness

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Uses a trickster character to explore and satirize competing theories of consciousness.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: CROW wrestles with monism, idealism, electromagnetic and quantum ideas, mirroring humanity’s confusion over the hard problem.

claims.title: Distinctive Flavor
claims.text: Blends humor, myth, and philosophy to capture the bewilderment of navigating the “Landscape of Consciousness.”

theories.name: Davies’s Consciousness in the Cosmos
theories.summary: Physicist and polymath Paul Davies asserts the heterodox view among scientists that consciousness is something very significant in the evolution of the universe. “Although we see consciousness only in response to some set of physical systems, nevertheless it seems to me to play an absolute and fundamental role.”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness is fundamental to the universe, shaping our understanding and potentially intertwined with cosmic evolution.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Suggests consciousness could influence quantum physics at the point of observation, altering reality’s unfolding.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Criticizes many-worlds interpretation for excluding consciousness, seeing quantum theory as its rightful place.

claims.title: Cosmic Vision
claims.text: Envisions a far future where conscious beings permeate the universe, making it entirely self-aware.

claims.title: Quantum Implication
claims.text: Proposes that future observations could select past histories, linking mind and cosmos across time.

theories.name: Delaflor's Model Dependent Ontology
theories.summary: A "Model Dependent Ontology" (MDO) seeks to advance a trans-ontological account of consciousness that operates by dissolving conceptual divisions without committing to any ontological substrate, whether material, mental, or otherwise. Consciousness is not the primitive; it is a "Cognition 2 (C2)" organization through which experience is rendered as language, self, and world (see below). In MDO, the world is not outside consciousness; it is part of what C2 renders. The framework is designed less as a competing theory of consciousness than as a structural device, in the manner of an extended Zen koan, for clearing the conceptual ground on which any theory of consciousness must operate.

theories.name: Eagleman’s Possibilianism
theories.summary: Neuroscientist, technologist, and author David Eagleman labels himself a “possibilian” in that he calls for “an openness in approaching the big questions of our existence.”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Advocates openness to multiple explanations for existence and consciousness, rejecting rigid atheism, theism, or passive agnosticism.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Treats consciousness like a CEO receiving only high-level summaries from vast, unseen neural processes unless something unexpected occurs.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Embraces uncertainty, insisting that both materialism and non-materialist explanations remain viable until evidence closes the question.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Encourages science to investigate without prematurely committing to one worldview, keeping alternative possibilities on the table.

claims.title: Open Question
claims.text: Admits science can link brain and mind but may never explain why experiences feel the way they do.

theories.name: Fodor's Principled Abstention: Intentionality Bracketing Phenomenality
theories.summary: Fodor deliberately declined to theorize phenomenal consciousness and argued that this was the correct strategy. His theory of consciousness is best understood as indirect and architectural. His Representational Theory of Mind explains cognition as computation over syntactically structured mental representations, and he explains thought as an internal Language of Thought. But he does not explain why any of this should have subjective phenomenal character. Nobody, Fodor held, has any idea how anything material could be conscious, nor even what having such an idea would be like.

theories.name: Gabriel’s New Realism and Field of Sense
theories.summary: Consciousness cannot be reduced to brain states of physical processes. “You are not your brain.” Consciousness is not a ‘substance’ but a ‘field of sense,’ ways in which the world becomes intelligible. Consciousness is the condition of appearance for intelligibility and meaning.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness is not the brain but the precondition for meaning, freedom, and intelligibility in human life.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Frames consciousness as a “field of sense,” the context in which the world appears and gains significance.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Rejects “neurocentrism” as a dangerous ideology, insisting the mind cannot be reduced to neural activity.

claims.title: Normative Dimension
claims.text: Sees consciousness as inherently tied to values, freedom, and the capacity to interpret and create norms.

claims.title: Anti-Physicalist Stance
claims.text: Argues that empirical science alone cannot explain the normative, semantic, and existential aspects of mind.

theories.name: Gómez-Marín’s Un-Theory
theories.summary: To come

theories.name: Hacker’s Skepticism
theories.summary: Consciousness is not a “thing” or a substance or a unitary phenomenon that can be isolated or explained by neuroscience. Instead, it refers to a complex array of capacities and states—like perception, thought, emotion, intention, and self-awareness.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness is not a thing or substance but a conceptual framework for describing human capacities and states.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Treats perception, thought, emotion, and self-awareness as interconnected capacities of persons, not brain parts.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Rejects the “hard problem” as a linguistic and conceptual confusion, not a genuine scientific or metaphysical puzzle.

claims.title: On Qualia
claims.text: Holds that subjectivity is already embedded in our language; no extra “qualia” need causal or mechanistic explanation.

claims.title: Limits of Neuroscience
claims.text: Argues neuroscience can’t solve conceptual questions; philosophy should clarify meaning, not hunt for inner entities.

theories.name: Hartford’s Eternal Conjecture
theories.summary: The Eternal Conjecture (EC) posits that “If there ever is Something, there always was Something, because no something (existence) comes from absolute Nothing (no existence)”. The EC theory of consciousness argues that because always is the single Source of all existence—including the 1st person mindedness we possess (consciousness)—that always Something (Source) must be Minded; otherwise, we couldn't be.

theories.name: Levin’s Technological Approach to Mind Everywhere
theories.summary: Developmental and synthetic biologist Michael Levin introduces "a framework for detecting, understanding, and communicating with cognition in unconventional substrates," which he calls 'TAME-Technological Approach to Mind Everywhere.'

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Minds can arise in many embodiments, including highly unconventional ones that humans currently find hard to think about. Cognitive agents must be detected empirically. Cognition is graded, and extends at least as far down as chemical networks. Consciousness likely does as well.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: TAME studies cognition in diverse systems, ranging across scales (from molecular networks to ecosystems) and across origin stories (evolved, engineered, and hybrid), by applying well-developed tools of behavior science far outside of conventional brain-based systems.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Consciousness may exist in cellular, bioengineered, or even non-physical “spaces of action.” See "Levin’s Ingressing Minds from Platonic Spaces.”

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Challenges the binary view of consciousness and redefines agency across biological and synthetic life. We do not make conscious minds, either in embryogenesis or in AI engineering; we facilitate its ingression through the interfaces we make.

claims.title: Open Issue
claims.text: Can first-person experience ever be meaningfully assessed in radically unfamiliar cognitive systems?

theorists.name: Michael Levin
theorists.role: Developmental & synthetic biologist and philosopher of biology

theories.name: McGinn’s Ultimate Mystery (Mysterianism)
theories.summary: Philosopher Colin McGinn argues that the bond between the mind and the brain is “an ultimate mystery, a mystery that human intelligence will never unravel.”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: The link between mind and brain is real but forever beyond human understanding due to our cognitive limits.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Distinguishes objective difficulty from subjective difficulty; consciousness may be biologically simple yet conceptually inaccessible.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Rejects supernatural or dualistic solutions, instead holding that the mystery is entirely natural yet permanently opaque.

claims.title: Illusion of Hardness
claims.text: Argues that consciousness seems harder to explain than language only because our access to it is limited.

claims.title: Brass Tacks Focus
claims.text: Urges study of neurons, axons, and dendrites as the physical substrate, while accepting we may never connect them to experience.

theories.name: Merriam’s Calculus of Qualia as Logical Primitives
theories.summary: The ‘Calculus of Qualia’ (CQ) is a formal system for consciousness studies that incorporates non-referential terms—logical primitives like █ that present phenomenal experiences (qualia) directly in awareness, rather than referring to them. This would mean that qualia are logical primitives, irreducible in themselves, and thus their intrinsic nature cannot be explained further.

theories.name: Musser’s “Is It Really So Hard?”
theories.summary: Science journalist George Musser explores the relationship between consciousness and physics with two explanatory arrows pointing in opposite directions. In addition to the normal using-science-to-explain-consciousness framework, he focuses on “why physicists are studying human consciousness and AI to unravel the mysteries of the universe.”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Explores a two-way link between physics and consciousness, asking if each could help explain the other.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Considers relational and perspectival theories, where properties (including qualia) arise only through interactions.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Rejects strict mysterianism, arguing there’s no evidence science has reached an insurmountable wall.

claims.title: Role of AI
claims.text: Suggests advanced AI might uncover theories about consciousness or physics beyond unaided human capacity.

claims.title: Optimistic Outlook
claims.text: Believes our evolved minds can, in principle, understand consciousness because we are part of the world we study.

theories.name: Nagasawa’s Mind-Body Problem in an Infinitely Decomposable Universe
theories.summary: Philosopher Yujin Nagasawa poses the disruptive idea: what would happen to the mind-body problem if there were no such thing as the deepest level of reality because the universe is infinitely decomposable? He argues that such a possibility would be devastating to theories of consciousness because it would undermine all traditional responses to the mind-body problem, such as physicalism, dualism, idealism, and neutral monism.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: If reality has no smallest parts, all standard mind-body theories collapse as unfalsifiable and unstable.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Infinite decomposability prevents locating a fundamental “bottom” level, undermining physicalism, dualism, idealism, and neutral monism.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Proposes “priority monism,” where the whole universe—not its parts—is the most fundamental entity.

claims.title: Eastern Resonance
claims.text: Aligns with some Eastern philosophies that see reality as an organic whole of entangled entities.

claims.title: Philosophical Shift
claims.text: Moves the search for fundamentality from the smallest components to the totality of existence itself.

theories.name: Nagel’s Mind and Cosmos
theories.summary: Philosopher Thomas Nagel famously shook up the philosophy of mind with his seminal article, “What Is It Like to Be a Bat?” He begins with the premise that “reduction euphoria,” which aims to explain consciousness by “some variety of materialism, psychophysical identification, or reduction,” gets it “obviously wrong,” and he states upfront and repeats at the conclusion that “we have at present no conception of what an explanation of the physical nature of a mental phenomenon would be.”

claims.title: Core Claims
claims.text: Consciousness cannot yet be explained physically; current reductionist approaches are “obviously wrong.”

claims.title: How it Works
claims.text: Subjective experience is irreducible; knowing “what it’s like” requires the subject’s own perspective.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Rejects both theism and strict materialism, seeking a secular alternative where mind is fundamental.

claims.title: Philosophical Implication
claims.text: Leans toward universal monism or panpsychism but focuses more on the depth of the problem.

theories.name: Owen’s Mind-Body Powers: NCC are Philosophically and Religiously Neutral
theories.summary: The search for neural correlates of consciousness is not only philosophically neutral but also religiously inclusive, inviting the atheist materialist as well as the theistic dualist to scientifically investigate the miraculous link between, as philosopher Matthew Owen puts it, “the wine of consciousness and the water of biological brains.”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Neural correlates of consciousness (NCC) can be studied without committing to physicalism, dualism, or other “-isms.”

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Uses Aristotle’s hylomorphism to frame consciousness as a mental power co-manifesting with bodily powers via neural mechanisms.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Rejects the view that consciousness emerges from the brain; instead, the brain exists to express a unified conscious form.

claims.title: Philosophical Neutrality
claims.text: NCC research invites both atheists and theists to investigate the intimate link between brain activity and experience.

claims.title: Religious Compatibility
claims.text: The model supports beliefs in life after death and bodily resurrection while remaining scientifically applicable.

theories.name: Pinker’s Naturalism
theories.summary: A naturalistic, computational-neuroscientific account of access consciousness joined to a carefully calibrated “mysterian-light” position on phenomenal consciousness: all evidence ties consciousness to brain activity and information processing, yet the subjective “what-it-is-like” character of experience may be a sui generis conceptual problem that human cognition is poorly equipped to solve.

theories.name: Raman’s Cosmic Significance
theories.summary: The emergence of awareness was not an insignificant event in cosmic history. Imagine the universe without anything like human consciousness. It would be dark, dreary, and dismal to unconscious entities, large or small. The spark of consciousness became a magical screen on which countless simple and complex attributes of the physical universe came to be projected.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Human consciousness gives meaning, beauty, and structure to a universe that would otherwise be inert and silent.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: The emergence of awareness—what Raman calls the “Third Big Bang”—reveals and enlivens cosmic reality.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: The universe’s grandeur is deciphered only through sentient perception; without mind, no meaning exists.

claims.title: Scientific/Philosophical Frame
claims.text: Consciousness is not just a product of the cosmos, but a turning point in its history.

claims.title: Implication
claims.text: Despite our physical insignificance, awareness makes us cosmically significant: we illuminate the universe from within.

theories.name: Reason's No-Go Theorem against Materialism/Supervenience
theories.summary: The "No-Go / No-Supervenience theorem" claims that self-certainty, or the capacity of healthy conscious humans to 'know' with certainty that they are conscious, is inconsistent with the properties possible in any meaningful definition of a physical system. Thus, a whole family of theories—materialist/physicalist, supervenience-based, and perhaps some forms of dual-aspect monism or panpsychist physicalism—cannot account for all the properties of human consciousness. Any physicalist theory that describes a self-aware, intelligent system must be internally inconsistent. Non-reductive physicalist theories are similarly pressured.

theories.name: RLK Reflections
theories.summary: Me, I just don't know … My own hunch, right here, right now—if I'm coerced to disclose it and for what little it's worth—might be something of a ....

theories.name: S. Harris’s Mystery of Consciousness
theories.summary: Philosopher, author, and neuroscientist Sam Harris, who is not known for timidity in offering opinions, does not offer his own theory of consciousness. Instead, he offers a mystery. The problem, he says, “is that no evidence for consciousness exists in the physical world.”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness is the only thing that reveals itself directly, yet no trace of it exists in the physical world.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Even perfect brain mapping can’t reveal subjective experience; physical events are silent on what they “feel” like.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Rejects “emergence” as a pseudo-explanation, calling it an incomprehensible restatement of a miracle.

claims.title: Limits of Science
claims.text: Argues no physical description, at any scale, can account for the fact of subjective awareness.

claims.title: Role of Introspection
claims.text: Holds that some truths about consciousness can only be found by examining experience directly.

theories.name: Schwitzgebel's Unreliable Introspection, Indeterminate Boundaries, Metaphysical Humility
theories.summary: Schwitzgebel holds that phenomenal consciousness is real while denying that introspection accesses it reliably, and that it has determinate boundaries: we can be mistaken about the character, structure, and even presence of our own experiences. He therefore resists building metaphysical conclusions directly from first-person certainty. His central metaphysical claim is borderline consciousness: mainstream naturalism must accept that for some systems—some animals, artificial systems, or unusual organisms—it is neither determinately true nor false that there is something it is like to be them. His broader “crazyism” holds that every metaphysics of mind has counterintuitive consequences. He thus combines phenomenal realism with introspective fallibilism, boundary indeterminacy, and metaphysical humility.

theories.name: Shermer’s Known Unknown…and Possibly Unknowable
theories.summary: Michael Shermer puts the hard problem of consciousness into the category of “a known unknown that may be unknowable.” He concludes that “the hard problem is asking of us a question that is impossible to answer: what’s it like to be the neural wiring? That is, what’s it like to be you? How should I know?”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: The hard problem of consciousness is a “known unknown” that may be logically impossible to solve.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Uses identity logic to argue you can’t truly know another being’s inner life without becoming that being.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Rejects dualism and “ghost in the machine” thinking, tracing such intuitions to essentialist views of the self.

claims.title: Illustrative Analogies
claims.text: Employs dolphins, body-swap comedies, and Kafka’s Metamorphosis to show why perspective-switching is conceptually flawed.

claims.title: Practical Limit
claims.text: While science can study brain function, only the subject can directly experience their own consciousness.

theories.name: Siler's Art of Consciousness
theories.summary: Metaphorming: Revealing the Nature of Consciousness with Metaphorms

theories.name: Tallis’s Anti-Neuromania Skepticism
theories.summary: Philosopher and humanist Raymond Tallis, a former geriatric neurologist and clinical neuroscientist, has a baffling yet coherent and penetrating perspective on consciousness.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Rejects the idea that neural activity alone can fully explain consciousness, calling reductionist approaches self-contradictory.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Argues that objective, quantitative science cannot capture subjective qualities like “aboutness,” unity, and lived time.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Critiques correlation-equals-identity claims, stressing that brain states look nothing like the experiences they supposedly are.

claims.title: Rejection of Alternatives
claims.text: Dismisses materialism, dualism, theism, and panpsychism as inadequate, leaving the problem unresolved.

claims.title: Skeptical Stance
claims.text: Advocates open-ended inquiry and ontological agnosticism, holding that the true basis of consciousness remains unknown.

theories.name: Wittgenstein's Grammatical Fiction
theories.summary: Wittgenstein does not offer a theory of phenomenal consciousness but rather an argument that the demand for one rests on grammatical confusion—treating sensation-words as names of private inner objects, on the model of nouns naming public things. A principal resource for deflationary treatments of qualia, his theory is not a specific ontology of mind but a grammatical therapy for the philosophical confusion generated by treating phenomenal consciousness as this private inner object. He does not deny pain, imagery, emotion, thought, or first-person immediacy; he denies that their intelligibility depends on an intrinsically private mental theater whose contents are named by inner pointing or designation.

theories.name: Zuboff’s Universalism
theories.summary: Arnold Zuboff's approach to consciousness is founded on a metaphysical position he terms ‘universalism,’ which states that there is exactly and only one subject of experience and that this one subject of experience is instantiated wherever awareness occurs. While Universalism is more a theory of personal identity than a theory of consciousness per se, it would, if true, directly affect the entire enterprise of theories of consciousness.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: There is exactly one subject of experience, shared by all conscious beings everywhere and everywhen.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Any experience with first-person “immediacy” is mine, independent of body, brain, or physical identity.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Personal identity depends on the shared “mineness” of experience, not on separate individuals or histories.

claims.title: Illusion of Selves
claims.text: We seem separate because our experiences are not integrated, creating a false sense of isolated ownership.

claims.title: Easy Game Argument
claims.text: It is far more probable you are all conscious beings than one extremely unlikely individual life.

theories.name: Aquinas’s Hylomorphism
theories.summary: Aquinas holds that the soul is the substantial form of the body, not a substance lodged within it, so a human being is one thing rather than two. He offers no theory of phenomenal consciousness in the modern sense, but his hylomorphic psychology provides a systematic account of embodied sensation, integrated awareness, intellectual cognition, and reflexive self-knowledge. Sensation is the reception of a form without its matter. What we call phenomenal consciousness falls chiefly to the sensus communis, the interior sense that unifies the external senses into one perceptual episode and accounts for our awareness that we are sensing. Intellect is immaterial yet must turn to sensory phantasms, and the mind knows itself only through its acts, never by direct inspection. Aquinas's treatment of soul and cognition sits within a theological account of the human being as made in the image of God.

theories.name: Aristotle’s Hylomorphism
theories.summary: Aristotle’s account of what we now call phenomenal consciousness is grounded in hylomorphism: soul as the form of an organic body rather than an entity within it, making awareness a capacity of the living animal instead of a property of a separate substance. Perception is the reception of sensible form without matter, and perceiving includes an awareness that one is perceiving, located in the common sense that also unifies the modalities and yields a single integrated experience. Aristotle profoundly shaped Aquinas’s psychology and remains relevant to contemporary hylomorphism, embodied cognition, functionalism, direct realism, and higher-order and self-representational theories, though he offers no solution to the modern hard problem. Intellect strains this naturalism: the active mind is called separate and everlasting, an ambiguity that generated the entire medieval controversy over its status.

theories.name: Avicenna’s Flying Man and Self-Present Soul
theories.summary: Avicenna combines an embodied psychology of sensory consciousness with a strongly dualist theory of the self, holding that the human soul is an immaterial, self-subsisting substance whose existence is identical with its awareness of itself. That self-awareness is primitive, permanent, and non-inferential: it requires no sensory input, no bodily awareness, and no second-order act, and it persists in sleep and in total absorption. His Flying Man thought experiment isolates it by subtracting all sensation. Intellect is nonbodily, and the individual soul survives bodily death. Avicenna’s architecture of internal senses strongly influenced medieval Latin psychology, including Aquinas, while his theory of self-presence profoundly shaped Suhrawardī and Mullā Ṣadrā and remains relevant to contemporary debates over minimal self-consciousness, embodiment, and first-person subjectivity.

theories.name: Bergson’s Multiplicity, Duration, Perception, Memory
theories.summary: Late 19th/early 20th-century philosopher Henri Bergson's non-reductive consciousness is an unapologetic, sophisticated challenge to Materialism Theories. Bergson distinguishes between consciousness and matter, between mind and body, according to the distinction between “time” (understood as “duration”) and “space”. In consciousness, he says, “we find succeeding states without distinction; and, in space, simultaneities which, without succeeding, are distinguished, in the sense that one is no longer there when the other one appears. Outside of us, reciprocal exteriority without succession: within, succession without reciprocal exteriority.”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness is a dynamic, non-reductive reality that bridges perception, memory, and time, challenging materialism.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Consciousness moves between pure perception and pure memory, with the brain filtering overwhelming awareness.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Matter is “images” without hidden powers; perception and memory define consciousness as temporal and creative.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Consciousness may persist beyond the brain, allowing for survival after death and rejecting strict materialist accounts.

theories.name: Chalmers’s Naturalistic Dualism
theories.summary: David Chalmers constructs a ‘naturalistic dualism’ to harmonize what he sees as two undeniable but ostensibly contradictory facts: (i) Mental states of phenomenal consciousness, the subjective experience of inner awareness, cannot be reduced to physical states of the brain. (ii) The physical world, the natural world, is all there is; there is nothing supernatural.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness is a fundamental feature of reality, irreducible to physical processes but fully part of the natural world.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Proposes unknown psychophysical laws linking physical states to subjective experience, much like physics links mass and gravity.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Rejects both reductive physicalism and supernatural explanations, keeping consciousness within a scientific worldview.

claims.title: Key Argument
claims.text: Conceivable “zombie worlds” show consciousness isn’t logically guaranteed by physical facts, requiring new basic properties.

claims.title: Philosophical Aim
claims.text: Adds consciousness to nature’s basic building blocks, expanding science’s laws without contradicting physical theory.

theories.name: Composite Dualism
theories.summary: Modern dualism in philosophy of mind begins with Descartes, who famously divides the world between the physical and the mental. He was motivated by the obvious distinction that the mind has thought but no extension, while the body has extension but no thought. Yet, body and mind both seem needed to have a human person.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: A human person is made of both a physical body and a nonphysical soul, each essential to identity.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: The body enables public interaction, while the soul carries ultimate, unanalyzable differences between individuals.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Souls may exist without bodies, but are typically recognized and distinguished through their bodily associations.

claims.title: Function Debate
claims.text: Some hold the soul can think independently; others believe it functions only when joined to a body.

claims.title: Ultimate Difference
claims.text: Each soul’s individuality is basic and unanalyzable, not derived from physical traits or relationships.

theories.name: Descartes’s Substance Dualism
theories.summary: Descartes’s theory of consciousness holds that phenomenal consciousness is a self-present mode of thinking belonging to an immaterial mind, but that much of its sensory and affective character arises only in the embodied union of mind and body. In other words, Descartes held that consciousness—which he called thought (cogitatio)—constitutes the essence of an immaterial mental substance (res cogitans) radically distinct from the extended, mechanical body (res extensa).

theories.name: Dualisms—Overview
theories.summary: Dualism is the theory of consciousness that requires two radically distinct parts: a physical brain, obviously, but also, in addition, a separate, nonphysical substance that is not only independent of the brain but also not of the physical world (as presently conceived). This would mean that reality consists of (at least) two ontological categories—physical and nonphysical, whether substances, properties, aspects, dimensions, or planes of existence. In general usage, “dualism” means “substance dualism.”

claims.title: Core Concepts
claims.text: Holds that consciousness requires both a physical brain and a distinct, nonphysical substance or property.

claims.title: Scientific Context
claims.text: Historically tied to soul doctrines; interactionism posits two-way causal influence between mental and physical realms.

claims.title: Why Meaningful
claims.text: Preserves personal identity beyond death; offers a framework for mind–matter causation outside physicalist limits.

claims.title: Major Challenges
claims.text: Faces causal closure objections, lack of evidence, and philosophical resistance due to complexity and non-parsimony.

theories.name: Emergent Dualism
theories.summary: Emergent dualism holds that mind is not fundamental in reality but arises naturally when sufficiently organized physical systems can generate a genuinely new, nonphysical conscious subject by as-yet-unknown meta-psychophysical laws rather than being created directly by God. William Hasker, who originated the theory, argues from the unity of consciousness that what emerges must be an individual rather than a property. Once generated, such a “soul” might persist beyond the brain, and the same laws could in principle operate in nonbiological systems. Thus, the theory accommodates strong brain dependence, evolution, animal consciousness, and potentially AI consciousness, while allowing possible postmortem survival.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Nonphysical minds naturally arise from certain complex physical systems, like brains, via unknown meta-psychophysical laws.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Physical complexity triggers the emergence of a new, tethered, nonphysical substance that becomes the conscious subject.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Souls are generated by the physical world itself, reducing the classic mind-body “pairing problem.”

claims.title: Possible Independence
claims.text: Once formed, a soul might persist beyond the brain, supporting interpretations of near-death and out-of-body experiences.

claims.title: Broader Scope
claims.text: Such laws could, in principle, generate consciousness in non-biological systems, including advanced AI.

theories.name: Epiphenomenalism (Dualism)
theories.summary: Epiphenomenalism is considered a kind of dualism—specifically a type of property dualism—because it maintains a fundamental ontological distinction between mental and physical properties, even though all mental states are instantiated in physical states or generated by physical processes.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Mental properties are real and non-physical but have no causal effect on the physical world.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Brain processes generate consciousness and qualia, but these mental states are purely byproducts without influence.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Unlike most property dualism, mental states here are causally inert—like a steam whistle on a train.

claims.title: Historical Shift
claims.text: Emerged as a retreat from full substance dualism when mental-to-physical causation lacked scientific evidence.

claims.title: Challenges & Tensions
claims.text: Critics question why evolution would produce consciousness if it plays no causal role in survival or behavior.

theories.name: Feser’s Neo-Thomistic, Neo-Aristotelian, Common-Sense Dualism
theories.summary: Catholic philosopher Edward Feser's account of consciousness combines a neo-Thomistic view that some mental faculties are immaterial and a neo-Aristotelian view that we perceive the world actually as it appears to be (i.e., direct realism, such that color and sound are properties of external objects as real as size and shape).

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Intellect is an immaterial faculty, and common-sense perception shows the world’s qualitative features are as real as physical ones.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Thought involves determinate, universal concepts irreducible to sensation or imagination, making it non-material in principle.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Rejects Descartes’s mechanistic view of matter, restoring colors, sounds, and meanings as objective features of reality.

claims.title: Critique of Materialism
claims.text: Modern materialism inherits a concept of matter that excludes qualitative features, making consciousness seem inexplicable.

claims.title: Proposed Solution
claims.text: Revive Aristotelian-Scholastic realism about matter and qualities, dissolving the “hard problem” as a conceptual mistake.

theories.name: God as the Supplier of Souls
theories.summary: Many in the Abrahamic religious traditions—Judaism, Christianity, Islam—believe that God dispenses souls actively to each individual (whether at birth, conception, or some arbitrary time is irrelevant here).

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: In Abrahamic traditions, God creates and assigns a soul to each person at or before life’s beginning.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Souls may be identical at creation or differ in innate traits; God’s act avoids bodies generating souls on their own.

claims.title: Philosophical Point
claims.text: Invoking divine creation sidesteps the challenge that physical matter must produce immaterial souls ex nihilo.

claims.title: Theological Extension
claims.text: Some Christian views add predestination, with God deciding each soul’s ultimate destiny at allocation.

claims.title: Controversy
claims.text: Predestination remains widely rejected in mainstream Judaism, Christianity, and Islam for its moral and theological difficulties.

theories.name: Gomatam’s GV Vedanta Consciousness
theories.summary: GV Vedanta can contribute novel, sophisticated notions of levels of matter to instantiate various features of consciousness without reducing consciousness itself to matter.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness is real and distinct from matter, though its traits can appear within structured levels of matter.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Conscious properties like thought and emotion are instantiated in “levels of matter,” without being reducible to matter itself.

claims.title: Distinguishing Ideas
claims.text: Matter can mirror traits of consciousness without being conscious, much like a painting reflects features of an object.

claims.title: Compatibility with Science
claims.text: This view accommodates materialist neuroscience by explaining how mental functions can arise from, but not be, matter.

claims.title: Illusion and Self
claims.text: Due to illusion (maya), we mistake materially reflected traits for our real conscious self, obscuring our true identity.

theories.name: Hasker's Unified Experience, Conscious Self, Causal Mind Requires a Brain-Generated Nonphysical Substance
theories.summary: Hasker’s emergent dualism holds that sufficiently organized brains naturally generate a unified, nonphysical conscious self rather than merely producing emergent mental properties. He argues that a unified conscious experience cannot exist distributed across the parts of a composite object, so the subject of experience cannot be the brain. What is required is not merely an emergent property but an emergent individual—a new substance generated by the brain in the course of biological development. Phenomenal consciousness is irreducible and essentially unified. The emergent self remains intimately dependent upon its brain but possesses genuine downward causal powers, including teleological agency and libertarian free will. This allows Hasker to combine strong brain dependence and evolutionary continuity with substance dualism. His theory leaves unexplained how matter generates a conscious individual and faces problems concerning causal closure and emergence, while allowing the theological possibility of postmortem survival through divine sustaining action

theories.name: Historical and Traditional Dualisms
theories.summary: Dualism is the oldest and most ubiquitous theory of consciousness in the sense that nonphysical aspects of the world and mind, such as animism and ancestor worship, had long seemed the default assumption of millennia of pre-modern human groups and cultures.

claims.title: Core Idea
claims.text: Dualism is humanity’s oldest view of mind, rooted in spiritual and cultural traditions.

claims.title: Cultural Roots
claims.text: Animism, ancestor worship, and ancient philosophical systems assumed nonphysical mind or soul.

claims.title: Religious Shaping
claims.text: Abrahamic faiths, despite varied scripture, reinforced belief in immortal souls beyond death.

claims.title: Philosophical Detail
claims.text: Historical theology often treated the soul as unified, continuous, and divinely created.

claims.title: Enduring Appeal
claims.text: These deep traditions still shape global belief, even as science challenges dualist assumptions.

theories.name: Indian Personal Consciousness: Plural Selves and Real Matter
theories.summary: A substantial minority of Indian traditions held that consciousness is irreducibly plural and matter irreducibly real, so the individual subject is an eternal existent rather than an appearance to be dissolved. Sankhya, Nyaya-Vaisheshika, Jainism, and the theistic Vedantas of Ramanuja, Madhva, and Chaitanya refuse both essential Advaitic (nondual) moves: reducing matter to appearance, and treating many subjects as one subject misperceived. Sankhya is the most consequential, placing intellect, ego, mind, memory, and emotion on the material side while reserving phenomenality alone for the self—a dualism drawn between consciousness and mind rather than between mind and body.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Indian traditions link individual consciousness to cosmic consciousness, either as a “part” or as the whole itself.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Schools like Advaita Vedanta see all reality as consciousness, while Samkhya posits dualism between spirit (purusha) and matter (prakriti).

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Some views hold the mind itself is subtle matter, illuminated by the soul’s inherent consciousness.

claims.title: Pluralist Perspective
claims.text: Gaudiya Vaishnava Vedanta treats God, matter, and innumerable individual consciousnesses as ontologically real and distinct.

claims.title: Philosophical Aim
claims.text: Encourages integrating meditative experience and spiritual practice into contemporary philosophy of mind debates.

theories.name: Interactive Dualism
