theories.summary: The primary problem of Dualism—many would say the defeater of Dualism—is how nonphysical substances could possibly interact with physical substances, especially given the common assumption that the physical world is a closed system.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Nonphysical minds and physical bodies can causally influence each other, despite objections from causal closure in physics.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Rejects epiphenomenalism, exploring quantum effects, extra dimensions, or non-classical physics as possible causal pathways.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Challenges 19th-century assumptions about matter and energy, suggesting physics may not be a fully closed system.

claims.title: Speculative Mechanisms
claims.text: Proposals include energy redistribution, overdetermination, divine assistance, or occasionalism as ways to bridge mind-body causation.

claims.title: Philosophical Tension
claims.text: The interaction problem remains a central challenge, with solutions often trading scientific plausibility for metaphysical possibility.

theories.name: Kind’s Dualism 2.0
theories.summary: Philosopher Amy Kind defends dualism 2.0, “a thoroughly modern version of dualism … decoupled from any religious or non-scientific connotations.” Her argument is direct and forceful: “A physicalist framework cannot adequately capture the full reality of our conscious experience”—which has a “qualitative nature.”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness has an irreducible qualitative nature that physicalism, in any form, cannot fully capture.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Treats phenomenal and physical activities as equally real but non-reducible, without invoking mental substances.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Offers a naturalistic, non-spooky dualism free of religious or mystical commitments.

claims.title: Contrast with Rivals
claims.text: Rejects Russellian Monism and panpsychism by not requiring phenomenality at the fundamental level.

claims.title: Philosophical Aim
claims.text: Seeks a broader account of causation that affirms the reality and efficacy of phenomenal states.

theories.name: Libet's Conscious Mental Field
theories.summary: Libet’s Conscious Mental Field (CMF) theory proposes that phenomenal consciousness is a unified, brain-generated but nonphysical phenomenon that is irreducible to the distributed neuronal activities producing it and may itself exert causal influence on neural processes. The proposal is strikingly counterintuitive in light of Libet’s famous readiness-potential experiments, which are widely invoked in materialist and epiphenomenalist arguments that unconscious physical brain activity initiates action before conscious intention, and consciousness is therefore causally secondary or even powerless. Yet Libet drew no such physicalist conclusion; instead, he explicitly characterized subjective consciousness as nonphysical and posited CMF partly to preserve both phenomenal unity and genuine mental-to-neural causation. The scientist whose experiments became emblematic of brain-first materialism thus developed one of neuroscience’s more explicit nonphysical theories of consciousness.

theorists.name: Benjamin Libet
theorists.role: Professor of Physiology; pioneering experimental investigator of consciousness

theories.name: Lorber’s Soul and Spirit
theories.summary: The Christian mystic Jakob Lorber asserts in his self-claimed revelations that the human being consists of a soul and a divine spirit, which, for a very short time, are incarnated in a material body.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Humans have a soul of countless “specifica” particles and a divine spirit, briefly incarnated together in body.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Spirit spark at birth guides soul via conscience, shielded to prevent overpowering developing free will.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Life’s goal is uniting soul and spirit through God-seeking, selfishness-resistance, and selfless love.

theories.name: Malebranche’s Divine Occasionalism: Inner Sensation and Phenomenal Experience
theories.summary: Malebranche’s theory of consciousness combines Cartesian substance dualism with occasionalism (the doctrine that God alone is a true cause and that creatures are only occasions for divine action) to produce a distinctive account of phenomenal experience: sensations, emotions, imaginings, pleasures, pains, and thoughts are real modifications of an immaterial soul, immediately known through inner sensation, yet bodily events do not themselves cause these conscious states. Rather, bodily changes serve as occasions on which God—the only genuine efficient cause—produces the corresponding phenomenal modifications in the soul according to general laws governing mind-body union.

theories.name: Mascari’s Qualion-Mind Paradigm
theories.summary: Stephen Arnold Mascari offers his “Qualion-Mind Paradigm” as a “biophysically generated dualism,” a “physicalistic/materialistic dualism that manifests supraphysical properties.” Mascari’s model was motivated by the recognition that something “new” is needed to explain our conscious mental life and that Nature could provide organic life-forms with a higher-level component, a “robust dualism,” that could account for mental phenomena in a fairly straightforward way.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness arises from “qualions,” stable microphysical energy structures in the body that manifest supraphysical mental properties.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: The brain (“Brain 1”) interacts with qualions (“Brain 2.0”), which generate unified consciousness fields and enable volition.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Qualions act as the physical substrate of a modern “soul,” bridging energy and consciousness more closely than neurons can.

claims.title: Ontological View
claims.text: Treats energy and consciousness as “ontological cousins,” reducing the explanatory gap between brain matter and mental life.

claims.title: Philosophical Aim
claims.text: Offers a scientifically framed dualism that preserves human freedom and responsibility, rejecting deterministic neuro-materialism.

theories.name: Moreland’s Christian Soul
theories.summary: Christian philosopher J. P. Moreland defines a robust “generic substance dualism” as the view according to which “(i) there is a substantial soul (self, ego, I, substantial form) that is wholly immaterial; (ii) the soul is not identical to its physical body; and (iii) the soul is that which grounds personal identity for human persons.”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Humans possess a wholly immaterial soul that grounds personal identity and gives form and life to the body.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: The soul animates and unifies the body, while the body enables the soul’s natural, fully realized state.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Conscious unity cannot arise from a brain’s separate parts; the soul explains unified, whole-field awareness.

claims.title: Philosophical Support
claims.text: Draws on introspection, self-awareness, modal arguments, and libertarian freedom to defend substance dualism.

claims.title: Value Implication
claims.text: A living body has intrinsic worth because it is ensouled; without a soul, it is merely a corpse.

theories.name: Nida-Rümelin’s Subject-Body Dualism
theories.summary: A version of dualism that is stronger than property dualism and that may be taken to be a version of so-called substance dualism. But because “substance dualism” invites associations that she would like to avoid, she uses “subject-body dualism” to describe her theory of consciousness. While not a dualist in the Cartesian sense, she endorses a non-reductive, non-physicalist account of consciousness, where phenomenal properties are ontologically basic.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: A conscious subject is neither identical to nor constituted by any material thing, though it has a body.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Phenomenal properties emerge from but are irreducible to physical substrates, grounding self-aware experience.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Rejects Cartesian “soul” talk; the person is identical with the experiencing subject, not a body-soul composite.

claims.title: Key Principles
claims.text: Builds on phenomenal essentialism, cognitive independence of concepts, and intrinsic pre-reflective self-awareness.

claims.title: Philosophical Aim
claims.text: Offers a scientifically compatible yet non-reductive dualism stronger than property dualism but softer than substance dualism.

theories.name: Nonphysical Component in the Human Mind
theories.summary: This theory of consciousness is a generalized notion that in order to make the human mind, some kind of “nonphysical component,” working with the human brain, might be needed.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Human mind may require a brain-linked “nonphysical component,” distinct from traditional immortal soul concepts.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Component has no awareness itself, but enables richer cognition; animals may have simpler equivalents.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Nebuchadnezzar’s biblical “mind change” illustrates possible alteration of such a nonphysical element.

theories.name: Nyāya’s Contingent Consciousness of the Enduring Self
theories.summary: Nyāya holds that the self is an eternal, all-pervading, nonphysical substance that is not conscious in its own nature. Phenomenal consciousness is not the essence of the self but a contingent set of qualities instantiated by an enduring, nonphysical ātman. Cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, and volition arise only when the self is appropriately connected through manas to bodily and sensory processes. First-order cognition reveals its object but not intrinsically itself; reflective awareness requires a later apperception (anuvyavasāya). Nyāya therefore combines substance dualism, external realism, and a non-reflexive account of ordinary cognition, while opposing Buddhist no-self and reflexivist theories, Sāṃkhya’s essentially conscious puruṣa, and Advaita’s self-luminous consciousness.

theories.name: Philosophical History of Dualism
theories.summary: Philosophical History of Dualism

claims.title: Historical Development
claims.text: Originates with Plato’s immortal soul vs. mortal body; shaped by early Christian theology and Neoplatonism.

claims.title: Key Turning Points
claims.text: Descartes’ res cogitans/res extensa distinction; rise of materialism and neuroscience challenged dualism; Chalmers’ naturalistic revival.

claims.title: Why Meaningful
claims.text: Frames mind and body as distinct realities, shaping religious belief, metaphysics, and the mind–body debate.

claims.title: Current Status
claims.text: Popular in public belief, rejected by most philosophers, with modern variants exploring interaction and causal roles.

theories.name: Pitts’s Interactionist Dualism: Energy Conservation and Mental Causation
theories.summary: The longstanding Leibniz-to-Dennett objection to interactionist dualism based on the conservation of energy and momentum suffers from circular reasoning, once neglected aspects of the physics of conservation laws are considered. Two typically neglected aspects of conservation laws are locality and the (bi)conditional relation to symmetries. With these features properly understood, non-conservation of energy and momentum could be a consequence of interactionism.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Conservation-law objections to dualism rest on outdated or circular reasoning, neglecting key features of modern physics.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Local conservation, symmetry relations, and Noether’s theorem show mental causation could naturally involve energy non-conservation.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Violations in specific places (e.g., brains) need not threaten physics globally and may be expected under dualism.

claims.title: Physics Engagement
claims.text: Uses classical field theory and symmetry principles to rebut conservation objections without relying on quantum mechanics.

claims.title: GR Complication
claims.text: General Relativity poses a novel challenge, but its force depends on one’s broader metaphysical and theistic commitments.

theories.name: Popper and Eccles's Interactionist Dualism: Three Worlds and the Liaison Brain
theories.summary: Popper and Eccles propose that phenomenal consciousness is non-physical and belongs to an irreducible mental domain that interacts causally with the physical brain, so the physical world is not causally closed. Popper's three-world ontology places subjective experience between physical states and the objective contents of thought, and his evolutionary argument holds that consciousness could not have been selected for unless it affected behavior; Eccles argues that a nonphysical self-conscious mind selects, interprets, and unifies activity in a cortical “liaison brain.” Later, Eccles posited “psychons” linked to neural dendrons and speculative quantum modulation of synaptic release by altering quantum exocytosis probabilities without transferring energy. Their theory influenced debates over interactionist dualism, emergence, mental causation, free will, and quantum consciousness, but its proposed mind–brain mechanisms remain empirically unsupported.

theories.name: Property Dualism
theories.summary: Property Dualism is the idea that while there is only one kind of substance in the world, physical substance, there are two kinds of properties, mental and physical properties, such that mental properties cannot be reduced to or explained by physical properties alone, even though both kinds of properties are generated by the same physical thing, namely brains.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Reality has only physical substance, but it holds two kinds of properties: physical and irreducible mental properties.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Brains generate both physical and mental properties, but mental ones can’t be reduced to physical explanations alone.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Mental properties have unique ontological status, even though they arise entirely from physical systems.

claims.title: Key Example
claims.text: You could know every brain fact about garlic smell yet not know its subjective feel without experiencing it.

claims.title: Challenges & Tensions
claims.text: Critics argue that positing nonphysical properties risks sliding toward substance dualism or metaphysical confusion.

theories.name: Realms of the Soul
theories.summary: Many, actually almost all, religious traditions present elaborate levels or stages or realms of the soul, accommodating the soul and its elaborate journeys before birth and after death—Yogācāra Buddhism, Sufism in Islam, Kabbalah in Judaism, Christian mysticism, occult sects such as Theosophy.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Many religions imagine structured realms mapping the soul’s journey before birth and after death.

claims.title: Shared Imagery
claims.text: Diverse traditions depict strikingly similar multi-level habitats for souls despite doctrinal differences.

claims.title: Philosophical Note
claims.text: Such visions presuppose a nonphysical, enduring soul, placing consciousness beyond the physical.

theories.name: Sāṃkhya's Pure Witness and the Material Mind
theories.summary: Sāṃkhya explains conscious experience through an ontological dualism between prakṛti and puruṣa, dividing reality between them. Prakṛti is active but insentient, unconscious nature and includes body, senses, intellect, ego, mind, cognition, affect, and qualitative contents; puruṣa is inactive, a plurality of contentless, changeless, inactive witnessing consciousness. Multiple puruṣas ground distinct subjects. Phenomenal experience therefore requires both structured psychophysical content and witnessing subjectivity. Decisively, the entire cognitive apparatus—intellect, ego, mind, senses, memory, emotion—falls on the material side, so the dualism separates consciousness from mind rather than mind from body. Because an effect pre-exists in its cause, sentience cannot arise from insentient constituents. Phenomenal experience arises from conjunction (saṃyoga), in which the insentient appears as if conscious and the indifferent witness as if an agent. Liberation (kaivalya) is cessation of that misidentification, leaving pure consciousness itself unchanged

theories.name: Soul in Indigenous Religions
theories.summary: The concept of the soul, in multifarious forms, has infused indigenous and folk religions throughout the world, and although we tend to categorize these ancient belief systems as “pre-modern” and “pre-scientific,” lacking the sophistication of the major Eastern and Abrahamic traditions, we may be remiss not to recognize the data and to assess its implications (if any).

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Indigenous traditions worldwide recognize spiritual aspects of humans, often as vital forces in both living beings and nature.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Souls may be internal, external, or multiple, able to depart the body in dreams or after death for new realms.

claims.title: Cultural Diversity
claims.text: Beliefs vary from ancestor reincarnation to multi-soul systems, with destinies shaped by trials, judgment, or transformation.

claims.title: Philosophical Note
claims.text: These concepts rarely match strict substance dualism but often distinguish body from enduring spiritual entities.

claims.title: Scientific Insight
claims.text: Cognitive science explains their universality through evolved “agent detection” while remaining agnostic on their truth.

theories.name: Soul in Islamic Philosophy
theories.summary: In Islam, the nature of the soul is a central concern and is not dissimilar to the soul in Christianity and Judaism (understandable because the three developed side by side during the Middle Ages, rather harmoniously, too). Building on ancient and Neo-Platonist philosophers, medieval Islamic philosophers, mainly al-Kindî, al-Farabi, Avicenna, and Averroes, developed an Islamic metaphysic of the soul by evaluating the concepts of intellect, soul, nafs, and body.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: The soul (nafs) is a self-aware, enduring essence that unites with the body yet can exist beyond bodily death.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Classical Islamic philosophers describe the soul as organizing the body, progressing through hierarchical faculties toward rationality.

claims.title: Spiritual View
claims.text: Consciousness is a “spiritual light” from God, polished through remembrance to reflect divine reality.

claims.title: Afterlife Development
claims.text: The soul continues to grow after death, ascending through paradisal levels toward union with the divine essence.

claims.title: Philosophical Roots
claims.text: Draws on ancient and Neo-Platonic thought, integrating metaphysics with Islamic theology and spiritual practice.

theories.name: Soul in the Hebrew Bible and Jewish Philosophy
theories.summary: If one wants to pay attention to the nature of consciousness or soul in the Hebrew scriptures (which is recognized as foundational by traditional Christianity and Islam as well as by Judaism), there are two essential words to consider: “nephesh” (נֶפֶשׁ), often translated as “soul,” and “ruach” (רוּחַ), often translated “spirit.”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Hebrew scripture’s key terms for “soul” (nephesh) and “spirit” (ruach) differ from modern notions, linking life, mind, and breath.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Nephesh denotes living beings and bodily life; ruach covers spirit, wind, and mental states, often tied to divine action.

claims.title: Philosophical View
claims.text: Segal defends preexistent souls that become thinking with bodily development, paralleling transformations in materialist animalism.

claims.title: Mystical Model
claims.text: Shyfrin’s Kabbalah of Information sees the soul as a self-aware information structure within a fractal cosmic hierarchy.

claims.title: Ontological Implication
claims.text: In this framework, material and spiritual are not fundamentally different, both arising from divine information creation.

theories.name: Soul in the New Testament and Christian Philosophy
theories.summary: Almost all Christian denominations feature an immortal soul as essential doctrine, and it is conventional wisdom that the immortal soul is supported by passages in the New Testament. Yet there are opposing views; for example, Peter van Inwagen's “Christian materialism.”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: In the New Testament, “soul” (psyche) typically means a living person, not an immortal, separable essence.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Life is tied to breath; death is unconscious “sleep” until bodily resurrection restores the whole person.

claims.title: Historical Shift
claims.text: Early Christianity absorbed Hellenistic ideas of an immortal afterlife, diverging from Hebraic bodily unity.

claims.title: Doctrinal Debates
claims.text: Traducianism, Creationism, and Pre-existence offer competing accounts of how individual souls originate.

claims.title: Philosophical Defense
claims.text: Contemporary Christian dualists argue the soul best explains consciousness and is ontologically linked to theism.

theories.name: Steiner’s Esoteric Soul and Consciousness
theories.summary: The esotericist, philosopher, and spiritual teacher Rudolf Steiner had a complex and changing relationship with Theosophy, from apologist and thought leader to competitor and reprobate.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness arises from the meeting of two currents—emotions from the future and visualizations from the past—within the soul.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Humans have physical, etheric, astral bodies, and the Ego; consciousness emerges where astral and etheric bodies intersect.

claims.title: Spiritual Journey
claims.text: After death, the etheric body detaches, dispersing experiences into the cosmic ether before the soul’s further evolution.

claims.title: Philosophical Aim
claims.text: Develops “spiritual science” to cultivate higher faculties—Imagination, Inspiration, Intuition—for conscious spiritual growth.

theories.name: Stump’s Thomistic Dualism
theories.summary: The influential Christian scholastic philosopher St. Thomas Aquinas gives an account of the soul that is non-Cartesian in character, according to Catholic philosopher Eleonore Stump, who has Aquinas taking the soul to be something essentially immaterial or configurational but nonetheless realized in material components.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: The soul is immaterial yet realized in matter, serving as the form that makes a body a living human being.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: The soul configures matter for life and intellect, existing naturally only as part of the body-soul composite.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Unlike Cartesian dualism, the soul here is not a separate substance but a form that can subsist apart unnaturally.

claims.title: Broader View
claims.text: All living things have souls as their life-giving forms, but only humans have rational, intellective souls.

claims.title: Philosophical Aim
claims.text: Challenges the sharp divide between materialism and dualism, offering a hybrid account rooted in Aquinas’s thought.

theories.name: Swinburne’s Substance Dualism
theories.summary: Christian philosopher Richard Swinburne is a leading advocate of substance dualism. “If you want to tell the whole story of the world, you must say what objects there are in the world, what substances there are, and what properties they have at different times,” Swinburne said on Closer to Truth. “Of course, that will include all the physical objects, all the tables and chairs and planets and atoms.”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Every person has a nonphysical soul that is essential to personal identity and conscious life.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: The soul is a separate mental entity, distinct from but associated with a physical body and brain.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Physical facts alone can’t determine “who is who”; souls uniquely track personal identity through time.

claims.title: Identity Argument
claims.text: Swapping bodies wouldn’t swap “you” and “me,” proving identity depends on souls, not just physical form.

claims.title: Non-Theological Basis
claims.text: Swinburne argues for the soul using philosophical reasoning, independent of religious texts or beliefs.

theories.name: Theosophy’s Eclectic Soul and Consciousness
theories.summary: Soul and consciousness are core doctrines of Theosophy, an occult amalgam of esoteric ideas from Western and Eastern religions, traditions, and philosophies. Theosophy defines itself as “Wisdom-religion” or “Divine Wisdom,” and considers itself “The substratum and basis of all the world-religions and philosophies, taught and practiced by a few elect ever since man became a thinking being.”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Theosophy blends Eastern and Western esoteric traditions, teaching that soul and consciousness are universal and fundamental.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Human beings have three soul aspects—animal, human, and spiritual—each linked to different planes of existence.

claims.title: View of Consciousness
claims.text: Consciousness pervades all matter, from atoms to humans, with self-consciousness fully developed only in humans.

claims.title: Philosophical Scope
claims.text: Consciousness pervades all matter, from atoms to humans, with self-consciousness fully developed only in humans.

theories.name: Trialism
theories.summary: Trialism is the theory of mind that posits reality as consisting of three fundamental substances or aspects, as opposed to the one of monism (e.g., materialism or idealism) or the two of dualism. There are two distinct kinds of trialism: a reinterpretation of René Descartes's dualism (implicitly in a religious context of the “soul”) and secular-philosophical three-part models of existence.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Trialism distinguishes three irreducible categories, aspects, or realms relevant to mind and consciousness, but different trialist theories assign very different meanings to the third category.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: In Cartesian trialism, mind-body union grounds irreducibly psychophysical experience; in Popper’s theory, physical reality, subjective experience, and objective knowledge constitute three interacting worlds.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: The third category need not be a third substance or a mediator between mind and body; its ontological and explanatory role varies among trialist theories.

claims.title: Cottingham’s Trialism
claims.text: Descartes’s mind-body union constitutes an irreducible primitive notion associated especially with sensation, passion, and embodied experience, without clearly requiring a third substance.

claims.title: Three-Worlds Theories
claims.text: Popper, Eccles, and Penrose each propose triadic models linking mind, matter, and abstract or cultural realms

claims.title: Indian Philosophy
claims.text: Several Indian traditions distinguish gross embodiment, subtle mind, and pure consciousness or spirit, while differing over whether this triadic structure is ultimately dualist, pluralist, or nondual.

theories.name: Albahari’s Perennial Idealism
theories.summary: Comparative philosopher Miri Albahari defends “Perennial Idealism” as a mystical solution to the mind-body problem. She faces the “vicious dilemma” of subjects arising from unconditioned consciousness. “If the manifest world of subjects is real, it irrevocably undercuts the purely unconditioned nature of the ground by imposing boundaries between subjects and the ground.”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: The ultimate ground of reality is unconditioned, nondual consciousness without subject–object structure.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Subjects and objects arise as appearances in the ground, like dreams depend on the dreamer.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Rejects cosmopsychism’s “cosmos as subject” model; consciousness itself is prior to all subjects.

claims.title: Implication
claims.text: Resolves the mind–body problem by rooting all existence in aperspectival consciousness.

theories.name: Arendsen’s Complex Idealism
theories.summary: Complex Idealism posits that reality is fundamentally a continuous, mental, and informational flow of duration, and that consciousness is an “unsplittable unity” that cannot be modeled computationally. Rather than viewing consciousness as an emergent property of material structures, the framework asserts the ontological primacy of a primary, continuous mental mobility. "Complex" signifies the dual-aspect architecture of existence, the intersection of "real" and "imaginary" domains.

theorists.name: Albert R.J. (Richard) Arendsen
theorists.role: Chemical engineer and computational modeling expert

theories.name: Bentley Hart’s Consciousness, Being, God
theories.summary: Philosopher, theological scholar, and intellectual provocateur David Bentley Hart constructs an ultimate unified monism, his form of idealism, first by showing that consciousness/mind and being/existence are profoundly inseverable. He argues that “rational thought and coherent order are two sides of a single reality” and that only by embracing God “as the absolute unity of consciousness and being” can the one ontological reality be confirmed.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness and being are inseparable, unified ultimately in God as one ontological reality.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Mental and material realms are irreducible to one another, both rooted in divine infinite mind.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: God is the absolute unity of consciousness and being, grounding both mind and reality.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Materialism fails to explain mind; reality is best understood as reason-infused and God-centered.

theories.name: Berkeley’s Immaterialist Idealism
theories.summary: Nothing exists but minds and the ideas they perceive, that the world we sense is constituted by the qualitative contents of perception themselves rather than by any mind-independent matter lying beneath them, and that these passive, perceived, lawfully ordered ideas are sustained as a coherent public world by the perception and will of an infinite spirit, God.

theories.name: Bhartṛhari’s Linguistic Idealism
theories.summary: Bhartṛhari integrates language and metaphysics to formulate a unique theory of consciousness, which can be called Linguistic Idealism. It posits that ultimate conscious reality is one indivisible linguistic principle, according to which language is not merely a tool for communication but the substance of which the universe is made.

theories.name: Bradley’s Absolute Idealism
theories.summary: Absolute Idealism has sentient experience as the sole reality, and phenomenal consciousness, at its most primitive level, is “feeling” or immediate experience: a pre-relational unity of qualitative diversity from which subject-object consciousness, judgment, body, self, and nature are abstracted, and within which finite sentient centers are partial appearances of one all-inclusive Absolute Experience.

theories.name: Buddhism’s Empty, Illusory Phenomenal Consciousness
theories.summary: Consciousness in Buddhism is sufficiently distinct, with its concepts of emptiness and illusion, that it could command a prime category of its own on the Landscape, yet it also fits decently in idealism, appropriately after Hinduism.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Phenomenal consciousness has no intrinsic nature; its apparent “what-it’s-like-ness” is a cognitive illusion.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Consciousness arises through interdependent processes, with no independent self or inner qualitative core.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Emptiness means lacking inherent nature, not lacking existence; all phenomena are conventionally real but ultimately empty.

claims.title: Philosophical Schools
claims.text: Madhyamaka sees mind and world as interdependent and empty; Yogācāra treats only mind as ultimately real.

claims.title: Implication
claims.text: Undermines the idea of private, irreducible subjective experience, shifting focus to public, process-based accounts of mind.

theories.name: Builes’s Modal Idealism
theories.summary: It is metaphysically necessary that Idealism is true, that every fundamental entity is conscious, and moreover that every fundamental property is a phenomenal property.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: It is metaphysically necessary that every fundamental entity and property is phenomenal.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Only one world is fundamental; all other possible worlds exist as thoughts in a divine mind.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Merges idealism with modal realism by reinterpreting possible worlds as mental representations.

claims.title: Implication
claims.text: Unifies philosophy of mind and modal metaphysics while preserving ontological parsimony.

theories.name: Chopra’s Only the Whole Is Conscious
theories.summary: Holistic physician Deepak Chopra defines consciousness as “It is what makes experience possible. It is what makes perception possible. It is what makes cognition possible.”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness is the non-physical source of all reality; only the whole cosmos is truly conscious.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Matter, energy, space, and time are expressions shaped from unitary, all-encompassing consciousness.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Individual beings aren’t independently conscious; they share in consciousness only as parts of the whole.

claims.title: Speculative Implication
claims.text: Pure awareness has no origin or cause; it simply is, beyond time and explanation.

theories.name: Dao De Jing’s Constant Dao
theories.summary: Among my favorite lines in all philosophical literature are the deceptively simple opening lines of the Dao De Jing, the Chinese classic text that is the foundation of Daoism. “The Dao [Ultimate Reality, Way] that can be spoken of [expressed] is not the Constant [Eternal] Dao; the Name that can be named [understood] is not the Constant [Eternal] Name” (道可道非常道; 名可名非常名). “Dao” (道) refers to “Ultimate Reality” but also means “Way” or “Path.” “Constant” comes from “Chang” (常), which also means “invariable” and may connote “eternal.”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: The Dao is ultimate reality and source of consciousness; beyond all names, concepts, and expression.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Dao (ultimate awareness) begets Name (cognition), leading through cosmic stages to all phenomena.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Consciousness is first and last; Daoist flow states deepen awareness beyond ordinary thought.

claims.title: Philosophical Implication
claims.text: If consciousness is fundamental, it endures until the deepest levels of metaphysical “Nothing.”

theories.name: Fichte’s Self-Positing I
theories.summary: Fichte’s theory of consciousness is a transcendental-idealist account in which phenomenal experience is not a passive reception of a mind-independent world but the lived manifestation of the finite I’s self-positing activity as checked, limited, affected, embodied, and socially summoned into determinate self-conscious experience.

theories.name: Forrest’s Intelligent Idealism
theories.summary: Intelligent Idealism argues that reality is best understood not as dead matter accidentally producing mind, but as Mind / Intelligence under constraint. Its deeper claim is that Mind is primary, constraint is the grammar of Mind, and intelligence is the signature of that grammar. It develops cumulatively across agency, qualia, evolution, perception, time, spacetime, physical actuality, biology, suffering, artificial intelligence, local selfhood, and the wider Mind-field. Rather than asking how mind emerges from matter, it asks what must be true of reality for law, agency, experience, structure, science, and intelligibility to be possible at all. Its central formula is: possibility before access, access before refinement, refinement through local avatars inside a rendered interface.

theories.name: Goswami’s Self-Aware Universe
theories.summary: Quantum physicist Amit Goswami proposes that consciousness, not matter, is the primary “stuff” of creation, and indeed it is consciousness that creates the material world, not the other way around.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness is the fundamental reality that collapses quantum possibilities into the physical world.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: A single universal consciousness “chooses” measurement outcomes, creating both mental and material objects.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: The ego is constricted consciousness; expanded states reveal our participation in the one cosmic subject.

claims.title: Implication
claims.text: Idealism resolves quantum paradoxes and affirms deep interconnectedness across all creation.

theories.name: Hegel’s Dialectical Consciousness in the Development of Spirit
theories.summary: Hegel’s theory of phenomenal consciousness is a developmental and social account in which immediate feeling, sensation, perception, self-consciousness, recognition, and rational spirit are not separate faculties but progressively articulated “shapes” through which experience becomes aware of its own conceptual, embodied, and intersubjective conditions.

theories.name: Hoffman’s Conscious Realism: The Case Against Reality
theories.summary: Cognitive psychologist Donald Hoffman's “Case Against Reality” argues that our visual perceptions are not veridical of ultimate reality because evolution selects for fitness to reproduce, not for access to ontological truth.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Perceptions are adaptive illusions, not accurate depictions of ultimate reality.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Consciousness is fundamental; spacetime and objects are icons in our perceptual interface.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Reality is a network of interacting conscious agents, not particles or matter in space-time.

claims.title: Speculative Implication
claims.text: Brain activity is created by consciousness, reversing the usual mind–brain causation.

theorists.name: Donald Hoffman
theorists.role: Professor Emeritus of Cognitive Science & Science Author

theories.name: How Consciousness Becomes the Physical Universe
theories.summary: Idealism works well as an explanation of creature consciousness, provided, of course, that one accepts its foundational premise that consciousness, and consciousness alone, is fundamental reality.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness is the ultimate reality; matter and energy are its complementary expressions.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Observation in quantum theory links observer, observed, and observation, giving rise to the physical world.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Consciousness can govern causation, generating matter and energy through quantum-like interactions.

claims.title: Speculative Implication
claims.text: Consciousness may be subject to relativistic effects, dilating with motion like time itself.

theories.name: Idealism Additional Theories
theories.summary: As creator and host of Closer To Truth, Robert Lawrence Kuhn receives ideas from viewers globally. These unsolicited papers are often elaborate treatises, the majority of which focus on consciousness or cosmology. He says he looks at all of them, keeps an open mind (with at least one eye squinty skeptical), learns some, and responds as he can. Here are some of them.

theories.name: Idealisms—Overview
theories.summary: Idealism is the theory that consciousness is ultimate reality, the fullness of the deepest level of all existence, the singular fundamental existent. It is the theory of consciousness that takes consciousness to its maximum meaning: Consciousness is rock-bottom reality.

claims.title: Core Concepts
claims.text: Holds that consciousness is ultimate reality; all physical worlds are derivative of mental fundamentals.

claims.title: Scientific Context
claims.text: Rooted in philosophy and religion; includes micro-, macro-, and cosmic forms with varied implications.

claims.title: Why Meaningful
claims.text: Reverses physicalism by making mind foundational; offers unifying metaphysics linking consciousness and existence.

claims.title: Major Challenges
claims.text: Faces incredulity, unclear mechanisms, and difficulty reconciling with empirical science’s physicalist assumptions.

theories.name: Indian Cosmic Consciousness
theories.summary: Indian traditions treat consciousness as the fundamental datum from which explanation begins rather than a phenomenon to be explained, and Advaita Vedanta takes this furthest: consciousness (Brahman) is the sole nondual reality, self-luminous and never an object, while body, mind, world, and the sense of being a particular subject are appearances within it. The qualitative character of experience belongs to a material and insentient inner organ; consciousness supplies only manifestation. The hard problem is thereby reframed, since the question is not how insentient matter generates experience, held impossible, but why one unlimited awareness appears as many bounded subjects. Superimposition (mistaking one thing for another) and ignorance claim to answer that question.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: In Advaita Vedanta, consciousness (Brahman) is the sole nondual reality; Atman and cosmic consciousness are identical.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Body, mind, and world are objects within consciousness; matter appears in consciousness, not vice versa.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Liberation comes from realizing oneself as limitless consciousness beyond space, time, and object boundaries.

theories.name: Kak’s Universal Consciousness
theories.summary: Computer scientist Subhash Kak proposes that consciousness is primary and that the very understanding of physical reality takes place in consciousness. He argues that consciousness cannot be a property of the brain; therefore, it is nonmaterial and transcends materiality. It is like a light that illuminates the physical universe.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness is primary, nonmaterial, and both illuminates and transcends the physical universe.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Quantum principles underlie brain–mind processes, with consciousness shaping perception, memory, and free will.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: The “outer cosmos” mirrors the “inner cosmos,” linking universal patterns to mental structures.

claims.title: Implication
claims.text: Consciousness interacts with materiality by influencing probabilities in physical state transitions.

theories.name: Kant’s Transcendental Idealism
theories.summary: Kant’s theory of consciousness holds that phenomenal consciousness is not a self-standing inner arena or an introspected mental substance, but the sensibly given, temporally ordered, and qualitatively affected side of experience that becomes experience of objects only through a priori forms of intuition, synthesis by imagination and understanding, and the unity of apperception by which representations can belong to one subject.

theories.name: Kashmir Shaivism’s Dynamic Non-Dualism
theories.summary: Consciousness (chit) is the fundamental reality of the universe. Kashmir Shaivism’s foundational doctrine is its steadfast emphasis on the intrinsic unity between the individual soul, known as Jiva, and the universal consciousness, identified as Shiva.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Supreme Consciousness (Shiva) and its dynamic power (Shakti) are identical, manifesting as all reality.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Consciousness vibrates as spanda, unfolding through 36 tattvas from pure awareness to physical matter.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: The world is a real, divine play of Consciousness, not an illusion to be transcended.

theories.name: Kastrup’s Analytic Idealism
theories.summary: Philosopher Bernardo Kastrup's “analytic idealism” is “a consciousness-only ontology” that has refocused attention, within the philosophical community and more broadly, on metaphysical idealism, that is, an idealism that is grounded in philosophical argument as opposed to promoted by religious tradition or spiritual belief.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Reality is entirely consciousness; all phenomena are patterns within a single cosmic mind.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Organisms are dissociated alters of cosmic consciousness; brain states are appearances of inner experience.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Idealism explains consciousness more parsimoniously than physicalism or panpsychism, avoiding their core problems.

claims.title: Speculative Implication
claims.text: Death may expand awareness, akin to psychedelic or near-death experiences.

theories.name: McGilchrist’s Relational, Creative-Process Idealism
theories.summary: Psychiatrist, neuroscientist, and literary scholar Iain McGilchrist's idealist metaphysics has consciousness as “irreducible, primordial and omnipresent.” But consciousness is “not a thing; it is a creative process,” he says.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness is irreducible, primordial, and omnipresent—a creative process from which matter is a phase.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Brain permits and shapes consciousness into bodily experience; all reality arises through relationships.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Cosmos evolves to know itself, with life introducing the capacity for value into cosmic consciousness.

claims.title: Speculative Implication
claims.text: Purposeful evolution is guided by attractors, not predetermined design, fostering truth, beauty, and goodness.

theories.name: Meijer’s Universal Knowledge Field
theories.summary: Biomedical scientist Dirk K. F. Meijer explains consciousness in the context of a “Universal Knowledge Field” (UKF), the concept that a collective storage of all information that is present and/or evolves in our universe can take on a universal character and that all information is present in a general knowledge field.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: All universal information resides in a unified, holographic-like field, encompassing consciousness and material reality.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Harmonic electromagnetic frequencies organize systems; a superfluid background field guides reality and brain–heart synchronicity.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: A holofractal memory workspace integrates past and future, making human awareness part of a universal field.

theories.name: Nader’s All There Is
theories.summary: Transcendental Meditation leader (and former neuroscientist) Tony Nader states “there is nothing other than consciousness, and that matter and the multiplicity of loci of consciousness, us, for one, are nothing but consciousness experiencing itself from limited perspectives that hide the true nature of both the observer and the observed.”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness is the only reality; matter exists only as an appearance within consciousness.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: One universal consciousness experiences itself through diverse perspectives, states, and flavors.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: A mathematical “monistic field theory” models all reality as triples of observer, observing, and observed.

claims.title: Implication
claims.text: Physical existence depends entirely on the interplay of consciousness’s three inseparable aspects.

theories.name: Nāgārjuna’s Empty Consciousness: Experience Without Essence
theories.summary: Every phenomenon whatsoever is empty (śūnyatā) of svabhāva—intrinsic nature, or existence from its own side or nature—because whatever arises in dependence on causes, parts, or concepts cannot possess a nature that is its own. Phenomenal consciousness or experience is not denied, but it has no intrinsic nature, no ultimate subject to whom it belongs, and no self-illuminating core, arising only in dependence on faculty, object, and conditions, and thus as empty as the objects it discloses.

theorists.name: Nāgārjuna
theorists.role: Buddhist philosopher; founder, Madhyamaka school of Mahāyāna Buddhism

theories.name: Philosophical History of Idealism
theories.summary: Philosophical History of Idealism in Eastern and Western Philosophy.

claims.title: Historical Development
claims.text: From the Upanishads’ non-dualism and Plato’s Forms, through Plotinus, to Berkeley’s immaterialism and beyond.

claims.title: Key Turning Points
claims.text: Berkeley’s 'esse est percipi', Kant’s transcendental idealism, Hegel’s absolute idealism, and Schopenhauer’s will.

claims.title: Why Meaningful
claims.text: Positions mind and consciousness as fundamental reality, shaping philosophy, theology, and modern consciousness debates.

claims.title: Current Status
claims.text: Echoes in British and American Idealism, and inspires today’s consciousness-first, spiritual, and metaphysical theories.

theories.name: Pulido-Moyano’s Consciousness Endomitosis Theory
theories.summary: Consciousness Endomitosis Theory (CET) offers a vision rooted in the non-dualist metaphysical tradition of Advaita Vedānta, reinterpreted through a contemporary philosophical and cosmological lens. CET posits that reality unfolds through a process of recursive self-division and self-recognition akin to cellular mitosis—but occurring within and by Consciousness itself. The cosmos, then, is not an object but a living, recursive grammar of self-consciousness.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness is the sole reality, recursively dividing and recognizing itself to manifest all forms in the cosmos.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Like cellular mitosis, awareness self-replicates into holons of being and knowing, appearing as particles, planets, and people.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: The phrase “I am aware that I am aware” is the primal vibration generating all multiplicity from unity.

claims.title: Scientific Parallels
claims.text: Links its metaphysics to cosmology and quantum theory, offering a “why” behind cyclic and multiverse models.

claims.title: Ultimate Aim
claims.text: Beyond theory, CET seeks liberation through direct recognition of one’s identity with pure, undivided awareness.

theories.name: Richheimer’s Ground Substance of Creation
theories.summary: Consciousness is the fundamental and ubiquitous feature of reality. In the cosmic cycle, consciousness is transformed first into cosmic mind and then into the material world. When conditions on a planet allow it, living organisms can arise and evolve, such that eventually sentient beings may evolve that strive to complete the creation cycle by becoming one with Cosmic Consciousness.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness is the primary “ground substance” of reality, generating cosmic mind and material world in a purposeful cycle.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Consciousness transforms into cosmic mind’s three layers, then material reality, enabling evolution toward reunion with Cosmic Consciousness.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: A “top-down” spiritual ontology explaining physics puzzles, psi phenomena, mystical states, and consciousness better than materialism.

claims.title: Implication
claims.text: Mind and matter form a unified, meaningful universe with purpose rooted in conscious return to cosmic source.

theories.name: Samarawickrama’s Fundamental, Frequency-Bearing Field
theories.summary: Computer/AI scientist Mahendra Samarawickrama posits that consciousness is a fundamental dimension of reality that brings experience prior to cognition or analysis, constructing knowledge, logic, or language. Within this framework, consciousness and its concomitants (e.g., feeling, perception, volition, attention, etc.) are attributed to the individual mind as a primary phenomenon. Consequently, knowledge emerges as a secondary construct of consciousness. Consciousness is directly experiential and independent of the brain’s cognitive, analytical, logical, or linguistic processes. This foundational layer of awareness underlies all knowledge constructs and can be experienced through meditation. During meditation, suspending external sensory input and internal brain cognition allows for direct confirmation of conscious experience.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness is fundamental, preceding cognition, and functions as a frequency-based field uniting physics and experience.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Hidden-variable “primion” model links quantum mechanics, relativity, and non-local conscious experience through sequential field dynamics.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Two modes of awareness: Gödel-limited self-referential knowledge and complete, non-referential direct causation perception.

theories.name: Śaṅkara's Self-Luminous Nondualism
theories.summary: Śaṅkara holds that pure self-luminous consciousness is ultimate reality and the true self (ātman) is numerically identical with Brahman. Consciousness is self-luminous (svaprakāśa), manifest without requiring a second awareness, and therefore never an object, property, act, or product. Phenomenal contents—perceptions, thoughts, affects, and self-representations—belong to mind, an insentient subtle-material instrument; consciousness manifests them without itself changing. Empirically, consciousness appears as an individual witness through reflection in and apparent limitation by mind, while ultimately there is only one nondual, non-intentional consciousness. Analysis of waking, dreaming, and dreamless sleep shows awareness persisting without content. Consciousness is thus real, irreducible, unindividuated, and identical with Brahman, while phenomenal individuality is appearance. Ignorance produces subject-object division and embodied self-identification; liberation is not a new conscious state but knowledge that one has always been Brahman

theories.name: Sarkar’s Infinite Supreme Consciousness
theories.summary: Spiritual guru and philosopher Prabhat Ranjan Sarkar’s monistic philosophy of infinite Supreme Consciousness is summarized in his 1962 book Ananda Sutram (“Bliss Sutras”): 85 Sanskrit sutras and brief explanatory purports that elaborate the spiritual and social philosophy of Ananda Marga (“Path of Bliss”), which is a synthesis of Vedic intuitional knowledge and Yogic intuitional practices. Sarkar’s philosophy of Infinite Consciousness, absolute reality, consists of uncaused, infinite, non-qualified Supreme Consciousness (Nirguna Brahman). This is composed of a Supreme Cognitive Principle—Shiva or Purusha—and an unexpressed Supreme Operative Principle or creative power—Shakti, Prakriti, or Maya.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Supreme Consciousness is infinite, non-qualified reality; all existence evolves through its cosmic cycle toward re-merger.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Creation cycles from subtle Supreme Consciousness to matter, then back via evolving minds and intuitional practice.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Spiritual goal is merging with Non-Qualified Supreme Consciousness through moral living and disciplined intuitional practice.

theories.name: Schelling’s Nature, Spirit, and the Identity of Mind
theories.summary: Schelling's theory of consciousness is that mind and nature are not two kinds of being but two poles or aspects of one absolute reality—captured in his formula that "nature is visible spirit, spirit is invisible nature"—so that consciousness is nature's own coming-to-awareness rather than a contingent anomaly imposed on physical matter: nature is a graded, self-organizing productivity harboring an unconscious, proto-mental dimension that ascends through successive stages until, in the human being, it awakens to full self-consciousness.

theories.name: Schopenhauer’s The World as Will
theories.summary: Schopenhauer’s theory of phenomenal consciousness holds that ordinary experience is the world as “representation”—objectified under the forms of subject-object cognition, space, time, and causality—while the embodied subject also has immediate inner access to itself as “will,” a blind striving that underlies both affective consciousness and the metaphysical character of nature as a whole.

theories.name: Shen’s Generative Principle of Physical Reality
theories.summary: The universe is the structured constraint architecture that consciousness imposes upon itself to make experience possible. Every conscious experience involves distinction—the ability to differentiate one state from another—and the structural features of consciousness closes the circle with modern physics. The challenge is to recognize that consciousness is not the question—it is the answer, and we have always been part of it.

theories.name: Spira’s Non-Duality
theories.summary: Spiritual teacher (and pottery artist) Rupert Spira espouses non-duality as “the recognition that underlying the multiplicity and diversity of experience there is a single, infinite and indivisible reality, whose nature is pure consciousness from which all objects and selves derive their apparently independent existence.”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: All apparent multiplicity arises from a single, infinite, indivisible reality whose nature is pure consciousness.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: By knowing the true nature of one’s own mind, one recognizes that self and ultimate reality are the same.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: This insight is echoed across major spiritual traditions, each affirming unity between self and the divine or absolute.

claims.title: Implication
claims.text: The highest form of knowledge is self-knowledge, as it reveals the nature of all reality.

theories.name: Sprigge’s Absolute Idealism
theories.summary: Absolute Idealism holds that phenomenal consciousness is the only intrinsically concrete reality, that physical reality as described by science is an abstract relational structure requiring an intrinsic experiential ground, that the countless momentary centers of experience composing nature are ultimately partial aspects of a single, all-inclusive cosmic experience (the Absolute), and that finite minds are perspectival, value-laden phases within a panpsychic Absolute or universal consciousness.

theories.name: Sri Aurobindo’s Evolving Consciousness
theories.summary: Indian philosopher and yogi (and nationalist) Sri Aurobindo envisions an ongoing, progressing evolution of consciousness as a prime feature of world meaning and human purpose. He envisions consciousness as the foundation of existence, but not in a way that negates the reality of the material world. Ultimately, reality is multi-tiered—matter, life, mind, supermind, spirit—all expressions of the same Divine Consciousness.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness is Divine reality unfolding through matter, life, and mind toward supramental transformation on Earth.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Evolution manifests pre-involved Divine Consciousness in ascending stages, bridging spiritual monism with material reality.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Final goal is supramental consciousness as intrinsic to life as current human mentality.

theories.name: Sri Ramana’s Self as Pure Consciousness
theories.summary: Sri Ramana highlighted the distinction between transitive awareness, which knows objects or phenomena, and intransitive awareness, which is awareness that knows nothing other than itself. In classical Advaita Vedanta, intransitive awareness is called pure consciousness because it is consciousness devoid of any content.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: The only real consciousness is pure intransitive awareness, aware only of itself as pure being, “I am.”

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Transitive awareness of objects is a fleeting appearance, borrowing existence and light from pure intransitive awareness.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Knowing consciousness requires turning attention inward toward one’s own being, not outward toward objects or phenomena.

claims.title: Philosophical Stance
claims.text: Classifies Advaita Vedanta as radical monism, not idealism, since mind and ego are ultimately unreal appearances.

claims.title: Ultimate Reality
claims.text: Pure, permanent, self-shining awareness is the sole existent, from which all seeming phenomena derive their appearance.

theories.name: Theise’s and Kafatos’s Fundamental Awareness and Complexity
theories.summary: The Fundamental Awareness Theory is a metaphysical framework that challenges conventional scientific materialism by positing consciousness, not matter, as the fundamental ontological reality of the universe. In this theory, awareness is not an emergent property of complex systems (like the human brain), but rather a foundational aspect of all that exists, even a multiverse.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness is the fundamental reality; matter and mind are complementary expressions of one awareness.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Quantum physics and systems biology reveal a non-dual, interconnected reality where observer and observed are inseparable.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Living systems are self-organizing, relational processes participating in a universal field of awareness.

claims.title: Ethical Implication
claims.text: If all entities share in awareness, this calls for compassionate, ecological relationships with all beings.

theories.name: Vișan’s Self-Reference
theories.summary: Cosmin Vișan proposes that self-reference, looking-back-at-itself, is the foundation of the structure and of the qualities of phenomenal consciousness within an idealist worldview.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness is identical with self-reference, a fundamental “looking-back-at-itself” that generates all qualia.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Self-reference recursively includes and transcends itself, producing layered structures and meanings in experience.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Qualia qualities arise from their meanings, which emerge from how self-reference perceives itself in various forms.

claims.title: Philosophical Stance
claims.text: Reality consists only of self-reference and its forms; no external or third-person entities truly exist.

theories.name: Ward’s Personal Idealism: Souls as Embodied Agents Created by God
theories.summary: Philosopher-theologian Keith Ward's “personal idealism” integrates his philosophical convictions about consciousness and souls, idealism in Eastern traditions, and his Christian faith. it's a heady brew.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness is irreducible; the soul is an embodied subject created by God.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Mind and body are subject and object, inseparable but not reducible to physical facts.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Embodiment is essential to mentality; the world is a construct of perceptions and thoughts.

claims.title: Implication
claims.text: The soul is an agent of intellectual and moral action within God’s creation.

theories.name: Yetter-Chappell’s Non-Theistic Idealism
theories.summary: Philosopher Helen Yetter-Chappell’s theory of consciousness integrates epiphenomenalist dualism with a non-theistic form of idealism. Her work challenges conventional physicalist and non-physicalist perspectives by proposing that consciousness is both fundamental and causally inert, yet central to the fabric of reality, a counterintuitive combination. She does this by developing a new quasi-Berkeleyan realist idealism, which does not depend upon God to do the metaphysical heavy lifting. This non-theistic idealism requires a fresh approach to the persistence and stability of the physical world.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness is fundamental yet causally inert; reality is a vast unity of experience without a theistic basis.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Physical laws sustain stable perceptions via a unified, non-agentive field of consciousness.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Combines epiphenomenalist dualism with quasi-Berkeleyan idealism while removing God from the metaphysical framework.

claims.title: Implication
claims.text: Perceptions are direct overlaps with universal consciousness, preserving direct realist intuitions.

theories.name: Yogācāra's Mind-Only: How Store Consciousness Makes Experience Cohere Without External Objects
theories.summary: Yogācāra understands ordinary phenomenal consciousness as a dependently conditioned flow that presents itself in the dual form of an experiencing subject confronting an independently existing world, although this subject–object division is itself a cognitive construction. Its “consciousness-only” or “cognition-only” thesis holds, at minimum, that what is directly experienced consists entirely of appearances within cognition; on stronger interpretations, consciousness and its transformations constitute the sole ultimate basis of phenomenal reality.

theories.name: Boyd’s Emergent Information Theory
theories.summary: Emergent Information Theory (EIT) bridges the mind-body gap by proposing that the brain creates a “non-material mind” (as defined in an informational context) that is capable of influencing events in the physical body. As such, EIT can be considered as an alternative form of emergent dualism that unifies all biological and technological information systems.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness arises from non-physical informational structures generated by the brain, not from physical matter alone.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Hierarchical information patterns built from neuronal states exert top-down causal control over physical brain activity.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Introduces a non-material “information dimension” where consciousness and other emergent phenomena reside.

claims.title: Biological–Technological Link
claims.text: While both brains and computers process information, only biological systems self-organize to produce consciousness.

theories.name: Chalmers’s Double-Aspect Theory of Information
theories.summary: Chalmers proposed a “double-aspect theory of information,” which holds information as ontologically fundamental, and it offers what it states: Information with two aspects: a physical aspect and a phenomenal (or experiential) aspect.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Information is fundamental and has both a physical and an experiential aspect.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: The same information structure is realized physically in systems and phenomenally as subjective experience.

claims.title: Philosophical Roots
claims.text: Extends neutral monism, linking Spinoza’s and Russell’s ideas to a naturalistic dualism.

claims.title: Hard Problem Link
claims.text: Offers information as the “common currency” bridging physical processes and consciousness.

claims.title: Contingency
claims.text: Even if this theory fails, Chalmers’ broader naturalistic dualism could still hold via another mechanism.

theories.name: Critiques of Integrated Information Theory
theories.summary: IIT has its critics, of course, as should every scientific theory. Some like to highlight IIT's “anti-common sense” predictions imputing consciousness to objects and things that just do not in any way seem to be conscious. The early exchange between theoretical quantum computer scientist Scott Aaronson and Giulio Tononi is illuminating.

claims.title: Core Critique
claims.text: Critics argue IIT makes “anti-common sense” claims, attributing consciousness to unlikely objects.

claims.title: Pseudoscience Controversy
claims.text: An open letter from 124 scholars labeled IIT “pseudoscience,” sparking widespread debate.

claims.title: Methodological Concerns
claims.text: Opponents say IIT’s predictions aren’t meaningfully testable given current scientific tools.

claims.title: Defense & Counterpoint
claims.text: Supporters argue IIT states its assumptions clearly and addresses the physical basis of consciousness.

claims.title: Field-Wide Impact
claims.text: The dispute highlights deep philosophical divides in consciousness research and risks polarizing the field.

theories.name: Davies’s Hidden Web of Information
theories.summary: Physicist Paul Davies speculates that information may be a fundamental principle in understanding the nature of reality, including life and mind, and that our current physical theories may be incomplete without incorporating both information and consciousness in a radically new way. Davies has long taken consciousness seriously and has woven it into his broader inquiries into physics, cosmology, and the informational structure of the universe. His views on “hidden webs of information” and consciousness appear throughout his work.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Information may be more fundamental than matter or energy, shaping life, mind, and reality itself.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Consciousness could emerge from or interact with deep informational structures underlying physical law.

claims.title: Distinctive Idea
claims.text: Proposes a “middle layer” of informational causation between physics and biological complexity.

claims.title: Cosmic Role
claims.text: Conscious observers may influence the universe’s history, echoing Wheeler’s participatory anthropic principle.

claims.title: Philosophical Implication
claims.text: Suggests science itself begins in consciousness, making mind central to understanding the cosmos.

theories.name: Doyle’s Experience Recorder and Reproducer
theories.summary: “Information Philosopher” Bob Doyle proposes the “Experience Recorder and Reproducer (ERR)” as an information model for the mind. He says that the mind, like software, is immaterial information; a human being “is not a machine, the brain is not a computer, and the mind is not processing digital information.” His proposal is that “a minimal primitive mind would need only to ‘play back’ past experiences that resemble any part of current experience,” because “remembering past experiences has obvious relevance (survival value) for an organism.”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness arises from replaying past experiences—sensory and emotional—when current events resemble them.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Neural assemblies store experiences with linked emotions, which are re-presented as unified wholes.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: ERR solves the “binding problem” by storing sensory and emotional data already integrated.

claims.title: Information Duality
claims.text: Treats information as having both physical and phenomenal aspects, potentially linking brain and mind.

theories.name: Hoel’s Causal Emergence
theories.summary: Erik Hoel’s theory of consciousness centers on ‘causal emergence,’ the idea that macroscopic structures in the brain can have stronger or clearer causal power than their microscopic components and that consciousness arises where macro-level causal structure is maximized. “Consciousness is what it’s like for information to be causally emergent.”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness arises where macro-level causal structures have greater causal power than their micro-level parts.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Higher-scale brain patterns maximize “effective information,” giving them unique causal efficacy.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Experience occurs at the level where causal emergence peaks, often structured as a narrative mind.

claims.title: Critique of Reductionism
claims.text: Rejects the idea that neurons alone explain mind; emergent stories and meanings are causally real.

claims.title: Broader Implication
claims.text: Links consciousness, free will, and meaning to the “world behind the world” of emergent structures.

theories.name: Information Additional Theories
theories.summary: Information additional theories include William Dembski arguing that “informational realism,” understood properly, can dissolve the mind-body problem; Jaime Cardenas-Garcia linking consciousness with “infoautopoiesis” (i.e., the self-production of information); and Jesse Bettinger proposing a fundamental, information driven ontological process.

theories.name: Koch Compares Integrated Information Theory with Panpsychism
theories.summary: Neuroscientist Christof Koch states that Integrated Information Theory (IIT) shares many intuitions with panpsychism, in particular that “consciousness is an intrinsic fundamental property of reality, is graded, and can be found in small amounts in simple physical systems.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Koch says IIT shares panpsychism’s view that consciousness is intrinsic, graded, and widespread.

claims.title: How It Differs
claims.text: IIT specifies which systems are conscious and addresses panpsychism’s combination problem.

claims.title: Explanatory Strength
claims.text: IIT explains adaptive value, qualitative differences, and when aggregates form one conscious entity.

claims.title: Quantitative Link
claims.text: Koch argues IIT shows how measurable causal powers map to subjective experiences.

claims.title: Philosophical Stance
claims.text: While open to panpsychism’s appeal, Koch sees IIT as offering a stronger research framework.

theories.name: Langan’s Cognitive-Theoretic Model of the Universe
theories.summary: Independent thinker, autodidact Christopher Langan claims that what he calls the “Cognitive-Theoretic Model of the Universe” (CTMU) provides the logical framework of a true Theory of Everything. It explains the connection between mind and reality, and proves the existence of God [as defined], the soul, and an afterlife. It identifies CTMU’s relationship to consciousness as a reflexive identity describing self-awareness, and must inevitably define the reality of self-aware beings.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Reality is a self-contained, self-processing system uniting mind, matter, and meaning into one reflexive framework.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: A “self-simulation” language (telesis) generates and models reality from within, coupling the physical and mental.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Consciousness is a generic property of reality, with all minds nested within the eternal “mind of God.”

claims.title: Metaphysical Reach
claims.text: Claims to unify physics, logic, and spirituality, proving God’s existence and outlining moral consequences.

claims.title: Self-Creation Principle
claims.text: Reality necessarily generates itself from possibility alone, requiring nothing outside itself to exist.

theories.name: Levin’s Ingressing Minds from Platonic Space
theories.summary: The “Ingressing Minds from Platonic Space” framework proposes that phenomenal consciousness is not generated by brains as self-sufficient, wholly physical devices, but rather, like mathematical truth and biological form, "ingresses" into the physical world from a structured, non-physical "latent [Platonic] space" of patterns—a space that contains not only “low-agency patterns” such as facts about triangles and prime numbers but also high-agency cognitive patterns such as "kinds of minds."

theorists.name: Michael Levin
theorists.role: Developmental & synthetic biologist and philosopher of biology

theories.name: Moll’s Multitrack Consciousness Conjecture
theories.summary: A Multitrack Consciousness Conjecture (MCC) suggests a new structure for consciousness in time, aiming to resolve the paradox of our subjective experience of a privileged now that seems fundamentally at odds with the physical model of block time (also known as the block universe).

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Each conscious self exists on its own track in time, experiencing a unique now within the block universe.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: These tracks are isolated in spacetime, with no cross-access—each one feels present only in its own moment.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Explains our sense of now without denying block time; uses its structure to ground temporal experience.

claims.title: Philosophical Impact
claims.text: Makes eternalist physics and our felt experience of time compatible, resolving the privileged now paradox.

theories.name: Resch’s Platonic Functionalism
theories.summary: Consciousness, reality, and computation are deeply integrated at a fundamental level. In philosophy of mind, functionalism says it's how a mind works that matters, not what stuff it's made of. In philosophy of mathematics, Platonism says that mathematical objects have an independent existence. Functionalism and Platonism are both leading theories in their respective fields, but when they are taken together, something extraordinary happens.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness depends only on functional organization, and all possible computations exist as real entities.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Functionalism’s substrate-independence plus Platonism’s real mathematics imply every computation—and mind—exists.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Physical reality emerges from computation, making minds and worlds Platonic structures with lawful order.

claims.title: Empirical Support
claims.text: Computational models from multiple researchers predict quantum, relativistic, and thermodynamic laws.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Suggests we may be computational “doppelgängers” in a mathematical universe, erasing the need for separate matter.

theories.name: Safron’s Integrated World Modeling Theory
theories.summary: The “Integrated World Modeling Theory” (IWMT) combines multiple theories into a unified model of consciousness to account for core aspects of phenomenology across computational/functional, algorithmic, and implementational/mechanistic (supervenient) levels of analysis.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Phenomenal consciousness is what it is like to be the spatiotemporally and causally coherent functioning of probabilistic generative model for the (valenced, affectively biased) sensoriums of embodied–embedded agents, entailing either perception or imagination when respectively coupled to or decoupled from sense-data.

claims.title: How It Works
