claims.text: IWMT draws upon both Integration Information Theory, Global Neuronal Workspace, and Predictive Processing theories, to describe how subnetworks of the brain can act as shared latent (work)spaces amongst heterogeneous sensory modalities, and arenas for Bayesian model selection, generating system-world estimates with sufficient rapidity to both inform and be informed by action-perception cycles, so affording more flexible adaptive behavior.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: IWMT is distinct from the theories it attempts to integrate in suggesting that no theory taken in isolation is capable of identifying sufficient conditions for explaining why there should be "something that it feels like" to be a physical/computational system.

claims.title: Empirical Support
claims.text: IWMT draws upon details of functional neuroanatomy in suggesting computational/algorithmic interpretations for mechanistic processes (e.g. the roles of neural synchrony, the brain's "rich club" organization whereby modules can be organized into a workspace architecture, etc.).

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Further developments in this theory may allow for sufficiently precise specifications of physical/computational substrates of consciousness in biological systems, so that they may be more skillfully understood and intervened upon, and potentially developed by artificial means.

theories.name: Tononi’s Integrated Information Theory
theories.summary: Integrated Information Theory (IIT), developed by neuroscientist Giulio Tononi and supported by neuroscientist Christof Koch, is an original, indeed radical, model that states what experience is and what types of physical systems can have it. IIT is grounded in experience, the phenomenology of consciousness, and it features mathematical description, quantitative measurement, scientific testability, broad applications, and nonpareil, intrinsic, cause-effect “structures.” In other words, “IIT addresses the problem of consciousness starting from phenomenology—the existence of my own experience, which is immediate and indubitable—rather than from the behavioral, functional, or neural correlates of experience.” Controversial to be sure, IIT has become a leading theory of consciousness.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness is identical to a maximally integrated cause–effect structure (“Φ-structure”) in physical systems.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Starts from universal properties of experience, formalizes them into physical postulates, and measures integration as Φ.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Treats consciousness as an intrinsic structural property of reality, not as a function or computation.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Offers a measurable test for consciousness, predicts brain regions involved, and claims true free will is possible.

claims.title: Challenges & Tensions
claims.text: Sufficiency of Φ for consciousness is disputed; critics question empirical support and ontological claims.

theories.name: Agüera y Arcas’s Computational Functionalism
theories.summary: Agüera y Arcas's “computational functionalism” exemplifies the theory of consciousness widely accepted in AI communities and other scientific disciplines: consciousness is simply an emergent function of the right kinds of computations.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness emerges from the right kinds of computations, as a natural function of life and intelligence.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Life is a self-constructing computational process; brains build predictive models, using sensory input as error correction, enabling modeling of self and others.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Theory of mind is the origin and mechanism of consciousness, evolving from a social “arms race” that drove self-reflection and the sense of self.

claims.title: Broader View
claims.text: Rejects dualism and the “hard problem” as illusions; consciousness is relational, distributed, and rooted in the computational nature of living systems.

theories.name: Awret’s Holographic Correspondence Theory of Consciousness
theories.summary: The ‘holographic principle’ of quantum gravity offers the possibility of “an admittedly very strange, single physical mechanism that can provide novel insights to many of the problems that bedevil our theories of consciousness,” especially how mental states of the mind are in some sense identical to physical states of the brain. That’s why, “we need a physics in which things that seem completely different are in some sense identical.”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness arises from a holographic duality, where mental states correspond to entangled physical states.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Like spacetime in AdS/CFT, consciousness may emerge from boundary-level quantum entanglement patterns in the brain.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Replaces metaphysical puzzles with “strange physics,” offering a naturalist explanation using quantum gravity tools.

claims.title: Philosophical Payoff
claims.text: Aims to resolve structural mismatch, mental causation, and conceivability arguments without abandoning physicalism.

claims.title: Open Question
claims.text: Can quantum entanglement in the brain persist long enough—and at sufficient scale—to support this correspondence?

theories.name: Bitar’s Architectural Theory of Consciousness
theories.summary: Philip Bitar proposes an architectural theory of consciousness (ATC) in which the structure of the mind is the basis for explaining consciousness.

claims.title: Structure of the mind
claims.text: Survival requires a parallel processing unit (a PPU) to maximize the response rate of the body. Survival also requires a serial-processing unit (an SPU) to centrally manage the body.

claims.title: Materialism
claims.text: Mental activity seems immaterial because it is private — not directly observable by our sensory systems. But assuming immateriality adds unnecessary complexity to a theory of the mind.

claims.title: Conscious vs. unconscious
claims.text: Operations of the SPU — the volitional unit — are conscious and are directly intentional, while operations of the PPU — the automatic unit — are unconscious and are not directly intentional.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Explains the mind in materialist terms that are consistent with mainstream science, thereby solving the mind-body problem. Explains the rationale for inferring that lower animals have minds but that computers do not.

claims.title: Consciousness
claims.text: Consciousness is nothing more than the subjective concept that we use to characterize the nature of information as represented by the volitional unit.

theories.name: Blums’ Conscious Turing Machine
theories.summary: The Blums contend that a machine capable of interacting with its environment through input sensors and output actuators, constructing internal models of its world, and viewing these models as being the world is the basis for its consciousness, both access and phenomenal. In their view, addressing the Hard Problem of consciousness reduces to demonstrating that subjective experience is computational in nature.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness is a computational process that can be modeled by a machine with internal world models.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Conscious awareness arises when all processors in the machine attend to and inspect globally broadcasted information.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Subjective experience is formalized as a function of internal model-building and synchronized inspection of data chunks.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: If correct, this theory suggests that machine consciousness is not only possible, but inevitable.

claims.title: Challenges & Tensions
claims.text: Critics may question whether formal definitions and symbolic processing can truly capture felt experience.

theories.name: Bostrom’s Computational Functionalism
theories.summary: Philosopher-futurist Nick Bostrom espouses a computational functionalism theory of consciousness, which is consistent with his view that there is a distinct possibility that our world and universe, our total state of affairs, is a computer simulation.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness arises from computational processes, regardless of the physical material they're built from.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Mental states are defined by what they do, not what they’re made of—software, not hardware, matters.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: If we’re in a simulation, then consciousness must be computable and substrate-independent.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Consciousness may come in degrees and help determine moral status and observer-based reasoning.

claims.title: Raises the Question
claims.text: If consciousness is computational, can artificial minds be conscious—and should they have rights?

theories.name: Complex Adaptive Systems Models
theories.summary: A complex adaptive system (CAS) is a dynamic network of interactions whose collective behavior may not be predictable from its component behaviors and that can “adapt” or alter its individual and collective behavior, creating novelties.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness is an emergent property of the brain as a complex adaptive system (CAS).

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: The brain adapts through nonlinear, self-organizing interactions across many levels of structure.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Consciousness shares CAS traits: unpredictability, recursion, history-dependence, and open boundaries.

theories.name: Computational Theories
theories.summary: Computational theories of mind developed organically as the processing power of computers expanded exponentially to enable the emulation of mind-like capabilities such as memory, knowledge structure, perception, decision-making, problem solving, reasoning and linguistic comprehension (especially with the advent of human-like large language models like ChatGPT). The growing field of cognitive science owes its development to computational theories.

claims.title: Core Concepts
claims.text: Sees mind as an information-processing system, modeled on algorithms, computation, and AI architectures.

claims.title: Scientific Context
claims.text: Draws from functionalism, neural networks, computational neuroscience, and AI research into reasoning, perception, and learning.

claims.title: Why Meaningful
claims.text: Offers a framework for simulating cognitive processes, potentially informing both neuroscience and machine consciousness design.

claims.title: Major Challenges
claims.text: Lacks a method to detect phenomenal consciousness in machines; risks overextending analogies between mind and current tech.

theories.name: Critical Brain Hypothesis
theories.summary: According to biophysicist John Beggs, the Critical Brain Hypothesis “suggests that neural networks do their best work when connections are not too weak or too strong.”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: The brain works best when its neural activity hovers near a “critical point” between order and chaos.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Neural networks self-organize at this balance point, maximizing information flow, storage, and flexibility.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Like a sandpile triggering avalanches, brain activity follows power laws at criticality.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Consciousness may emerge from this dynamic balance, optimizing awareness and adaptability.

claims.title: Challenges & Tensions
claims.text: It's unclear how brains stay tuned to criticality or distinguish it from mere random noise.

theories.name: Dennett’s Multiple Drafts Model
theories.summary: In his intellectual memoirs, I've Been Thinking, philosopher Daniel Dennett highlights two fundamental questions on which his career is founded—the two related philosophical problems he set himself to solve. “First, how can it be that some complicated clumps of molecules can be properly described as having states or events that are about something, that have meaning or content.”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness is not a unified stream but a competition among parallel brain processes for temporary dominance.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Different brain modules draft interpretations; one becomes “famous” by winning attention and shaping the moment.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: There is no “inner observer” or central theater—just distributed processes editing a narrative on the fly.

claims.title: On Qualia
claims.text: What we call “qualia” are user illusions—real effects, but not mysterious, private mental properties.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: To understand consciousness, we must adopt a third-person scientific view, not rely on introspective intuition.

theories.name: Grossberg’s Adaptive Resonance Theory
theories.summary: To computational neuroscientist Stephen Grossberg, “all conscious states are resonant states.” The conscious brain is the resonant brain where attentive consciousness regulates actions that interact with learning, recognition, and prediction. Grossberg's idea is that the mind is an activity, not a thing; a verb, not a noun—it's what you do, not what you have or use.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness emerges when the brain enters a resonant state that integrates attention, learning, and prediction.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Bottom-up inputs match top-down expectations, creating a feedback loop that produces stable, resonant awareness.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Only resonant states involving feature-based representations (like color or shape) can become conscious.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Consciousness enables fast, stable learning in a changing world by marking meaningful, complete representations.

claims.title: Raises the Question
claims.text: Can artificial systems achieve resonance deep enough to support real conscious awareness?

theories.name: Jackendoff’s Intermediate-Level Cognitive Representations
theories.summary: Linguist/philosopher Ray Jackendoff presents an “intermediate-level cognitive representations” theory of consciousness as a cognitively and computationally grounded, representational theory that accounts for consciousness, not by locating it in specific brain structure (as in the neural correlates of consciousness), but by identifying which types of mental representations are accessible to consciousness and why. There is no “central observer,” no “Cartesian Theater.”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness happens at a middle layer of mental processing—not raw data or abstract thoughts.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: We experience representations like shapes, sounds, and spatial layouts—not the brain’s inputs or concepts.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Consciousness is tied to how information is formatted, not where it happens in the brain.

theories.name: Malinkovic and Aru’s Biological Computationalism
theories.summary: Biological computationalism postulates that the specific physical and energetic properties of biological substrates are constitutive of the computations capable of supporting consciousness. Biological systems support conscious processing because they (i) instantiate scale-inseparable, substrate-dependent multiscale processing as a metabolic optimisation strategy, and (ii) alongside discrete computations, they perform continuous-valued computations due to the very nature of the fluidic substrate from which they are composed.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness depends on biological computation where physical, energetic, and chemical properties are part of the computation itself.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: The brain computes through inseparable multiscale dynamics, combining discrete spikes with continuous fluid and field-based processes.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: In biology, the substrate is the algorithm; computation cannot be separated from its physical realization.

claims.title: Metabolic Shaping
claims.text: Severe energy constraints force the brain to optimize computation through coarse-graining and cross-scale integration.

claims.title: Digital
claims.text: Digital AI lacks consciousness because it separates hardware from computation and cannot replicate living, energy-bound dynamics.

theories.name: Markwell’s Process Identity Theory
theories.summary: “Process Identity Theory” proposes that conscious experience is identical to the brain’s recursive, temporally integrated, embodied self-modeling dynamics. This view extends classical mind–brain identity theories by identifying consciousness with ongoing dynamical activity rather than static neural states, much as weather arises from atmospheric dynamics.

theorists.name: J. Kevin Markwell
theorists.role: Flight Surgeon and Head and Neck Surgeon, US Navy

theories.name: Mathematical Theories
theories.summary: Mathematics can apply to consciousness in two ways. The first approach involves methods, models, and simulations that are increasingly rigorous and sophisticated, describing and explaining essential features and mechanisms of conscious experience, primarily its structure, level, content, and dynamics.

claims.title: Core Concept
claims.text: Consciousness can be modeled mathematically or even be fundamentally mathematical in nature.

claims.title: Approaches
claims.text: One treats math as a descriptive tool; the other makes math the ontological basis of mind.

claims.title: Applications
claims.text: Theories like Integrated Information Theory and the Free Energy Principle quantify structure, level, and content.

claims.title: Speculation
claims.text: Tegmark and Penrose argue consciousness is mathematics, not just represented by it.

claims.title: Key Challenge
claims.text: Whether math can capture subjective experience or only its measurable correlates remains unresolved.

theories.name: Mikkilineni and Michaels’s Emergent Optimization Process
theories.summary: Consciousness evolved in biological systems as a regulatory mechanism to manage the uncertainties of life. Consciousness, in this view, is an “emergent optimization process” situated at the intersection of material and mental structures, enabling life to navigate metastable states without succumbing to disorder.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness evolved as a regulatory process to manage uncertainty in complex, metastable biological systems.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: It integrates stored knowledge with real-time feedback to preserve coherence and enable adaptive survival.

claims.title: Scientific Context
claims.text: Combines General Theory of Information, evolutionary biology, and complex systems to model consciousness functionally.

claims.title: Distinguishing Ideas
claims.text: Frames consciousness as functional, not mysterious; proposes “Mindful Machines” as ethical, knowledge-driven successors.

claims.title: Why Meaningful
claims.text: Links life and death as genomic processes; urges morally guided AI development grounded in biological principles.

theories.name: Minsky’s Society of Mind
theories.summary: Artificial intelligence pioneer Marvin Minsky calls the multiple semi-independent modules in the human mind, generated by physically locatable modules in the human brain, The Society of Mind (not coincidentally the name of his book). It is a model of human cognition constructed, step by step, from the nonconscious interactions of simple mindless elements he calls “agents.”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: The mind is made up of many simple, mindless “agents” working together like a society to produce cognition.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Nonconscious agents interact across layers, forming semi-independent modules that build complex mental functions.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: There's no single “self” or control center—just a decentralized network of specialized mental components.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Understanding thought requires high-level models, not low-level neuron behavior—like grasping software, not transistors.

claims.title: Raises the Question
claims.text: If no part of the brain knows everything, where does our sense of unified self come from?

theories.name: O'Reilly-Shah's State Space Theory and Computational Dynamic Monism
theories.summary: State Space Theory (SST) proposes that phenomenal consciousness arises from hierarchical delay coordinate embedding (DCE) in plastic recurrent neural networks, in which the brain reconstructs the dynamical history of its own states and its environment through recurrent feedback. The accompanying metaphysical framework, Computational Dynamic Monism (CDM), identifies consciousness with the temporally extended computational process itself, not with any static neural state, functional role, or intrinsic property of matter. The claim is that this dissolves the hard problem through identity rather than explanation

theories.name: Pribram’s Holonomic Brain Theory
theories.summary: Pribram’s holonomic approach relates phenomenal consciousness to distributed activity in synaptic and dendritic networks, modeled through holographic mathematics and Gabor analysis. Sensorimotor transformations help organize this activity into experienced objects, while a temporal-hold hypothesis associates awareness with delayed matching between incoming signals and established responses. Pribram also explored quantum mechanisms and neutral monism, neither of which follows simply from holographic coding. The framework offers hypotheses about the neural organization of experience, but does not establish why distributed processing possesses phenomenal character or uniquely distinguish conscious from unconscious processing.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Phenomenal consciousness depends on organized activity in synaptic and dendritic networks, described using the mathematics of holography.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Distributed neural activity encodes perceptual and memory information through wave-like relationships; prolonged processing of novel input is proposed to bring awareness.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Information is distributed within particular neural networks, with mathematical transformations linking spectral patterns to the spatial and temporal organization of experience.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Offers a framework for perceptual organization, associative memory, and partial recovery of information from damaged networks, while inviting reconsideration of the mind–matter relationship.

claims.title: Open Issues
claims.text: Evidence for dendritic processing does not establish holonomic consciousness. Proposed quantum mechanisms remain unconfirmed, and why the relevant neural organization produces subjective experience remains unresolved.

theories.name: Putnam’s Machine Functionalism
theories.summary: Functionalism is the theory that mental states are generated by their functional roles—i.e., by what they do rather than by what they are made of. Functionalism contends that all mental states (like sensations, beliefs, emotions) are defined by their causal roles or functional states of the system, such that what really matters is not the physical composition or structure of the brain, not the neurobiology, but the causal relations between inputs (stimuli), internal states, and outputs (behavior).

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Mental states are defined by what they do (their functions), not what they’re made of physically.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Consciousness results from input-output patterns and internal causal roles, like software running on hardware.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Minds can exist in many physical forms; brain structure doesn’t uniquely define mental states

claims.title: Challenges & Revisions
claims.text: Putnam later rejected strict functionalism for ignoring meaning, embodiment, and conscious experience.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Consciousness can’t be fully reduced to computation; it requires context, environment, and pragmatic understanding.

theories.name: Sejnowski’s Computational Two Tiers and Traveling Waves
theories.summary: Sejnowski’s theory of consciousness is a computational framework that focuses on the global dynamics of spiking neurons and traveling waves. He proposes that consciousness arises from a sophisticated, "two-tier" organizational structure within the cerebral cortex, where high-level cognition coexists with, but remains functionally distinct from, standard sensorimotor processing.

theorists.name: Terrence J. Sejnowski
theorists.role: Distinguished Professor, Pioneer of Computational Neurobiology

theories.name: Turing’s Imitation, Machine Thought, and the Hidden Mind
theories.summary: Turing offered no positive theory of phenomenal consciousness; instead, he transformed how machine mentality could be assessed. His 1936 universal machine establishes that computation is fixed by formal organization rather than physical medium, supplying the premise for multiple realizability. He acknowledged consciousness as mysterious but argued that its first-person privacy need not prevent rational attribution of thought to machines, proposing the imitation game as an evidential test of intelligent behavior. His computational framework, learning-machine proposals, and substrate-neutral conception of intelligence helped inspire machine functionalism, computational theories of mind, and artificial intelligence. Yet nothing in Turing establishes that computation or behavioral equivalence suffices for subjective experience. Contemporary AI-consciousness research therefore inherits his other-minds problem while supplementing behavior with architectural, cognitive, and mechanistic indicators.

theories.name: Wang’s Layered Architecture and Cognitive Informatics
theories.summary: Wang’s Layered Reference Model of the Brain treats consciousness as the highest-level, collectively organized state within a formal architecture of natural intelligence. Consciousness integrates information about the organism’s bodily and emotional condition, its external environment, and the relations between them, while depending on lower layers of sensation, memory, perception, action, homeostasis, unconscious processing, and subconscious processing.

theories.name: Ambron’s Local Field Potentials and Electromagnetic Waves
theories.summary: Biologist and pain researcher Richard Ambron suggests that understanding the specific consciousness of pain might help to understand the mechanism of consciousness in general.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness may arise from electromagnetic (EM) waves generated by local field potentials around neurons.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Pain signals transfer from action potentials to local EM waves, which may influence nearby brain circuits.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: EM waves could unify diverse sensory inputs, potentially solving the binding problem of consciousness.

claims.title: Testable Hypothesis
claims.text: Ambron claims his theory can be empirically tested, unlike many other consciousness theories.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Understanding pain’s EM signature might reveal a general mechanism for how consciousness emerges in the brain.

theories.name: Becker’s Analog Body Electric
theories.summary: Robert Becker’s bioelectric theory of consciousness proposes that phenomenal experience emerges not merely from discrete synaptic transmissions, but from continuous, slow direct-current (DC) electromagnetic fields generated by the perineural network involving glial and Schwann cells. He hypothesized that this primitive, brain-spanning analog electrical network regulates both physiological healing and cognitive states. Changes in these potentials correlated with wakefulness, sleep, anesthesia, hypnosis, and pain, suggesting that DC organization helps determine both whether consciousness is present and aspects of its contents. In this view, continuous spatial voltage gradients provide the unified physical substrate required to bind isolated sensory inputs into the singular, cohesive gestalt of phenomenal consciousness, positioning electromagnetism as the fundamental architect of subjective experience,

theories.name: Electromagnetic Field—Overview
theories.summary: Electromagnetic (EM) Field Theories treat minds as identical to, or derivative from, the broader, brain-spanning EM fields generated by the cumulative aggregate of multiple, specific neural currents. The brain is packed with an intricate three-dimensional web of these EM fields—the question is what functions do these EM fields serve (if any), and whether these fields in any way relate to consciousness?

claims.title: Core Concepts
claims.text: Consciousness arises from large-scale electromagnetic fields generated by synchronized neural activity and resonant physical processes.

claims.title: Scientific Context
claims.text: Empirical studies link EM field patterns, phase alignment, and brain-wide wave dynamics to cognitive processing and conscious states.

claims.title: Why Meaningful
claims.text: Proposes a physical, field-based substrate that can unify diverse neural activity into coherent, dynamic conscious experience.

claims.title: Panpsychist Extension
claims.text: General Resonance Theory adds that all matter has rudimentary consciousness, which combines through resonance into richer minds.

claims.title: Major Challenges
claims.text: It's unclear whether EM fields generate consciousness or merely reflect deeper processes; causal evidence remains limited.

theories.name: Ephaptic Coupling
theories.summary: An ephaptic coupling theory of consciousness leverages the idea that neurons, being electrogenic, produce electric fields, which, if sufficiently strong and precisely placed, can influence the electrical excitability of neighboring neurons near-instantaneously.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Neurons influence nearby neurons through electric fields, not just synapses.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Tiny brain-generated fields modulate excitability and synchronize activity across cells.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Consciousness may partly arise from local, non-synaptic electrical interactions.

theories.name: Fingelkurts and Fingelkurts’s Operational Architectonics
theories.summary: The Operational Architectonics (OA) framework of brain-mind functioning is a unified theoretical model that bridges neurophysiological processes and subjective mental experience. At its foundation lies the concept of the operation—a spatiotemporally bounded, functionally meaningful event that serves as a common denominator for both brain activity and phenomenological experience.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness arises from nested, dynamic patterns of brain-generated electromagnetic fields. The concept of the operation—a spatiotemporally bounded, functionally meaningful event that serves as a common denominator for both brain activity and phenomenological experience.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: EEG-detectable electromagnetic field patterns, called operational modules, bind sensory and cognitive content into unified moments. Widespread endogenous local fields generated by transient, functional neuronal assemblies.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: The brain and mind share a spatiotemporal structure, forming a functional isomorphism across levels.

claims.title: Emergence Framework
claims.text: Consciousness emerges at the operational level, bridging neurobiology and phenomenology without full reduction.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Offers EEG-based tools to assess altered or minimal consciousness in meditation, coma, and beyond.

theories.name: Hunt and Schooler’s General Resonance Theory
theories.summary: General Resonance Theory (GRT) proposes that consciousness arises from synchronized resonance across multiple scales of nature, with electromagnetic fields serving as the primary seat of consciousness rather than merely correlating with it. GRT bridges electromagnetic field theories with panpsychist foundations, offering a solution to panpsychism's combination problem of consciousness.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness arises from synchronized resonance across physical systems, especially in nested electromagnetic fields.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Resonance between brain/body fields enables phase transitions, creating unified, richer states of conscious experience.

claims.title: Panpsychist Foundation
claims.text: All matter has some level of consciousness; resonance allows simple experiences to combine into complex minds.

claims.title: Solves Combination Problem
claims.text: Explains how micro-conscious entities unite into macro-consciousness through shared rhythmic synchronization.

claims.title: Beyond Biology
claims.text: Suggests that artificial systems could host consciousness if they replicate the right resonant structures.

theories.name: Jones’s Electromagnetic Fields
theories.summary: Philosopher Mostyn Jones gathers, explains, and classifies various electromagnetic-field theories, each with its own theoretical foundation: computationalist, reductionist, dualist, realist, interactionist, epiphenomenalist, globalist, and localist. He uses three questions to classify the field theories: 1. How do minds exist relative to fields? 2. Are minds unified by global or local fields? 3. How extensively do fields and neurons interact?

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Minds may be brain-generated electromagnetic fields, not just products of neurons.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Field patterns unify conscious experience, potentially solving the binding problem better than neural circuits.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Proposes “neuroelectrical panpsychism”: consciousness arises by merging simple experiences via electrical activity.

claims.title: Theory Classification
claims.text: Jones maps field theories across eight models (e.g., realist, dualist, globalist) using three core questions.

claims.title: Open Question
claims.text: Can electromagnetic fields fully explain qualia, or is more than field integration needed?

theories.name: Lewis and MacGregor’s Phase of Energy Resonator Model
theories.summary: A phases of energy resonator model of consciousness is a two-way exchange of energy between the conscious mental realm and the physical realm of the brain—the mental and physical phases of energy are likened to the phases (e.g., gas/liquid) of matter—and a possible realization in the form of a generic resonator.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness involves a two-way energy exchange between mental and physical realms via resonant systems.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Brain activity generates mental states; mental states return influence through a novel “dispositional energy.”

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Consciousness is like a new phase of energy, akin to vapor rising from liquid, with causal power.

claims.title: Mechanism Proposal
claims.text: Resonator structures, possibly at astroglial–pyramidal interfaces, mediate this bidirectional energy flow.

claims.title: Raises the Question
claims.text: Can a new kind of energy—beyond known physics—explain mind–brain interaction without violating science?

theories.name: Llinás’s Mindness State of Oscillations
theories.summary: Neuroscientist Rodolfo Llinás’s theory of the “mindness state” is centered on the concept of oscillations. Many neurons possess electrical activity, manifested as oscillating variations in the minute voltages across the cell membrane.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness arises from synchronized neural oscillations across the brain.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Neurons resonate like cicadas, generating unified activity that gives rise to mind.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Reality is partly constructed—consciousness is a brain-generated “virtual reality.”

theories.name: McFadden’s Conscious Electromagnetic Information Theory
theories.summary: Molecular geneticist Johnjoe McFadden proposes conscious electromagnetic information (CEMI) field theory as an explanation of consciousness.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness arises from information encoded in the brain’s electromagnetic (EM) field—not from neurons.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: EM fields unify brain activity by integrating information in space, forming a conscious “gestalt.”

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Conscious EM fields don’t just mirror neural activity—they causally influence thoughts and actions.

claims.title: Challenges Neural Theories
claims.text: Neural correlates drift, but EM fields remain stable across trials, tracking conscious content better.

claims.title: Scientific Dualism
claims.text: Mind isn’t nonphysical—it’s energetic; a field-based property distinct from matter but still natural.

theories.name: Miller’s Brain Waves’ Analog Organization of Cortex
theories.summary: Cognition and consciousness emerge from the fast and flexible dynamic organization of the cortex produced by traveling brain waves performing analog computations. Consciousness is the tip of the iceberg of cognition and may be a natural outcome of analog computation. Consciousness is good for flexibility and planning, and for the kind of big-picture stuff that needs a unified representation. When the analog computations create brain wave patterns that are large enough to unify the cortex, you get consciousness.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness emerges when traveling brain waves analog-organize the cortex into a unified, flexible system.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Brain waves dynamically coordinate millions of neurons, using analog computations to organize information across the cortex.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Waves don’t just communicate information; they actively structure and control cortical processing in real time.

claims.title: Executive Control
claims.text: Alpha and beta waves impose goals on faster gamma activity, enabling top-down, goal-directed thought and behavior.

claims.title: Consciousness Link
claims.text: When wave patterns grow large and coordinated enough to unify the cortex, conscious experience naturally arises.

theories.name: Pockett’s Conscious and Non-Conscious Patterns
theories.summary: Psychologist Susan Pockett's electromagnetic field theory of consciousness proposes that “while conscious experiences are identical with certain electromagnetic patterns generated by the brain” have always been acknowledged, it is critical to “specify what might distinguish conscious patterns from non-conscious patterns … the 3D shape of electromagnetic fields that are conscious, as opposed to those that are not conscious.”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Conscious experiences are specific electromagnetic (EM) field patterns produced by the brain.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: The 3D shape of an EM field determines whether it’s associated with consciousness or not.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Consciousness isn’t a process—it’s a thing: a spatial EM pattern, separable from attention or cognition.

claims.title: Testable Hypothesis
claims.text: Conscious EM fields can, in principle, be identified and replicated—even in hardware.

theories.name: Singer and Melloni’s Large-Scale Synchrony
theories.summary: A biologically grounded account of consciousness centered on large-scale neuronal synchrony. Conceiving consciousness as an emergent process from a dynamical system, this theory reframes consciousness not as a function of isolated brain areas or fixed representational codes, but as an emergent, temporally structured phenomenon arising from transient synchronization across distributed neural assemblies in different brain areas.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness emerges from transient synchronization across distributed brain regions, not from any specific area.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Neurons across the brain synchronize in timing (especially in gamma and theta bands) to unify perception.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Consciousness is a dynamic, temporal coordination—not content or location based, but interaction based.

claims.title: Solves the Binding Problem
claims.text: Synchrony binds features like color and motion into unified experience without needing special neurons.

claims.title: Philosophical Shift
claims.text: Consciousness isn’t layered on top of brain activity—it is the brain’s large-scale synchrony in motion.

theories.name: Zhang’s Long-Distance Light-Speed Telecommunications
theories.summary: Synaptic neuroscientist Ping Zhang suggests that “the long-time puzzle between brain and mind” might be solved by “a light-speed telecommunication between remote cells that are arranged in parallel.”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness may rely on light-speed electrical fields that synchronize distant brain cells beyond synaptic transmission.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Action potentials create traveling electrical fields that link parallel neurons instantly, enabling rapid coordination.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Unlike slow synapses, these fields allow non-local, flexible, and ultra-fast brain communication.

claims.title: Raises the Question
claims.text: Could light-speed neural signaling be the missing link between brain activity and unified conscious experience?

theories.name: Blackmore’s “It’s All Models”
theories.summary: All mental models are conscious. These models all have ‘something it is like’ to be them, while bats, cats, and humans do not. If we ask, “What is it like to be a bat?”, we cannot answer. We cannot even be sure whether the bat (or dog, cat, robot, or even another human) is, or is not, conscious at all. On the other hand, if we ask, “What is it like to be the bat’s model of the world?” we can answer. The answer is that if that creature is building models of its world, then there is something it is like to be whatever those models describe—whatever they say it is like.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness doesn’t belong to brains or bodies, but to the mental models they build.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: All predictive models have “something it is like” to be them—experience is model-based, not self-based.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: There is no experiencer behind experience—only self-models that give the illusion of one.

claims.title: Research Shift
claims.text: Stop asking who is conscious; ask what models are being built and how they generate experience.

claims.title: Delusionism
claims.text: Consciousness is a compelling self-deception, a model mistaken for a metaphysical reality.

theories.name: Churchland’s Eliminative Materialism
theories.summary: Eliminative Materialism is the maximalist physicalist position that our common-sense view of the mind is misleading and that consciousness is a kind of illusion generated by the brain—a contingent, evolutionary, inner adaptation that enhanced fitness and reproductive success.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Our common-sense ideas of the mind are wrong; consciousness as we know it is likely an illusion.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Folk psychology will be replaced—not reduced—by a future neuroscience that better explains behavior.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Consciousness is a brain-generated construct, useful for survival, not a literal inner reality.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: If qualia are illusions, then selfhood, agency, and inner life must be reinterpreted scientifically.

claims.title: Challenges & Tensions
claims.text: Critics argue that denying subjective experience defies both intuition and direct evidence.

theories.name: Dennett’s Illusionism
theories.summary: Daniel Dennett's theory of consciousness is illusionist, and or even eliminativist, because he denies the existence of qualia as they are traditionally conceived—private, inner, felt experience, the non-physical building blocks of subjectivity. Instead, he argues that consciousness is not what it seems to be from the first-person perspective. "There are no qualia," he states.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness is not what it seems; qualia are illusions, not inner, non-physical realities.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: The brain produces a “user illusion” of experience through complex, unconscious processes.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Rejects traditional qualia entirely—there’s no private, ineffable mental essence to explain.

claims.title: Misunderstood View
claims.text: Dennett doesn’t deny experience exists; he denies it exists as people think it does.

claims.title: Philosophical Impact
claims.text: Sparked the illusionist movement by challenging the very reality of felt experience.

theories.name: Feyerabend's Revisable, Disposable Mind
theories.summary: Feyerabend’s early philosophy of mind argues that phenomenal consciousness may be real as lived experience while our ordinary mental concepts—pain, sensation, thought, image, feeling—may not reveal its ultimate ontology. He challenged the idea that introspective certainty proves the existence of irreducibly mental properties and helped establish eliminative materialism by suggesting that mature neuroscience might replace, rather than reduce, common-sense psychological categories. Yet Feyerabend did not consistently endorse eliminativism as settled truth. His later pluralism resisted granting scientific-materialist language exclusive authority. His enduring contribution is methodological: theories of consciousness should remain open to radical conceptual revision without denying the reality of experience.

theories.name: Frankish’s Illusionism
theories.summary: “Illusionism” is a term coined by the philosopher Keith Frankish for a revisionary view of consciousness, which builds on earlier work on qualia eliminativism (notably that of Daniel Dennett). The key idea is that consciousness, though real, is not what it seems. What we call 'phenomenal consciousness' is a brain-generated impression, not an intrinsic metaphysical feature of the mind. While not denying that conscious experiences are real, Frankish argues that the mysterious “phenomenal properties” or “qualia” often ascribed to them are, in fact, an introspective illusion.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness is real but not what it seems. Conscious experiences are real, but we are wrong to believe that they possess irreducibly subjective “phenomenal properties” or “qualia.” Their phenomenal qualities are illusions—brain-generated impressions, not intrinsic mental properties.

claims.title: Represented but not instantiated
claims.text: The phenomenal properties of consciousness are merely intentional objects, similar to impossible objects, which can be represented but not instantiated.

claims.title: Functional not phenomenal
claims.text: The distinctive properties of conscious experiences are functional (“quasi-phenomenal”) ones. Consciousness is a complex, multifaceted functional state, which supports a rich sensory engagement with the environment.

claims.title: Introspective distortion
claims.text: Introspective processes create a simplified, schematic model of our psychological responses to stimulation, which we mistake for direct apprehension of subjective qualities.

claims.title: Economical
claims.text: Illusionism is an explanatorily economical strategy, which avoids the need for radical revisions to our scientific worldview and avoids the threat of epiphenomenalism.

claims.title: A more inclusive ethical framework
claims.text: By removing imaginary metaphysical barriers to understanding other minds and moving beyond a binary view of consciousness, illusionism encourages us to study and appreciate the rich variety of conscious experience across the natural world.

theories.name: Graziano’s Attention Schema Theory
theories.summary: Advanced by neuroscientist Michael Graziano, attention schema theory asserts that for the brain to handle a profusion of information, it must have developed a quick and dirty model, a simplified version of itself, which it then reports “as a ghostly, non-physical essence, a magical ability to mentally possess items.”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness is the brain’s internal model of attention, not a mysterious essence.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: The brain builds a simplified “attention schema” to monitor and control its own focus.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: This self-model feels like a ghostly inner self—but it’s a useful, evolved illusion.

theories.name: Humphrey’s Magical-Compelling User Illusion
theories.summary: Nicholas Humphrey’s theory of consciousness is a form of illusionism and compatible with eliminativism, because phenomenal consciousness—what it's like to feel inner experience—is not what it seems to be. Rather than revealing a deep metaphysical reality, consciousness is a user-illusion evolved to enhance our survival. He says, “Phenomenal consciousness is a magical mystery show that the brain lays on for itself.”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness is an evolved illusion—an inner show that feels real but isn’t what it seems.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: The brain creates a rich self-model that simulates qualia, but no intrinsic properties exist.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Consciousness is “performance art” for the self—adaptive, enchanting, and misleading.

claims.title: Evolutionary Function
claims.text: The illusion boosts survival by enhancing self-worth, social bonding, and meaning.

claims.title: Ontological Stance
claims.text: There are no qualia—just compelling representations that trick us into believing in them.

theories.name: Irvine’s Scientific Eliminativism
theories.summary: Scientific eliminativism claims that consciousness does not exist and/or that talk of consciousness should be eliminated from science. These are strong positions to take, and require serious defense.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness may not exist as a unified phenomenon and should possibly be dropped from science.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Consciousness is likely a cluster of capacities, not a single natural kind with clear scientific boundaries.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Introspective reports are unreliable; science should prioritize measurable, operational definitions.

claims.title: Research Strategy
claims.text: Replace metaphysical speculation with empirical, pluralistic methods grounded in cognitive science.

theories.name: Kammerer’s Introspective Illusionism
theories.summary: Philosopher François Kammerer defends an illusionist conception of phenomenal consciousness, according to which phenomenal consciousness does not exist but simply seems to exist. He thinks that such a conception defends physicalism better than other more standard versions of physicalism.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Phenomenal consciousness doesn’t exist—only the illusion of it does, created by introspective misrepresentation.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: We form beliefs about inner experience using flawed introspective concepts shaped by a “naïve” theory of mind.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: The illusion feels real because we treat our introspective access as epistemologically special.

claims.title: Defense of Physicalism
claims.text: Illusionism offers the strongest response to anti-physicalist arguments by denying their key assumption.

claims.title: Challenges & Tensions
claims.text: Intuition rebels against illusionism—but that resistance itself may be part of the illusion.

theories.name: Mandik’s Qualia Quietism
theories.summary: ‘Qualia quietism’ to support an anti-realist theory of consciousness, labeled ‘neurofunctionalism,’ which integrates representationalism, self-representationalism, and neurobiological realism, aiming to naturalize phenomenal consciousness by tying it to brain-based representational structures. This is a naturalistic theory: phenomenal states are real, physical states in the brain with both causal powers and intentional content.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness is real and physical, but talk of "qualia" adds confusion rather than clarity.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Conscious states are brain-based representational states with self-representing structures—no special inner glow.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Avoids both realism and eliminativism about qualia by treating the term as conceptually empty.

claims.title: Key Argument
claims.text: The concept of qualia is circular, chaotic, and unnecessary—better replaced by precise alternatives.

claims.title: Neurofunctionalist View
claims.text: Consciousness arises from neural processes that both represent and reflexively model themselves.

theories.name: Ostendorf’s Predictive, Pattern-Driven Interface
theories.summary: Consciousness is a recursive illusion: a simulated interface generated by a pattern-completion machine built for survival—not for truth. Consciousness is the byproduct of sensory data, memory that enables prediction, and a persistent self-narrative.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness is a recursive illusion—an adaptive simulation, not a real inner self or causal force.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Sensory data, predictive memory, and self-narrating language combine to generate the illusion of experience.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: The brain’s goal is survival, not truth; consciousness is a compressed, biased interface.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: There is no true agent or self—only post-hoc narration over pre-programmed neural outputs.

theories.name: Ryle’s Category-Dissolution of Inner-Theater Consciousness
theories.summary: Ryle’s theory of consciousness is a conceptual, ordinary-language critique of the Cartesian picture that consciousness is an inner private theatre inhabited by mental episodes, qualia, images, volitions, and acts of introspection. He offers not a theory of phenomenal consciousness but a diagnosis of why the demand for one is malformed. His argument is that Cartesian dualism—"the dogma of the Ghost in the Machine"—rests on a category mistake: it treats mental predicates as naming occult inner episodes belonging to the same logical type as bodily events. Consciousness is not a private theater illuminated by an inner eye but an adverbial feature of intelligent performance;

theories.name: Enactivism
theories.summary: Enactivism is the way of thinking that to explore mental activities, one must examine living systems interacting with their environments, agents bringing forth a mental world through embodied, sensorimotor coupling with the physical world. Cognition is characterized, not by representations in the brain, but by embodied activities and organisms-environment dynamics. A mind without a body would be as if incoherent.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Minds arise through dynamic interactions between living bodies and their environments.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Cognition is not passive reception but active, embodied engagement with the world.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Mental activity is inseparable from sensorimotor interaction; no body, no mind.

theories.name: Frank/Gleiser/Thompson’s “The Blind Spot”
theories.summary: Astrophysicist Adam Frank, theoretical physicist Marcello Gleiser, and philosopher Evan Thompson elevate and promote “the primacy of consciousness” in that “There is no way to step outside consciousness and measure it against something else. Everything we investigate, including consciousness and its relation to the brain, resides within the horizon of consciousness.”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness is the inescapable condition of knowing; we can't step outside it to explain it.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Consciousness and embodiment form a “strange loop” that science typically overlooks or denies.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: The “hard problem” is an illusion caused by ignoring the primacy of lived experience.

claims.title: Challenges Standard Views
claims.text: Rejects both reductionism and dualism as caught inside the “Blind Spot” worldview.

claims.title: Proposed Approach
claims.text: Calls for a science grounded in experience itself, via neurophenomenology and embodied methods.

theorists.name: Marcello Gleiser
theorists.role: Professor of Natural Philosophy, Physics & Astronomy

theories.name: Froese’s Irruption Theory
theories.summary: Irruption Theory of consciousness takes phenomenology to be dynamically relevant, yet thermodynamically non-reductive, treating the subjective mind as a causally efficacious “black box” that makes a measurable difference in the living body. Subjective states are not an epiphenomenon, but a distinct aspect of reality that interacts with measurable matter through specific entropy exchanges: intentions “irrupt” into bodily dynamics as deviations that initiate action, and lived experience “absorbs” physiological variations into perceptual awareness.

theories.name: Gefter’s Enactive-QBist Engagement
theories.summary: Amanda Gefter’s theory of consciousness unifies QBist physics with enactive cognitive science. Qbism is a quantum-Bayesian interpretation that treats quantum theory as a normative ‘user’s manual’ for agents in a participatory universe. Enactivism is the adaptive, embodied cognitive science framework in which cognition is the enactment of a subject–object boundary through ongoing sensorimotor engagement with the environment. Taken together, they offer the possibility of a unified metaphysics—one that brings subject and object, mind and world, back together again.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness arises from the participatory co-creation of subject and object, where agents and worlds are enacted together through interaction.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: QBism explains how the world is constituted through agent–system interactions; enactivism explains how agents arise through organism–environment engagement. Combined, they describe a dynamic, bidirectional process of mutual enactment.

claims.title: Scientific Context
claims.text: Bridges quantum Bayesianism and enactive cognitive science, offering a unified metaphysics that grounds physics and mind in participatory, relational terms.

claims.title: Distinguishing Ideas
claims.text: Rejects the absolute subject–object divide; emphasizes anti-representationalism, second-person primacy, and normativity in both physics and cognition.

claims.title: Why Meaningful
claims.text: Proposes a post-Cartesian metaphysics where agency, meaning, and reality are inseparable from the acts that bring them forth—reuniting self and world.

theories.name: Gibson’s Ecological Psychology
theories.summary: Experimental psychologist James J. Gibson proposes an “embodied, situated, and non-representational” approach to perception (which, while not a surrogate for phenomenal consciousness, has features in common). Gibson attacks both behaviorism and cognitivism (e.g., information processing), arguing for direct perception and direct realism.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Perception is direct and action-guided, not based on internal representations or processing.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Organisms detect real-world information (invariants) through active engagement with their environment.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Introduces “affordances”—action possibilities the environment offers relative to the perceiver.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Shifts the unit of analysis to the organism-environment system, aligning with embodied views of mind.

claims.title: Raises the Question
claims.text: If we perceive affordances, not properties, what exactly is the content of conscious experience?

theories.name: Hurley’s Sensorimotor Loops and Embodied Interaction
theories.summary: Perception and action are not just inputs and outputs but dynamically interwoven components of cognition. Thus, consciousness is not merely the result of internal representations processed in isolation but emerges from sensorimotor loops between perception and action and embodied interaction with the world.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness arises from dynamic loops between perception and action, not isolated brain activity.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Perception and action continuously influence each other through real-time feedback with the environment.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Rejects the “input-output sandwich” model; sees mind as embodied, embedded, and interactive.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Consciousness may extend beyond the brain, involving body and world in its very structure.

claims.title: Raises the Question
claims.text: If perception and action co-constitute consciousness, where exactly does the mind stop?

theories.name: Lakoff and Johnson’s Embodied Realism and Embodied Mind
theories.summary: Embodied realism is the view that the mind is inherently embodied: we think with a brain that evolved to run a body, and so every concept—even color—is shaped by our sensorimotor makeup rather than read off a mind-independent world. On this account, phenomenal consciousness is real and neurally grounded, but that its experienced contents, categories, unity, imagery, affective salience, and conceptual articulation arise through the embodied brain’s interaction with the world, structured by unconscious frames, image schemas, and metaphorical mappings rather than by disembodied reason, direct access to reality “in itself,” or a separable mental substance.

theories.name: Noë’s “Out of Our Heads” Theory
theories.summary: Philosopher Alva Noë argues that only externalism about the mind and mental content, which requires active and continuous engagement between the brain and its environment, body and beyond, can succeed as a theory of consciousness.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness is not in the brain alone; it emerges from dynamic engagement with the world.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Consciousness arises through active bodily interaction with our environment, not internal processes alone.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Consciousness is a kind of skilled activity—like dancing—not something the brain simply produces.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Shifting consciousness “outside our heads” reframes neuroscience’s goals and limitations.

claims.title: Raises the Question
claims.text: Can brain-based models ever fully explain a phenomenon that depends on world-involving activity?

theories.name: Pretel-Wilson’s Human Systems Theory
theories.summary: Understanding human systems requires discovering “an anatomy of the universe that does away with the mind-body dualism” and replacing it with “the spatial and temporal dualities that constitute everything that exists from the ground up.” Thus, consciousness becomes superseded by the actual-possibility duality intrinsic to human systems that avoids postulating a “collective person” with a consciousness of its own or an “artificial man” without its own purpose.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness is replaced by a deeper duality: actual vs. possible states within human systems.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Human beings shape the world through shared systems grounded in spatial and temporal dualities.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Rejects mind-body dualism; reframes human nature as inherently world-shaping, not merely thinking.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Consciousness becomes unnecessary as a core concept for explaining human experience or agency.

claims.title: Raises the Question
claims.text: If consciousness is redundant, what anchors subjective experience in this systems framework?

theories.name: Shanahan’s Embodied Insights from Disembodied Minds
theories.summary: Murray Shanahan explores the conceptual boundaries of consciousness by examining the plausibility and coherence of disembodied ‘minds’—in particular, AI/LLMs in computers—‘minds’ that exist without bodies or sensory interaction with the physical world, and in doing so, he assumes and supports an embodied and enactive understanding of biological consciousness, where cognition is inseparable from embodiment.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness is deeply tied to embodiment; disembodied minds may be conceptually incoherent.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Cognition arises from brain–body–world interactions, not from computation alone.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Disembodied AI challenges the limits of our concepts of time, self, and mind.

claims.title: Raises the Question
claims.text: Can a conscious mind exist without a body, world, or social embeddedness?

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Exploring “minds without bodies” reveals the boundaries and blind spots of human-centered intuitions.

theories.name: Thompson’s Mind in Life
theories.summary: Philosopher Evan Thompson heralds “the deep continuity of life and mind.” His foundational idea is “Where there is life there is mind, and mind in its most articulated forms belongs to life,” and his organizing principle is “Life and mind share a core set of formal or organizational properties, and the formal or organizational properties distinctive of mind are an enriched version of those fundamental to life.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Mind is continuous with life; consciousness emerges from life’s self-organizing, bodily processes

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Consciousness arises from the same dynamic, embodied patterns that make living systems autonomous.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Life and mind are not separate domains but share deep structural and functional roots.

claims.title: Phenomenology’s Role
claims.text: Lived experience helps guide and shape scientific inquiry into consciousness.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Bridges biology and subjectivity, aiming to dissolve the “hard problem” by reframing it.

theories.name: Vucolova’s Collapse into Translation
theories.summary: Consciousness is an emergent, embodied, energy-driven phenomenon. It is unified in principle, diverse in implementation, and fully grounded in physical processes. It emerges from sensory–motor interactions between an organism and its environment, mediated through embodied brain–body dynamics. It arises from the collapse of both first-order perceptual states and higher-order symbolic states that enable the translation of physical stimuli into symbolic representations, thereby creating subjective awareness.

theories.name: Carruthers’s First-Order Representationalism
theories.summary: Peter Carruthers’s theory of consciousness is a first-order theory because it holds that conscious experience arises directly from non-meta-representational, first-order perceptual states—that is, from representations of the world, rather than from representations of those representations (which are central to higher-order theories).

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness arises from first-order perceptual states that represent the world, not from meta-representations.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: A mental state becomes conscious when it’s globally broadcast and available to guide thought, speech, or action.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Carruthers rejects higher-order awareness as necessary; consciousness needs no inner monitoring or self-representation.

claims.title: Evolving View
claims.text: He once critiqued first-order theories, but later reversed position, affirming their strength over higher-order models.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Supports a parsimonious, brain-based model where global availability—not introspection—marks a state as conscious.

theories.name: Direct Perception Theory
theories.summary: Direct Perception Theory is the idea that “the information required for perception is external to the observer; that is, one can directly perceive an object based on the properties of the distal stimulus alone, unaided by inference, memories, the construction of representations, or the influence of other cognitive processes.” Philosopher Ned Block describes non-mainstream views of phenomenal consciousness that take it to work via this kind of “a direct awareness relation to a peculiar entity like a sense datum [i.e., that which is immediately available to the senses] or to objects or properties in the environment.”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: We perceive the world directly, without relying on mental representations or internal processing.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Perception is an immediate relation to external objects, based solely on their physical properties.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: The phenomenal feel of an experience depends on the actual object perceived—not just brain activity.

theories.name: Dretske’s Information and Representationalism
theories.summary: Philosopher Fred Dretske's theory of consciousness centers around the informational and representational nature of mental states and a naturalistic account of intentionality, all within a scientific, materialistic framework. Dretske's representational theory is considered a first-order theory because it holds that conscious experiences consist in, or are identical to, certain kinds of first-order mental representations—that is, representations of the external world, not of other mental states.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness consists in first-order mental representations of the external world, shaped by information use.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: A brain state becomes conscious when it carries information and is poised to guide reasoning or behavior.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: You’re not aware of representations themselves, but of what they represent—this is the “transparency” thesis.

claims.title: Naturalizing Qualia
claims.text: Qualia are just features of representational states, not mysterious inner properties.

claims.title: Challenges & Tensions
claims.text: Critics question whether this fully explains the subjective feel—the “what-it’s-like”—of experience.

theories.name: First-Order—Overview
theories.summary: First-order representationalism (FOR) seeks to account for consciousness in terms of, or by reducing to, external, world-directed (or first-order) intentional states. In other words, consciousness can be explained, primarily, by understanding how the directedness of our mental states at objects and states of affairs in the world is generated directly by those objects and states of affairs.

claims.title: Core Concepts
claims.text: First-order representationalism explains consciousness via direct, world-focused mental representations without requiring higher-order awareness.

claims.title: Scientific Context
claims.text: Links conscious states to sensory cortical and thalamic activity, emphasizing representational content over metacognitive processes.

claims.title: Why Meaningful
claims.text: Offers a content-based account of phenomenal experience that may align closely with specific neural states.

claims.title: Major Challenges
claims.text: Must explain cases where neural representation exists without corresponding conscious experience, and address critiques from higher-order theories.

theories.name: Hill's Representationalism: Qualia’s Appearance and Reality
theories.summary: Hill’s mature theory holds that phenomenal consciousness is fundamentally representational, including introspective awareness of qualitative states such as pain: whenever a subject is aware of something, the subject is in a mental state that represents it. Experiential awareness of qualia is typically nonconceptual, allowing experience to outrun linguistic and conceptual capacities. Because representations can succeed or fail, Hill extends the appearance/reality distinction even to qualia, thereby challenging claims that introspection reveals their intrinsic metaphysical nature. His account applies to vision, pain, emotion, and introspection and supports materialism without requiring his earlier type-identity theory. Its central difficulty is whether representational structure explains phenomenal character rather than merely accompanying or organizing it.

theories.name: Jackson’s Representationalism and the Knowledge Argument
theories.summary: Philosopher Frank Jackson develops a representationalist view about perceptual experience. “That experience is diaphanousness (or transparent) is a thesis about the phenomenology of perceptual experience. It is the thesis that the properties that make an experience the kind of experience it is are properties of the object of experience.”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Conscious experience is nothing over and above how it represents the world—its phenomenal character is representational.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: We access the experience itself only by accessing the properties of what we’re perceiving—experience is transparent.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Jackson uses this view to reject his earlier anti-physicalist Knowledge Argument by showing Mary gains no new truths.

claims.title: Raises the Question
claims.text: If phenomenal experience is fully representational, why does it feel like something more?

claims.title: Challenges & Tensions
claims.text: Critics argue representationalism still can’t explain Mary’s “aha” moment when she sees red.

theories.name: Lamme’s Recurrent Processing Theory
theories.summary: Neuroscientist Victor Lamme proposes Recurrent Processing Theory, which stresses brain sensory systems that are massively interconnected and involve feedforward and feedback connections, as being necessary and sufficient for consciousness. The visual system provides a case where “forward connections from primary visual area V1, the first cortical visual area, carry information to higher-level processing areas, and the initial registration of visual information involves a forward sweep of processing.”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness arises when sensory brain areas engage in recurrent (feedback) processing, not just feedforward flow.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Recurrent loops within visual circuits (Stage 3) are both necessary and sufficient for conscious perception.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Consciousness doesn’t require global broadcasting; local sensory feedback alone can generate awareness.

claims.title: Challenges & Tensions
claims.text: Critics argue background brain conditions are still needed—recurrent loops alone may not be enough.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Suggests we can have visual experience without access or report, separating “seeing” from “knowing.”

theories.name: T. W. Clark’s Content Hypothesis
theories.summary: Naturalism philosopher Thomas W. Clark posits phenomenal consciousness as the representational content of a cognitive system's sufficiently structured representational processing. Conscious experience exists only for the conscious system, so it is categorically subjective, and its basic elements are irreducibly qualitative. As a general rule, he says, we don't find representational content in the world it participates in representing, which can help explain subjectivity. Qualitativeness is entailed by the system’s need for representational primitives that aren’t themselves objects of representation.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness is the structured representational content within a cognitive system's internal processing.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Sensory qualities arise as irreducible contents that can't be further broken down without regress.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Subjective experience exists only for the system itself—it’s not part of the world it represents.

claims.title: Compatible Frameworks
claims.text: Fits with other representational theories like IIT, Global Workspace, and Predictive Processing.

claims.title: Philosophical Implication
claims.text: Consciousness creates a self-contained world immune to its own disappearance.

theories.name: Transparency Theory
theories.summary: Transparency theory makes the argument that because sensory (e.g., visual) experience represents external objects and their apparent properties, experience has no other properties that pose problems for materialism. We “see right through” perceptual states to external objects and take no notice that we are actually in perceptual states; the properties we perceive in perception are attributed to the objects themselves, not to the perception.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: We experience the world by directly perceiving external objects, not internal mental states.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Conscious perception represents objects so transparently that we “see through” mental states to the world.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: If experience had extra mental features, we’d notice them—but introspection reveals only the world’s features.

claims.title: Supports Representationalism
claims.text: Transparency backs the view that phenomenal experience is just representational content, nothing more.

claims.title: Challenges Inner Access
claims.text: Denies that first-person experience reveals intrinsic mental properties beyond what's represented.

theories.name: Tye’s Contingentism
theories.summary: Philosopher Michael Tye has proposed a theory of consciousness he calls “contingentism,” which is a kind of identity theory (i.e., phenomenal states and physical/brain states are literally the same) but with a novel twist: while the identity is indeed true in our world, it is not metaphysically true in all possible worlds. More recently, however, he has come to hold that, at the most fundamental level, there is a kind of 'consciousness*' or a protoconsciousness, a version of panpsychism (see “Tye's Irreducible Consciousness*” under Panpsychism).

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness is identical to physical states in this world, but not in all possible worlds.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Conscious experiences arise from physical or functional brain states, but only contingently so.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
