claims.text: Unlike classic identity theory, it allows for zombies or inverted qualia in other possible worlds.

claims.title: Solves the Hard Problem
claims.text: Claims that metaphysical possibility of disconnection doesn’t undermine physicalist explanation here.

claims.title: Shifting Ground
claims.text: Tye later leans toward panpsychism, suggesting basic consciousness pervades physical reality.

theories.name: Armstrong’s Higher-Order Perception Theory
theories.summary: Armstrong’s higher-order perception theory proposes that a first-order mental state becomes introspectively conscious when the subject has a distinct, perception-like awareness of that state. On his materialism, both levels are neural: one brain process “scans” or represents another, producing phenomenal consciousness. This makes Armstrong's the founding modern version of Higher-Order Perception (HOP), or inner-sense, theory, and, because the scanning is a physical process operating on physically realized first-order states, it extends his materialism to consciousness.

theories.name: Brown’s “HOROR” Higher-Order Representationalism
theories.summary: The central idea of HOROR theory (Higher-Order Representation of a Representation) is that consciousness arises not from a higher-order representation of a mental state (like sights or sounds) but rather from a higher-order representation of a representation. In other words, for a state to be conscious, the subject must represent the fact that there is a representation going on, without necessarily representing the first-order content directly. This second-order awareness is still conceptual or cognitive, but it targets the representational status of the first-order state.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: A mental state is conscious when you represent a representation of that state—not the state itself.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Consciousness arises from a higher-order cognitive state that tracks the existence of a first-order representation.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Unlike standard HOT theories, HOROR targets the representational status, not the specific perceptual content.

claims.title: Solves Misrepresentation
claims.text: Avoids false positives by not requiring the lower state’s content to be accurately matched.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Consciousness is tied to cognitive access and self-modeling, not just sensory richness or introspection.

theorists.name: Hakwan Lau
theorists.role: Professor of Biomedical Engineering & Neuroscience Researcher

theories.name: Cleeremans’s Learned Consciousness via Radical Plasticity
theories.summary: Cleeremans proposes that consciousness is not an intrinsic property of certain neural states but something the brain learns to do. His Radical Plasticity Thesis takes consciousness not as an intrinsic feature of particular neural states, but as an acquired capacity: the brain learns to represent, evaluate, and predict the consequences of its own representational activity.

theories.name: Deacon’s Symbolic Communication (Human Consciousness)
theories.summary: Neuroanthropologist Terrence Deacon asserts that symbolic communication has radically altered the nature of human consciousness, whereas consciousness broadly is coextensive with the development of brains in animals that regulate their movement with the aid of long-distance senses, such as vision, because of the predictive capacity this affords and requires.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Human consciousness is transformed by symbolic communication into a virtual, meaning-seeking awareness.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Symbol use lets us think beyond the immediate world, accessing others’ minds and abstract concepts.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Symbolic thought makes us a "symbolically eusocial" species with extended, shared mentality.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Enables memory, emotion, ethics, and aesthetics far beyond what animal consciousness supports.

claims.title: Raises the Question
claims.text: Does symbolic communication create a fundamentally different kind of mind in humans?

theories.name: Higher-Order—Overview
theories.summary: According to Higher-Order Theories of consciousness, what makes a perception conscious is the presence of an accompanying cognitive state about the perception. This means that phenomenal consciousness is not immediate awareness of sensations. Rather, it is the higher-level sensing of those sensations, a product of second-order thoughts about first-order perceptions or mental states—a two-level process.

claims.title: Core Concepts
claims.text: Higher-Order Theories explain consciousness as arising from cognitive states about first-order perceptions, creating a two-level awareness.

claims.title: Scientific Context
claims.text: Supported by work linking conscious perception to sensory metacognition and prefrontal–parietal activity beyond primary sensory regions.

claims.title: Why Meaningful
claims.text: Offers a clear mechanism for distinguishing conscious from unconscious mental states, influencing debates on self-awareness and reflexivity.

claims.title: Major Challenges
claims.text: Must clarify how higher-order states generate phenomenology and address competing same-order or reflexive accounts.

theories.name: Humphrey’s Mental Representations and Brain Attractors
theories.summary: Neuropsychologist Nicholas Humphrey employs an evolutionary framework, combining mental representations with what he calls “attractor states in the brain,” to develop a novel materialistic theory of phenomenal consciousness, which he sees as a late and not ubiquitous evolutionary development. His multidisciplinary argument follows.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Conscious experience is a brain-generated interpretation of sensory input, not just raw brain activity.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Sensory input is reinterpreted in time through feedback loops and attractor states, producing qualia.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Consciousness is not widespread; it evolved late for animals needing a robust sense of self.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: The phenomenal self may be “fake news,” but evolutionarily useful for survival and social navigation.

claims.title: Challenges & Tensions
claims.text: Consciousness arises only in interpretation, making neural correlates harder to pinpoint directly.

theories.name: Ismael's Reflexive Representation and Situated Self
theories.summary: Ismael explains the first-person structure of phenomenal consciousness through reflexive representation without claiming that self-representation constitutes consciousness. Mental states can simultaneously represent the world and present their own occurrent character, enabling immediate self-identification, phenomenal concepts, and distinctive first-person knowledge. This dual-content architecture helps explain privacy, ownership, apparent incorrigibility, and the persistent explanatory gap without requiring ontological dualism. Her later perspectival and virtual-machine work embeds such minded agents within physics, while explicitly leaving phenomenality unreduced. She distinguishes self-consciousness, a formal property of reflexive media, from consciousness, a qualitative property that only some such media possess. The theory explains the architecture and epistemology of subjectivity more fully than why subjective experience exists at all.

theories.name: Kriegel’s Cross-Order Self-Representation
theories.summary: Kriegel’s Cross-Order Integration theory holds that a phenomenally conscious state is a single, unified representational state containing two integrated components: a first-order representation of an object or condition and a higher-order representation of that very first-order state. Unlike standard higher-order theories, which posit one mental state representing another, Kriegel’s self-representationalism makes the awareness of experience internal to the experience itself.

theories.name: Lau’s Perceptual Reality Monitoring Theory
theories.summary: Cognitive neuroscientist Hakwan Lau introduces Perceptual Reality Monitoring Theory, which he says is an empirically grounded higher-order theory of conscious perception. He proposes that conscious perception in an agent occurs “if there is a relevant higher-order representation with the content that a particular first-order perceptual representation is a reliable reflection of the external world right now.”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Conscious perception happens when a higher-order process tags a sensory state as reflecting real-world truth.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: A non-conscious higher-order representation monitors perception for reality status and enables subjective awareness.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Consciousness sits between perception and cognition, not identical with either; it’s a functional “reality check.”

claims.title: Blindsight Explained
claims.text: Sensory info without higher-order tagging yields perception without awareness, as seen in blindsight cases.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Consciousness may not require biology; even AI systems with reality monitoring could, in principle, be conscious.

theorists.name: Hakwan Lau
theorists.role: Professor of Biomedical Engineering & Neuroscience Researcher

theories.name: LeDoux’s Higher-Order Theory of Emotional Consciousness
theories.summary: Neuroscientist Joseph LeDoux's Higher-Order Theory of Emotional Consciousness combines his approach to higher-order representationalism and his commitment to the centrality of emotion. His thesis is that “the brain mechanisms that give rise to conscious emotional feelings are not fundamentally different from those that give rise to perceptual conscious experiences.”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Emotional feelings arise from higher-order representations, just like perceptual consciousness does.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Conscious emotion occurs when cortical systems rerepresent lower-order inputs, including self-related content.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Fear (and other emotions) requires more than subcortical reactions—it needs higher-order self-modeling.

claims.title: Introspection Levels
claims.text: Consciousness involves “noticing” higher-order states; deeper introspection adds more cognitive layers.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Conscious agency may emerge from layered narratives in the brain, blending thought, emotion, and self-modeling.

theories.name: Lycan’s Homuncular Functionalism
theories.summary: Philosopher William Lycan defends a materialist, representational theory of mind that he calls “homuncular functionalism” and that posits that “human beings are ‘functionally organized information-processing systems’ who have no non-physical parts or properties.” Lycan does recognize “the subjective phenomenal qualities of mental states and events, and an important sense in which mind is ‘over and above’ mere chemical matter.”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness arises from hierarchically organized, representational brain systems functioning in a material, information-processing way.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Mental states are built from simpler “sub-agents” (homunculi) that represent and monitor other states, like nested systems.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Even phenomenal qualities (like “what it’s like” to see yellow) are fully captured by representational functions.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: The “explanatory gap” exists, but it’s about ineffability, not evidence against materialism or science.

claims.title: Challenges & Tensions
claims.text: Some argue Lycan downplays qualia or brushes aside the Knowledge Argument too quickly.

theories.name: Melnyk’s Realization Physicalism
theories.summary: Consciousness is a reductive but non-eliminative physicalism: phenomenal properties are real but non-fundamental mental properties, best understood as physically realized representational properties of sensations, while the “hard problem” arises largely from a misleading but psychologically formidable “intuition of distinctness” that makes such properties seem unable to be physical or functional, even though, in fact, they are.

theories.name: Metzinger’s No-Self Representational Theory of Subjectivity
theories.summary: Philosopher Thomas Metzinger presents a representationalist and functional analysis of subjectivity, the consciously experienced first-person perspective. What has been traditionally called “conscious thought,” he argues, is actually “a subpersonal process, and only rarely a form of mental action.”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: The self is an illusion; consciousness builds a transparent model that creates the feeling of selfhood.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Subjective experience arises from dynamic brain processes that represent a self-model, not a real self.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Conscious thought is mostly passive and subpersonal, lacking agency or active mental control.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Consciousness enables social responsibility and cultural evolution by generating the illusion of agency.

claims.title: Challenges & Tensions
claims.text: Rejecting the self undermines common ideas of free will, autonomy, and personal identity.

theories.name: Rosenthal’s Higher-Order Thought
theories.summary: Philosopher David Rosenthal proposes “a higher-order-thought [HOT] theory of consciousness, according to which a sensation, thought, or other mental state is conscious if one has a higher-order thought that one is in that state.”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: A mental state is conscious only if you have a thought that you're in that state.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: A higher-order thought (even if unconscious) makes a first-order state conscious.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Consciousness isn’t just perception—it’s awareness of perception through a second-level thought.

claims.title: Qualia Explained
claims.text: Qualia are mental qualities structured by perceptual discrimination, not mysterious inner properties.

claims.title: Challenges Simpler Views
claims.text: Rejects first-order theories for failing to explain what makes a state conscious.

theories.name: Thagard’s Neural Representation, Binding, Coherence, Competition
theories.summary: Philosopher Paul Thagard poses big questions upfront. “Why do people have conscious experiences that include perceptions such as seeing, sensations such as pain, emotions such as joy, and abstract thoughts such as self-reflection? Why is consciousness central to so much of human life, including dreams, laughter, music, religion, sports, morality, and romance? Are such experiences also possessed by other animals, plants, and robots?”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness arises from four interacting brain mechanisms: representation, binding, coherence, and competition.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Neural representations compete and cohere across brain areas to bind sensory, emotional, and cognitive content.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Explains complex experiences (e.g., awe, humor, dreams) using only empirically grounded brain functions.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Provides a neuroscience-based checklist to assess consciousness in animals and AI systems.

claims.title: Physicalist Confidence
claims.text: Claims the mystery of consciousness dissolves once we grasp how the brain physically builds it.

theories.name: Budson’s Consciousness as a Memory System
theories.summary: Consciousness evolved as part of the episodic memory system, likely to enable a flexible recombining of information, and it was subsequently co-opted to produce other functions, such as problem-solving, abstract thinking, and language. The theory challenges traditional views that consciousness is a mechanism for perceiving the immediate present or making real-time decisions. Rather, episodic memory required a conscious system to create and retrieve explicit event memories in the first place.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness evolved to support episodic memory, not to perceive the present or guide immediate action.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: The brain stores selected inputs as unified memories, which consciousness replays to imagine and plan future outcomes.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Conscious experience is delayed; we remember the world rather than perceive it in real time.

claims.title: Evolutionary Function
claims.text: Consciousness makes humans flexible by enabling creative recombination of past experiences to simulate future scenarios.

theories.name: Buzsáki’s Neural Syntax and Self-Caused Rhythms
theories.summary: Neuroscientist György Buzsáki presents the brain as “a foretelling device that interacts with its environment through action and the examination of action's consequence,” restructuring its internal rhythms in the process.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: The brain is a self-organizing system that creates internal rhythms to guide action and cognition.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Neural rhythms segment and synchronize cell assemblies, generating “neural syntax” that supports cognition.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: The brain doesn’t absorb information; it generates patterns internally, then matches them to the world.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Consciousness may arise from internalized action: thinking is simulated doing, grounded in rhythmic brain loops.

claims.title: Raises the Question
claims.text: If meaning is selected by the world, how does spontaneous neural activity become subjective experience?

theories.name: Carhart-Harris’s Entropic Brain Hypothesis
theories.summary: Psychopharmacologist Robin Carhart-Harris proposes the Entropic Brain Hypothesis in which the entropy of spontaneous brain activity indexes the informational richness of conscious states (within upper and lower limits, after which consciousness may be lost).

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness reflects the brain’s entropy level: higher entropy means richer, looser experience; too high or low means loss.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Brain states vary along an entropy scale; psychedelics increase entropy and neural flexibility.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Normal waking consciousness suppresses entropy, favoring order, stability, and self-awareness.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Shifting entropy may help treat depression and disorders of consciousness by loosening rigid brain patterns.

claims.title: Raises the Question
claims.text: Is consciousness more vivid or fundamental in high-entropy “primary” states like psychedelics enable?

theories.name: Damasio’s Homeostatic Feelings and Emergence of Consciousness
theories.summary: Neuroscientist Antonio Damasio's perspective on consciousness is distinctive in a variety of ways. Crucially, the root process behind consciousness, he argues, is that of feelings related to the interior of complex organisms endowed with nervous systems.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness begins with feelings that monitor and regulate the internal state of the body.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Interoceptive signals generate “homeostatic feelings” that inform the brain about bodily well-being.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Feelings are inherently conscious and serve as the biological foundation for subjectivity.

claims.title: Biological Priority
claims.text: Consciousness evolved from affective (internal) processes, not cognitive (external) ones

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Consciousness enables deliberate regulation of life, giving it survival and evolutionary value.

theories.name: Deacon’s Self-Organized Constraint and Emergence of Self
theories.summary: Neuroanthropologist Terrence Deacon, whose research combines human evolutionary biology and neuroscience, asserts that the origins of life and the origins of consciousness both depend on the emergence of self: the organizational core of both is a form of self-creating, self-sustaining, constraint-generating processes.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness emerges from self-organizing processes that generate and sustain their own constraints.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Neural systems resist entropy by dynamically preserving internal order, shifting activity as needed.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Consciousness isn’t in one place—it's a shifting pattern of constraint-driven organization.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Consciousness is linked to life-like self-maintenance, not just information or complexity.

claims.title: Raises the Question
claims.text: Can constraint-generation explain subjective experience, or only self-regulating behavior?

theories.name: Entropic Theories
theories.summary: Entropic theories explain consciousness in special relationships with the Second Law of Thermodynamics—entropy. While the brain is always and obviously involved, here there is something special about entropy in endowing consciousness with its deceptive sense of a nonphysical nature.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness arises from thermodynamically constrained dynamics, where local decreases in entropy must be balanced according to physical law.

claims.title: Mechanism
claims.text: Van Hamme: coherence crossing microtubular thresholds; Lugten: computational emergence requiring simultaneous information deletion to repay the “entropy debt.”

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Qualia are not metaphysical add-ons but intrinsic structural features—either stabilized coherence patterns (Van Hamme) or hidden computational histories (Lugten).

claims.title: Scientific Grounding
claims.text: Both root consciousness in thermodynamics and information theory, with Van Hamme invoking quantum coherence fields and microtubules, and Lugten referencing Landauer’s principle.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Consciousness is real, evolutionarily constrained to living systems, and—per Lugten—supports genuine free will by proving unpredictability.

theories.name: Freud's Surface Consciousness and Irreducible Affect
theories.summary: Freud’s theory of consciousness is a depth-psychological account in which phenomenal consciousness is real but derivative, intermittent, and structurally limited: the mind is not coextensive with awareness, and what appears in consciousness is shaped by unconscious wishes, affects, conflicts, defenses, memories, and symbolic substitutions. His importance for consciousness studies is that he breaks the Cartesian identification of mind with consciousness and makes phenomenal life dynamically stratified.

theories.name: Friston’s Free-Energy Principle and Active Inference
theories.summary: Theoretical neuroscientist Karl Friston conceptualizes consciousness as the natural outcome of his “free-energy principle for action and perception (active inference),” which stresses the primacy of minimizing in all organisms the difference between perceptual expectations (required for homeostasis) and real-time sensory inputs.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness is a process of minimizing surprise by predicting and adapting to sensory inputs.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: The brain creates internal models that infer causes of sensations to reduce prediction errors.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Consciousness isn't a thing but a dynamic, inferential process like evolution or the weather.

claims.title: Biological Basis
claims.text: Organisms stay alive by maintaining “attractor” states—stable patterns with low surprise.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Consciousness enables flexible predictions about future states, grounding selfhood and action.

theories.name: Giannakopoulos’s Entropy-Resisting Amplifier of Persistence
theories.summary: Consciousness is an entropy-resisting amplifier of persistence, a fractalized, bootstrapped, reversible computation—a recursively coherent information structure that persists at the boundary of collapse.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness is a recursive, entropy-resisting structure: an amplifier of persistence at the edge of collapse.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Consciousness buffers fragile information patterns using fractalized, bootstrapped, reversible computation to resist disorder.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Qualia are structural echoes—glows of stabilized coherence—that register persistence in the face of entropy.

claims.title: Scientific Support
claims.text: Builds on thermodynamics, information theory (GTI), reversible computing, and metastable states in complex systems.

claims.title: Challenges & Tensions
claims.text: Difficult to test empirically; risks metaphorical language outpacing formal, falsifiable scientific modeling.

theories.name: Homeostatic and Affective Additional Theories
theories.summary: Theorists offer their Homeostatic and Affective theories

theories.name: Mansell’s Perceptual Control Theory
theories.summary: Clinical psychologist Warren Mansell proposes Perceptual Control Theory (PCT) in which “reorganization is the process required for the adaptive modification of control systems in order to reduce the error in intrinsic systems that control essential, largely physiological, variables.”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness emerges as the brain reorganizes to reduce error in systems that control internal goals.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Adaptive feedback loops adjust perception and action to maintain internal stability under changing conditions.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Consciousness has three layers—phenomenal, access, and self-awareness—built on purposeful control.

theories.name: Marchetti’s Attention-Based Theory
theories.summary: Giorgio Marchetti maintains, following Damasio (1998), that the phenomenal aspect of consciousness (PAC) provides the agent with a sense of self and with information about how its own operations affect its self. The PAC, Marchetti argues, is produced by attentional activity, which modulates the energy level of the neural substrate—namely, the organ of attention—that underpins this activity.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness arises from attention modulating energy levels in a specialized neural system.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Different aspects of conscious experience map to how attention alters energy: where, how much, and in what direction.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Attention doesn't just select content—it creates consciousness and a minimal sense of self.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Without attention, there is no consciousness; without consciousness, the self cannot develop.

claims.title: Raises the Question
claims.text: Can attention exist without some level of selfhood—or does one always imply the other?

theories.name: Panksepp’s Primal Affective Consciousness
theories.summary: Panksepp’s affective-neuroscience theory holds that the most basic form of phenomenal consciousness is not perceptual representation, reflective thought, or cortical access, but felt affect generated by evolutionarily ancient subcortical action systems. Consciousness therefore grows upward from a bodily, affective core rather than downward from higher cognition. In other words, phenomenal consciousness in its most basic form is affective rather than cognitive or perceptual, and that raw feeling is generated by ancient subcortical circuitry homologously conserved across mammals rather than by neocortex.

theories.name: Pepperell’s Organization of Energy
theories.summary: Artist and perceptual scientist Robert Pepperell suggests that while energetic activity is fundamental to all physical processes and drives biological behavior, consciousness is a specific product of the organization of energetic activity in the brain.

theories.name: Pereira’s Sentience
theories.summary: Neuroscientist Antonio Pereira, Jr. hypothesizes that cognitive consciousness depends on sentience. He distinguishes “two modalities of consciousness: sentience, in the sense of being awake and capable of feeling (e.g., basic sensations of hunger, thirst, pain), and, second, cognitive consciousness, i.e., thinking and elaborating on linguistic and imagery representations.”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness has two layers: basic sentience and higher-level cognitive awareness.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Sentience arises from biochemical homeostasis; cognition depends on neural electrical activity.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Feeling comes first—thinking requires sentience, but sentience doesn’t require thinking.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Medical care should prioritize signs of sentience, not just higher cognitive functions.

claims.title: Raises the Question
claims.text: Can a person feel pain or hunger without showing any signs of mental activity?

theories.name: Predictive Theories (Top-Down)
theories.summary: Top-down predictive theories highlight brain-based, central-to-peripheral, efferent influence on sensory organs more than peripheral-to-central, afferent sensory perceptions—and while top-down predictive models may or may not be themselves explanations of consciousness, they give insight into the nature of consciousness and its evolutionary development. Top-down is a fundamental principle of how brains work, and it would be surprising if it were not relevant for understanding consciousness.

claims.title: Core Concept
claims.text: Conscious perception arises from top-down brain predictions shaping and integrating sensory input.

claims.title: Context
claims.text: Includes reentry theories and predictive processing, both emphasizing active brain modeling of reality.

claims.title: Applications
claims.text: Explains perception as Bayesian error minimization, linking awareness to survival and adaptation.

claims.title: Speculation
claims.text: Predictive brains may extend beyond the skull, forming part of larger cognitive systems.

claims.title: Key Challenge
claims.text: Unclear if prediction alone explains consciousness or merely underpins perceptual processes.

theories.name: Rudrauf's Projective Consciousness Model
theories.summary: The Projective Consciousness Model (PCM) is a mathematical model of embodied consciousness that “relates phenomenology to function, showing the computational advantages of consciousness.”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness arises from the brain’s ability to model space and experience through projective geometry.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: The brain selects spatial viewpoints to integrate sensory input, memory, and goals via active inference.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Projective transformations structure conscious perspective and guide the switch between perception, imagination, and action.

claims.title: Embodied Anchor
claims.text: The “lived body” acts as a stable reference point for conscious control and survival.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Consciousness evolved to simulate spatial information, helping organisms anticipate and adapt to their environment.

theories.name: Sebastian’s Predictive Machine
theories.summary: The brain is a control system operating as a multi-layered predictive engine that constructs a future-oriented world model by minimizing qualia potential—a latent dynamical quantity analogous to the gunas of Sāṅkhya philosophy. Within this parallel predictive architecture, top-down priors are continuously calibrated against bottom-up sensory signals through a delayed error-integration loop. Consciousness is modeled as an emergent process observing the world model, experiences variations in qualia potential, and can identify with a self-model embedded within it, offering a formal account of subjective phenomena emphasized in Eastern philosophy.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness emerges from a predictive feedback loop that minimizes qualia potential and updates a dynamic world model.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Brain rhythms process sensory prediction errors in hierarchical loops, integrating them over time to refine perception.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Introduces “qualia potential” as a scalar driver of motivation and perception, expanding on predictive coding models.

claims.title: Explains Subjective Phenomena
claims.text: Accounts for vision persistence, illusions, altered states, and self-model embodiment via temporal integration.

theories.name: Seth’s “Beast Machine” Theory
theories.summary: Neuroscientist Anil Seth extends top-down predictive theories with his neuroscience-informed “beast machine” theory that conscious experiences can be understood as forms of brain-based perceptual prediction within the general framework of predictive processing accounts of brain perception, cognition, and action.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness arises from the brain’s predictive guesses about sensory inputs, not the inputs themselves.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: The brain constantly generates top-down “controlled hallucinations” to interpret ambiguous sensory signals.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Conscious experience is a kind of waking dream, reined in by bodily and sensory feedback.

claims.title: Biological Roots
claims.text: Prediction evolved to regulate the body’s internal state—consciousness helps organisms stay alive.

claims.title: Raises the Question
claims.text: If reality is prediction-driven, what does it mean to accurately perceive the world?

theories.name: Solms’s Affect as the Hidden Spring of Consciousness
theories.summary: Neuroscientist and psychoanalyst Mark Solms applies Friston's free energy principle to the hard problem of consciousness. He identifies the elemental form of consciousness as affect and locates its physiological mechanism (an extended form of homeostasis) in the upper brainstem.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness is fundamentally affective; it begins with feelings rooted in homeostasis.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: The brainstem tracks bodily needs; affective states signal prediction errors in survival terms.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Feelings, not thoughts, are the original form of consciousness—subjectivity begins with affect.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Consciousness exists to help organisms flexibly meet needs in unpredictable environments.

claims.title: Challenges AI
claims.text: Only systems with real survival needs and affective inference could ever be truly conscious.

theories.name: Brand Deisler’s Linguistically Attributed Biographical Self and Conscious Action
theories.summary: Brand Deisler proposes that the human biographical Self arises when other people’s linguistic attributions construct an enduring referent linked to the child, which becomes coupled with the organism’s accumulated history and eventually functions as the entity to which actions are unconsciously attributed. Although the theory does not explain why experience exists or why any state has qualitative character, it may explain how human phenomenal consciousness becomes organized around selfhood—the importance of language in how experiences acquire autobiographical significance, personal ownership, temporal extension, anticipated consequences, and the character of happening to or being enacted by a persisting person.

theories.name: Chomsky’s Language and Consciousness
theories.summary: Philosopher and linguist Noam Chomsky revolutionized the theory of language, and although language-related theory of consciousness has not been a focus of his contributions, its relevance remains.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness may not be a solvable mystery, but a reflection of how little we understand matter itself.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Language is an innate capacity grounded in deep mental structures, revealing internal, not external, processes.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: The real mystery isn’t the mind—it’s matter; we don’t yet know what the physical even is.

claims.title: Challenges & Tensions
claims.text: Rejects the “hard problem” of consciousness as a pseudo-question with no coherent formulation.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Consciousness might someday be explained by future science—but not by current physicalist assumptions.

theories.name: Dewart’s Assertive Speech and Self-Presence
theories.summary: Dewart holds that all animals experience but only humans experience consciously, and that consciousness is generated by speech rather than by genetic natural selection. He argues that human consciousness emerged when speech transformed animal experience into self-present experience, because assertive speech enables a subject simultaneously to encounter reality, its own act of experiencing, and itself as experiencer, without requiring a separate introspective act. Internalized speech then develops into thought, while culture becomes a new inheritance mechanism through which consciousness continues to evolve. Dewart’s naturalistic theory therefore links phenomenology, language, and cultural evolution, but it explains self-conscious phenomenal experience more directly than basic sentience and does not explain why prehuman experience has phenomenal character.

theories.name: Drabkin’s “Language” as Fundamental Expression
theories.summary: Conscious experience is a property of human behavioral immersion (contra functioning) within an environment empowered by a particular understanding of 'language' as the fundamental expression or self-manifestation of reality.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness emerges from immersion in a reality that expresses itself through “language” as fundamental manifestation.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Language is not a tool or system, but the world’s way of expressing itself, shaping agency and experience.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Shifts focus from mature cognition to early language acquisition as key to conscious self-manifestation.

claims.title: Challenges Hard Problem
claims.text: Rejects “what-it’s-like” talk as a philosophical dead end; all thought is already expressive.

claims.title: AI Implication
claims.text: AI lacks true expression because it is not immersed in an expressive environment; it cannot develop agency.

theories.name: Fedotov's Communication Hypothesis of Consciousness
theories.summary: Consciousness is a highly specialized brain function that enables the encoding of personal information into communicative messages. On a subjective level, awareness of mental images signifies the readiness of information to be transmitted to an interlocutor. The Communication Hypothesis allows us to determine the position of conscious processes in relation to other cognitive processes, such as sensory detection, decision-making, and emotions. Consciousness can influence only those components of behavior that are related to the transmission of messages between people.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness is a state in which a person demonstrates the ability to potentially share information with another person through universal conditioned signals (words, gestures, and other language signs).

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Encoding information into messages (ability in the state of consciousness) is a cognitive process that can be defined as the awareness of events in the context of their significance.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Provides a basis for an objective analysis of subjective phenomena by investigating the formation of messages both at the neural level and in interpersonal interactions.

claims.title: Scientific Framing
claims.text: Provides a basis for an objective analysis of subjective phenomena by investigating the formation of messages both at the neural level and in interpersonal interactions.

claims.title: Bridges the Gap
claims.text: Sensory detection, decision-making, emotions, and other cognitive processes are projected into consciousness only during their encoding of the information.

theories.name: Hickey’s Language and Consciousness
theories.summary: There is an intimate relationship between language and consciousness. The phenomenon of thought and that of sensation form the two main aspects of conscious experience. Thought is a collective term encompassing individual thoughts, cognitive phenomena with which we organize the rational flow of consciousness.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Language organizes thought and communicates experience, but consciousness can exist without it.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Language structures inner and outer experience using symbolic syntax and vocabulary generated in the brain.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Syntax enables abstract thought, freeing language from immediate context and shaping conscious awareness.

claims.title: Evolutionary Angle
claims.text: Human language evolved alongside brain and anatomy changes, enabling symbolic, structured expression.

claims.title: Open Issue
claims.text: Without language, how can other beings express or verify their conscious experience?

theories.name: Jaynes’s Breakdown of The Bicameral Mind
theories.summary: Psychohistorian Julian Jaynes's 1976 book, The Origin of Consciousness in the Breakdown of the Bicameral Mind, proposes that consciousness, particularly “the ability to introspect,” is a learned behavior rooted in language and culture and arises from metaphor; consciousness is neither innate nor fundamental.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness, especially introspection, is a learned, language-based behavior that emerged culturally, not biologically.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Ancient humans followed hallucinated “voices” (gods); consciousness arose as these voices faded.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Conscious thought is built from metaphor and analogy, modeling external behavior internally.

claims.title: Challenges & Tensions
claims.text: Most scholars reject the historical and neurological accuracy of the bicameral mind hypothesis.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: If true, consciousness is a cultural invention—not a biological given—shaped by language and social complexity.

theories.name: Koch’s Consciousness Does Not Depend on Language
theories.summary: Neuroscientist Christof Koch asserts without ambiguity, “Consciousness doesn't depend on language,” and he offers vivid clinical cases of brain trauma or insult where language is obviously lost and consciousness is obviously retained.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness exists independently of language and is not unique to humans.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Consciousness arises from brain processes, even when language ability is lost.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Language shapes experience but is not required for basic awareness or sentience.

theories.name: Language Relationships—Overview
theories.summary: Language obviously enriches the content of consciousness, perhaps provides a framework for human consciousness, but is there a deeper relationship? While it is generally (but not universally) accepted that language does not generate theories of consciousness per se, it features in some and is rejected in others, both of which are worth exploring.

claims.title: Core Concepts
claims.text: Explores whether language and consciousness are causally linked, mutually dependent, or largely independent phenomena.

claims.title: Scientific Context
claims.text: Research spans philosophy, neuroscience, and linguistics, from language-facilitated self-awareness to pure perception without linguistic content.

claims.title: Why Meaningful
claims.text: Clarifies how language shapes higher-order consciousness while recognizing non-linguistic forms of awareness in humans and animals.

claims.title: Major Challenges
claims.text: Defining “language” and “consciousness” precisely, avoiding anthropocentric bias, and reconciling developmental, evolutionary, and cross-species evidence.

theories.name: Parrington’s Language and Tool-Driven Consciousness
theories.summary: Biologist John Parrington proposes that a qualitative leap in consciousness—“human self-conscious awareness”—occurred during human evolution as “our capacity for language and our ability to continually transform the world around us by designing and using tools” transformed our brains.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Human self-consciousness emerged from the co-evolution of language and complex tool use.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Language and tools reshaped brain structures, enabling abstract thought and inner speech.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Human consciousness is uniquely symbol-driven, with tools and grammar as its scaffolding.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: The self is real, grounded in neural binding and concept-based unity, not a mere illusion.

claims.title: Challenges & Tensions
claims.text: Critics say it explains cognition, not the deeper mystery of subjective experience.

theorists.name: John Parrington
theorists.role: Professor of Molecular and Cellular Pharmacology & Researcher

theories.name: Quine's Linguistic Demotion of Phenomenal Consciousness
theories.summary: Quine offered no theory of phenomenal consciousness, but his philosophy of language supplies one of the most consequential instruments for demoting it: the linguistic machinery through which the phenomenal is stripped of foundational standing. Quine's claim is not that qualia are unreal but that they are second-grade—admissible in the loose idioms of daily life yet excluded from the extensional, public language in which he holds that the true structure of reality must be described.

theories.name: Searle’s Language and Consciousness
theories.summary: To philosopher John Searle, language is crucial for consciousness, just as consciousness is crucial for language, because much of our consciousness is shaped by language and because the parts of language that are most important to us are precisely those that are conscious.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Language and consciousness enrich each other in a bootstrapping loop across evolution and development.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Language shapes what we can consciously think, feel, and imagine—expanding our inner lives.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Many conscious experiences (like longing or regret) are impossible without linguistic thought.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Human consciousness is not just richer than animals’; it’s structurally different because of language.

theories.name: Skopelitou’s Logos: Language Before Consciousness?
theories.summary: Psychologist Stella Skopelitou offers a fundamental theory of everything, which she calls “Logos,” according to which, if “everything” is, first of all, a word (which includes time, space, selfhood, the universe), then so is consciousness a word, and all that it entails. The theory of Logos proposes that language is not merely a communicative tool or cognitive supplement but the fundamental structure by which consciousness manifests and the world becomes intelligible or meaningful. In this view, consciousness does not precede language; rather, it is through language that consciousness becomes possible in the first place.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness arises through language; without language, consciousness could not appear or be recognized.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Language (Logos) is the deep structure making awareness, selfhood, and meaning possible at all.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Logos is not a tool for consciousness, but its precondition—language comes first, not mind.

claims.title: Challenges & Tensions
claims.text: Claims even questions about consciousness rely on language, making empirical testing paradoxical.

claims.title: Raises the Question
claims.text: If all thought is mediated by words, can consciousness without language ever be known?

theories.name: Smith’s Language as Classifier of Consciousness
theories.summary: Philosopher Barry Smith states that while we think of consciousness as “moments of experience,” the way we capture what's similar or different in our experiences over time is via language.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Language helps us group, compare, and communicate our conscious experiences across time.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: By labeling and categorizing, language structures how we perceive and organize the world.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Losing words can fragment perception, suggesting language partly shapes consciousness itself.

theories.name: Toomela’s Language-Mediated Structural-Systemic Theory
theories.summary: Consciousness is a language-mediated psychic process whose result is the experiencing of one's own psyche—a capacity that emerges neither in the brain nor from sensory experience alone but with the acquisition of the linguistic sign, because a word is a dual system pointing simultaneously outward to the sensory world and inward to another sign within the mind, such that every use of a word is at once a reference to the world and an experience of one's own mental content, rendering consciousness a socially constituted, developmentally acquired, and (as far as is known) a distinctively human phenomenon

theories.name: Armstrong’s Causal-Role Central-State Materialism
theories.summary: Armstrong’s central-state materialism combines a functional analysis of mental concepts with an empirical identity theory: a mental state is identified by the causal role it normally plays among stimuli, behavior, and other mental states, while science determines which physical state occupies that role. In humans, the occupants are states and processes of the brain, so sensations, perceptions, beliefs, desires, and conscious experiences are not merely caused by brain states but are brain states. For phenomenal consciousness, the upshot is deflationary: their felt qualities carry no ontological weight—the precise point at which critics locate the explanatory gap.

theories.name: Feigl's Double Knowledge of Raw Feels
theories.summary: Feigl’s mind–brain identity theory holds that phenomenal consciousness—the “raw feels” of color, sound, pain, emotion, imagery, and thought as directly lived—is empirically identical with neural processes. The phenomenal and neurophysiological vocabularies are not the same; first-person acquaintance and third-person scientific description provide two epistemic routes to the same event. Feigl described his position as “double knowledge”: A phenomenal report and a neural description can refer to one event. The subject knows the event by acquaintance; scientists know it by behavioral evidence, causal theory, and neurophysiological description.

theories.name: Kripke’s Modal Argument Against Mind–Brain Identity
theories.summary: Kripke’s theory of phenomenal consciousness is not an affirmative psychophysical model but a modal-metaphysical argument that conscious states such as pain are essentially characterized by their felt phenomenal character, so that any attempted identity between such states and brain states would have to be necessary if true, yet appears not to be necessary. As such, it remains the most influential modal argument against the physicalist reduction of phenomenal consciousness.

theories.name: Levine’s Explanatory Gap
theories.summary: Levine coined the term "explanatory gap" for a failure: granting that a conscious state is identical with a neural state, we still cannot see why that state should feel as it does. His contrast is between "heat is molecular motion," which fully explains heat's behavior, and "pain is C-fiber firing," which leaves qualitative character unaccounted for. Even a complete account of the brain appears unable to explain why particular neural processes possess particular phenomenal qualities. Originally formulated as an epistemological response to Kripke, Levine argues that phenomenal-concept strategies tend merely to relocate the problem because first-person acquaintance itself resists physical explanation. His later work increasingly favors strong emergentism, with consciousness governed by basic psychophysical laws. The theory’s challenge is whether phenomenal explanation requires an intelligibility unavailable elsewhere in fundamental science.

theories.name: Lewis’s Analytic Functionalism and Causal-Role Identity Theory
theories.summary: Lewis’s theory of phenomenal consciousness is a reductive materialism combining functional analysis with psychophysical identity: experiences are characterized by their causal relations to stimuli, behavior, and other mental states, while science discovers which physical states occupy those roles, typically neural states. Applied to experience, Lewis's reductive materialism yields a deflationary but non-eliminative account: qualia are real, but they are the occupants of a functional role, not intrinsic felt properties transparently revealed in having them.

theories.name: McLaughlin's Neurobiologicalism
theories.summary: McLaughlin’s neurobiologicalism is an a posteriori type-identity theory of phenomenal consciousness: for every type of subjective experience, there is a neurobiological state type with which it is numerically identical. He accepts an explanatory gap as genuine, but denies that this epistemic gap implies an ontological one. He recognizes the absence of a priori entailment that runs from neurobiological to phenomenal truths, arguing that sufficiently strict phenomenal-neural correlations could justify identity by inference to the best explanation, avoiding brute psychophysical laws. Psychophysical identities, if true, are necessary though empirically discovered. Anti-physicalist arguments from conceivability are met by locating the gap in the recognitional character of phenomenal concepts rather than in the world. Phenomenal consciousness is thereby substrate-dependent, not merely functionally organized. The principal challenges are multiple realization, neuroscientific variability, and whether identity genuinely explains phenomenal character

theorists.name: Brian P. McLaughlin
theorists.role: Professor of Philosophy and Cognitive Science

theories.name: Mind-Brain Identity Theory—Overview
theories.summary: Mind-brain identity theory holds that states and processes of the mind are identical to states and processes of the brain and, as such, can be considered the exemplar of materialism.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: The mind is the brain; every mental state is identical to a brain state.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Conscious experiences arise directly from neural processes—no extra mental layer exists.

claims.title: Challenges & Tensions
claims.text: Critics argue minds could exist in different physical forms, weakening strict identity claims.

theories.name: Papineau’s Mind-Brain Identity
theories.summary: Papineau defends an unabashed neurobiological physicalism on which conscious states simply are brain states, and argues that the sense of an explanatory gap is a cognitive illusion rather than evidence against the identity.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Conscious states are brain states—no more, no less; identity, not causation, explains the link.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Mind-brain identities are inferred abductively from robust correlations, as salt was identified with NaCl

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: The explanatory gap is a real feeling with no evidential force—it’s a psychological illusion rooted in dualist habits of thought, the "antipathetic fallacy," generated by how phenomenal concepts work.

claims.title: Zombie Rejection
claims.text: If consciousness is physical, zombies are metaphysically impossible, however conceivable they remain.

claims.title: Limits of Precision
claims.text: There is no hidden “essence” of consciousness; no fact fixes precisely which neural property "pain" refers to; phenomenal concepts are vaguer than they seem.

theories.name: Place’s Empirical Identity and the Phenomenological Fallacy
theories.summary: Place’s theory holds that phenomenal consciousness is not merely caused by or correlated with neural activity but is literally constituted by processes in the brain. Descriptions of experience and descriptions of physiology differ in meaning and verification, yet may identify the same event. He combines this claim with the “phenomenological fallacy,” which mistakes descriptions of how things appear for descriptions of private objects possessing the apparent qualities.

theories.name: Quine’s Naturalized Mind and the Demoted Phenomenal
theories.summary: Quine is a physicalist who advocates the identity theory of mind—"mental states are states of the body." Consciousness is real but wholly bodily—a condition of the nervous system—while particular mental events are identical with physical events even when mental classifications cannot be reduced to neurological classifications. His account explains how sensory stimulation, behavioral dispositions, and public language support knowledge and mental attribution, but leaves unexplained why neural activity has subjective, qualitative character.

theories.name: Sellars’s Sensa Beyond the Given
theories.summary: Sellars’s theory of consciousness distinguishes conceptual thought from sensory consciousness and gives each a different naturalistic treatment; both are identity theories, but of distinct types. Thoughts are functionally classified inner episodes modeled on public language, whereas sensations are nonconceptual, intrinsically qualitative states—“sensa”—postulated to explain phenomenal qualities. Sellars looks to a completed scientific image that must expand beyond present-day physics to accommodate qualitative sensory processes in a wholly physical world.

theories.name: Smart’s Topic-Neutral Identity
theories.summary: Smart’s identifies sensations and phenomenal experiences with processes in the brain while denying that ordinary experience reports mean the same as neuroscientific statements. Scientific evidence and ontological parsimony eliminate irreducibly psychical “nomological danglers” from an otherwise physical account of nature. The properties we introspect are "topic-neutral," so that experience does not commit us to irreducibly non-physical properties. Sense data and mental images are not entities in the world.

theories.name: Baars’s and Dehaene’s Global Workspace Theory
theories.summary: Proposed originally by Bernard Baars, extended with neuroimaging and computer modeling by Stanislas Dehaene, along with Jean-Pierre Changuex, Lionel Naccache, and others, Global Workplace Theory (GWT) proposes that brain-wide presence and broad accessibility of specific multi-sensory, multi-cognitive information is what constitutes conscious awareness.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness arises when information is globally broadcast across the brain’s processing systems.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: A “global workspace” integrates local brain processes into a unified field of attention and awareness.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Only information that enters this workspace becomes conscious; the rest remains unconscious background activity.

claims.title: Role of Prefrontal Cortex
claims.text: The prefrontal cortex is central—it's thought to coordinate and sustain global broadcasting of conscious content.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Offers a bridge between neuroscience and psychology by explaining how attention shapes conscious thought.

theories.name: Bach’s Cortical Conductor Theory
theories.summary: Cognitive scientist Joscha Bach posits a functional explanation for phenomenal consciousness, the cortical conductor theory (CTC), where “cortical structures are the result of reward-driven learning, based on signals of the motivational system, and the structure of the data that is being learned.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness is a memory of what the brain’s "conductor" last attended to and integrated.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: A prefrontal “conductor” regulates cortical activity, coordinates functions, and builds a protocol for reflection.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Experience is not lived in real time—it’s the system’s recall of recent, integrated attentional states.

claims.title: Neural Basis
claims.text: The conductor operates via prefrontal cortex structures like the ACC and dorsolateral PFC.

claims.title: Functionalist Frame
claims.text: Consciousness is explained by function, not intrinsic qualities—aligned with other functionalist theories.

theories.name: Bieberich’s Fractal Loops and Sentyons of Bright Matter
theories.summary: Bieberich’s Fractality Principle of Consciousness posits that the unity of phenomenal experience arises when information distributed across neural networks is recursively mapped into self-similar structures at progressively smaller scales, reaching the dendrites and neuromolecules of individual neurons. This cross-scale “fractalization” closes a "psychic loop" between the external world and an internal phenomenal "endospace." Bieberich postulates “bright matter” composed of hypothetical conscious units called sentyons, whose internal fractality would make each unit both local and connected to the whole conscious system.

theories.name: Block’s Biological Reductionism
theories.summary: Philosopher Ned Block represents a majority of philosophers (and a large majority of scientists) who hold that “phenomenal consciousness is reducible to its physical basis.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness is real and reducible to complex neurobiological processes in the brain.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Electrochemical activity in neurons explains conscious states without invoking anything nonphysical.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Consciousness arises from perception more than cognition—no need for higher-order thought.

theories.name: Brain Circuits and Cycles Theories
theories.summary: Brain circuits and cycles as mechanisms of consciousness are older explanations, no longer considered sufficient in themselves, having evolved into more sophisticated theories. Brain circuits cover the following kinds of large-scale brain structures: lateral pathways across the cerebral cortex linking diverse cortical areas (e.g., especially in the prefrontal, cingulate, and parietal regions of the cortex, which are involved in higher-level activities such as planning and reasoning).

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness arises from rhythmic activity and recurrent loops within large-scale brain circuits.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Thalamocortical and cortico-cortical pathways process and synchronize information via neural oscillations.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Brain rhythms (e.g., gamma waves) and feedback loops are necessary but not sufficient for consciousness.

claims.title: Modern Legacy
claims.text: These models evolved into richer frameworks like Global Workspace and Integrated Information Theory.

claims.title: Open Issue
claims.text: Can oscillatory synchronization alone explain subjective experience, or is a deeper mechanism still needed?

theories.name: Bunge’s Emergent Materialism
theories.summary: Philosopher and physicist Mario Bunge rejects any “separate mental entity,” calling it “a stumbling block to progress.” It is “unwarranted by the available data and the existing psychological models,” he says, and it collides “head-on with the most fundamental ideas of all modern science.” Rather, Bunge argues that the mind-body problem requires a psychobiological approach, based on the assumption that behavior is an external manifestation of neural processes—an approach that also abandons ordinary language in favor of a “state space language, which is mathematically precise and is shared by science and scientific philosophy.”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Mental states are real but fully material, emerging from complex brain activity.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Mind is a set of neural functions shaped by learning, not reducible to physics or chemistry.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Rejects both dualism and reductionism; mind emerges from brain like music from an orchestra.

claims.title: Philosophical Reframe
claims.text: Argues for psychoneural monism using systems theory and mathematically precise models.

claims.title: Critique of Other Views
claims.text: Dismisses zombies, panpsychism, and computationalism as unscientific or conceptually confused.

theories.name: Calvin’s Darwinian Mechanism in Neocortex
theories.summary: Consciousness emerges as “the current winner of Darwinian copying competitions in cerebral cortex,” competitions among a multitude of subconscious mindsets—spatiotemporal firing patterns of cerebrocortical neurons, particularly within the association areas of the neocortex. This process is dynamic, not static, recursive, and shaped by selective pressures similar to natural selection. In this view, consciousness is not a constant state of awareness but rather the fleeting victor in an ongoing Darwinian struggle within the brain.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness is the momentary winner of Darwinian competition among spatiotemporal patterns of neural activity in cerebral cortex.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Neural patterns copy with variation, compete for cortical territory, and preferentially propagate when favored by experience, current conditions, and goals.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Darwinian selection operates within the brain on behavioral timescales, generating and refining the patterns underlying thought.

claims.title: Conscious Contents
claims.text: Temporarily dominant patterns shape conscious perception and thought; their competition and recombination support flexible problem-solving and creativity.

claims.title: Explanatory Limit
claims.text: The proposed mechanism addresses how conscious contents are selected, while leaving unresolved why a winning neural pattern should possess subjective place-timing of conscious access.

theories.name: Crick and Koch’s Neural Correlates of Consciousness
theories.summary: The neural correlates of consciousness (NCC) are defined as the minimum activities in the brain jointly sufficient (and probably necessary) for any one specific conscious perception and, extended, for subjective experience in general, the inner awareness of qualia.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness arises from specific patterns of brain activity that are necessary and sufficient for experience.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Neurons fire, transmit chemicals, and form circuits that correlate with particular conscious states

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Consciousness research should target its physical correlates, not abstract metaphysics.

claims.title: Key Example
claims.text: The claustrum may act like a conductor, synchronizing brain regions to unify conscious perception.

claims.title: Open Issue
claims.text: Even with perfect correlations, it's unclear how brain activity produces subjective experience at all.

theories.name: D. Freeman's Primitive Felt Theory
theories.summary: Freeman's Primitive Felt Theory holds that phenomenal consciousness is built from a finite repertoire of irreducible felt states—thirst, pain, fear, but also familiarity, confidence, and urgency—instantiated in conserved subcortical structures near the midline of the diencephalon and upper brainstem. Cortical networks compute the content of thought unconsciously; their outputs descend through corticofugal pathways and are experienced as compressed, shifting combinations of these primitives. Cognitive phenomenology is thus a low-dimensional readout of cortical computation, and phenomenal unity is tied to the spatial cohesion of a compact subcortical substrate.

theories.name: Dalla Barba's Temporal Consciousness
theories.summary: Dalla Barba distinguishes two irreducible modes in which objects and events appear in consciousness: knowing consciousness, which presents them through general knowledge, and temporal consciousness, which presents them as uniquely situated within one’s personal past, present, or future. The theory’s central claim is that episodic remembering, present orientation, and future projection are expressions of a single first-person temporal mode rather than separable memory operations.

theories.name: Dendritic Integration Theory
theories.summary: Dendritic Integration Theory (DIT) is a neurobiological theory of consciousness that emphasizes the role of dendrites—the branched extensions of neurons—in integrating information and posits that conscious experience arises from nonlinear computations occurring in the apical dendrites of pyramidal neurons, particularly in the neocortex. Linking neurobiology and phenomenology, DIT relates cellular-level mechanisms to conscious experience by leveraging the intricate complexities of dendritic processing in brain circuits.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness arises from nonlinear integration in the apical dendrites of pyramidal neurons.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Dendrites combine top-down and bottom-up signals; calcium spikes amplify matching inputs into awareness.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Conscious access depends on local cellular mechanisms, not just large-scale brain networks.

claims.title: Experimental Clue
claims.text: Anesthesia blocks dendrite-soma coupling, halting consciousness while sparing other brain activity.

claims.title: Integrative Potential
claims.text: DIT complements global theories by explaining how microcircuits might gate conscious content.

theories.name: Edelman’s Neural Darwinism and Reentrant Neural Circuitry
theories.summary: Nobel laureate biologist Gerald Edelman presents a purely biological theory of consciousness, founded on Darwinian natural selection and complex brain morphology. His foundational commitment is that “the neural systems underlying consciousness arose to enable high-order discriminations in a multidimensional space of signals,” that “qualia are those discriminations,” and that “differences in qualia correlate with differences in the neural structure and dynamics that underlie them.”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness arises from evolutionarily selected neural circuits and their dynamic reentrant activity.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: The brain constantly selects and synchronizes neural groups through recursive signaling to integrate experience.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Consciousness is not computed; it’s selected, like immune responses, from massively variable neural patterns.

claims.title: Primary vs. Higher-Order
claims.text: Primary consciousness builds scenes in the “remembered present”; higher-order adds language and self.

claims.title: Hard Problem Reframed
claims.text: Qualia are just neural discriminations; the mystery fades once mechanisms are fully understood.

theories.name: Gray’s Brain-Built World-Model: Qualia, Comparators, Late-Error Detection
theories.summary: Phenomenal consciousness is a brain-built, multimodal “display” of the organism and its world, generated too slowly to direct most immediate behavior but useful for detecting failures in the unconscious systems that do. Conscious experience supplies an arena in which actual outcomes can be compared with prediction. It is a naturalistic account of conscious contents and their adaptive function, while conceding that it does not explain why the relevant neural processes should feel like anything at all

theories.name: Hawkins’s Thousand-Brain Remembered Modeling
theories.summary: Hawkins’s Thousand Brains Theory is primarily a theory of neocortical intelligence; its relevance to consciousness lies in explaining how massively parallel cortical models yield the unified, stable, object-centered perceptual world we experience. Consciousness is a brain-generated phenomenon dependent on neocortical modeling, voting, prediction, and action.

theories.name: He’s Joint Determinant Theory
theories.summary: Joint Determinant Theory is a pluralistic and integrative neurobiological approach to understanding consciousness, encompassing the diverse neural underpinnings of conscious experience. It emphasizes the complexity and diversity of conscious experiences that arise from the interplay of multiple neural determinants rather than a single neural correlate.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness arises from multiple interacting brain systems, not a single neural mechanism or region.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Different kinds of awareness (e.g., perception, memory, emotion) involve distinct but overlapping neural circuits.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Rejects the idea of a universal neural correlate of consciousness; favors a pluralistic, context-sensitive approach.

claims.title: Spontaneous Activity Matters
claims.text: Ongoing brain activity—not just responses to stimuli—helps determine what enters consciousness.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Consciousness science should study varied experiences separately, not assume one unifying explanation fits all.

theories.name: Hirstein’s Mindmelding
theories.summary: William Hirstein argues that it is “the assumption of privacy”—the deep, metaphysical impossibility for one person to ever experience the conscious states of another—that has led philosophers and scientists to claim wrongly that the conscious mind can never be explained in straightforwardly physical terms and thus to “create vexing dualisms, panpsychisms, views that would force changes in our current theories in physics, views that deny the reality of consciousness, or views that claim the problem is insoluble.”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness isn’t inherently private; it could, in principle, be shared via brain-to-brain links.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: “Mindmelding” would connect one brain’s control network to another’s sensory processing.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Undermining privacy shows that consciousness can be fully explained in physical terms.

theories.name: Libet's Mind Time: Readiness Potential, Unconscious Initiation, Delayed Awareness, Antedating Consciousness
theories.summary: Libet investigates phenomenal consciousness by comparing the objective timing of brain processes with the subjective timing of experience, leading him to propose that appropriate neural activity must develop for a substantial interval, up to about half a second, before conscious sensory experience appears, and that voluntary actions begin with unconscious cerebral activity before conscious intention is reported. His “readiness-potential” experiments consequently became iconic evidence for materialist, determinist, and epiphenomenalist interpretations of consciousness—the physical brain appears to initiate an action before the conscious mind knows that it intends to act. Ironically, Libet himself explicitly rejected the inference that consciousness is therefore purely physical, ultimately proposing instead that phenomenal consciousness constitutes a nonphysical, brain-generated Conscious Mental Field with possible causal efficacy.

theorists.name: Benjamin Libet
theorists.role: Professor of Physiology; pioneering experimental investigator of consciousness

theories.name: McComas's Hippocampal Memory-Stream Theory
theories.summary: Phenomenal consciousness is identified with the ever-changing sequence of short-term memories produced by the patterned electrical firing of hippocampal neurons, so that the hippocampus—not the cerebral cortex—is the primary generator of experience, and qualia are held to be, in principle, a function of neuronal impulse activity rather than any exotic or non-physical property.

theories.name: Merker’s Midbrain-Centered Reality Space
theories.summary: Merker’s mid-brain proposal holds that basic phenomenal consciousness can be generated without the cerebral cortex, principally through an evolutionarily ancient upper-brainstem system that solves one control problem: matching needs to opportunities in a mobile body by integrating perception, motivation, and action within an egocentric world model. The cortex enriches the content of consciousness but does not constitute it, a claim supported by decortication in mammals and by children born without cortex.

theories.name: Mitchell’s Free Agents
theories.summary: While neuroscientist Kevin Mitchell argues, contra many scientists and philosophers, that free will, or agency, is not an illusion—that “we are not mere machines responding to physical forces but agents acting with purpose”—he still asserts that “you cannot escape the fact that our consciousness and our behavior emerge from the purely physical workings of the brain.”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Humans are genuine agents with real free will, not just machines obeying physical forces.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Agency emerges from evolved brains that model, simulate, and choose among possible actions.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Free will is real and fully physical—no ghost, just the machine doing the work.

theories.name: Morsella’s Passive Frame for Action Conflict Resolution
theories.summary: Passive Frame Theory assigns phenomenal consciousness a narrow, evolutionarily grounded function: it provides a common field in which otherwise encapsulated systems can jointly constrain skeletal-muscle action when their action tendencies conflict. Consciousness does not exercise executive command; unconscious mechanisms do the work. The conscious field is “passive” because its causal contribution lies in making incompatible action-relevant contents simultaneously available to the somatic nervous system

theories.name: Neurobiological—Overview
theories.summary: This overview sets out the organizing logic of the subcategory: framing first, then method, then the mainstream cortical case, then two entries that reframe what a neurobiological answer can look like, then mechanism descending from function through memory to brainstem and single dendrites, and finally the consequences for privacy and for free will. The sequence is neither chronological nor fame-driven; it is an argument about where the disputes lie.

theories.name: Northoff’s Temporo-Spatial Sentience
