theories.summary: Psychiatrist and neuroscientist Georg Northoff postulates what he calls “sentience” as “a more basic and fundamental dimension of consciousness,” and he proposes that sentience arises via “temporo-spatial mechanisms”—characterized by brain activity, spatiotemporal relationship, and structure—with which “the brain constructs its own spontaneous activity [that] are key for making possible the capacity to feel, namely sentience.”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness rests on sentience, which arises from the brain’s spontaneous temporo-spatial activity.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: The brain integrates internal and external inputs through dynamic patterns of space and time.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Shifts focus from cognition to structure—the form and flow of brain activity, not just content.

claims.title: Philosophical Reframe
claims.text: Replaces the mind-body problem with a “world-brain” relation rooted in nested timescales.

claims.title: Open Question
claims.text: Can temporo-spatial structure alone explain why experience feels the way it does?

theories.name: Prinz’s Neurofunctionalism: Attention Engenders Experience
theories.summary: Philosopher Jesse Prinz accounts for consciousness with two main claims: first, consciousness always arises at a particular stage of perceptual processing, the intermediate stage; and second, consciousness depends on attention. “Attention” is Prinz's focus in that it “changes the flow of information, allowing perceptual information to access memory systems.”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness arises when attention makes perceptual information available at an intermediate processing stage.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Attention binds features into a unified, viewpoint-based format and passes it to working memory.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Only perceptual content—not thoughts or intentions—can be conscious; all consciousness is sensory.

claims.title: Neural Basis
claims.text: Consciousness depends on synchronized neural firing during attention-driven information flow.

claims.title: Challenging Dualism
claims.text: Claims a fully materialist, empirically grounded theory can solve the hard problem.

theories.name: Sapolsky’s Hard Incompatibilism
theories.summary: Neuroendocrinologist and biological anthropologist Robert Sapolsky counts himself as a “hard incompatibilist,” affirming the truth of determinism (i.e., all events and actions are the product of prior events and actions) and denying the existence of free will. There is no possibility, he says, “of reconciling our being biological organisms built on the physical rules of the universe with there being free will, a soul, a ‘Me’ inside there which is somehow free of biology.”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Free will is an illusion; all human actions are fully determined by biology and environment.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Brain activity precedes conscious intention, making choice a post hoc story, not a cause.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Consciousness is not a driver of action, but a “hiccup” or emergent side effect of brain processes.

claims.title: Reluctant Position
claims.text: Admits bafflement at consciousness itself, calling it a “complex emergent property” that explains little.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Undermines moral responsibility; challenges law, ethics, and the notion of personal agency.

theories.name: Schiff’s Anterior Forebrain Mesocircuit of Conscious Recovery
theories.summary: Schiff’s mesocircuit hypothesis explains severe impairment and recovery of consciousness after widespread brain injury through the dynamics of an anterior forebrain loop linking central thalamus, frontal cortex, striatum, and globus pallidus interna. Multifocal injury reduces excitatory drive throughout this circuit, producing a self-reinforcing downregulated state; recovery occurs when surviving networks regain sufficient activity to restore thalamocortical and corticostriatal function.

theories.name: Searle’s Biological Naturalism
theories.summary: “Biological Naturalism” is the name philosopher John Searle gave to a neurobiological solution to the mind-body problem. His approach is to ignore the mind-body problem's philosophical history and focus on “what you know for a fact.” He starts with a mundane, working definition of consciousness: “Conscious states are those states of awareness, sentience or feeling that begin in the morning when we wake from a dreamless sleep and continue throughout the day until we fall asleep or otherwise become ‘unconscious.’”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness is a real, irreducible, biological feature of the brain—part of the natural world.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Brain processes cause conscious states, which are higher-level features with causal power.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Consciousness has a first-person, subjective ontology that can't be reduced to third-person terms.

claims.title: No Need to ‘Naturalize’
claims.text: Consciousness doesn’t require redefinition—it’s already a natural biological phenomenon.

claims.title: Philosophical Position
claims.text: Rejects materialism, dualism, and illusionism—just start with what’s plainly true.

theories.name: Sergent’s Global Playground
theories.summary: Cognitive neuroscientist Claire Sergent's nuanced theory of consciousness emphasizes the temporal flexibility of conscious access. Her work suggests that conscious perception is not strictly tied to the immediate processing of sensory stimuli but can occur "offline," allowing for retrospective awareness of events. She proposes an update to previous formulations of the global neuronal workspace model that she labels a “global playground.”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness can operate “offline,” bringing past stimuli into awareness after they’ve disappeared.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: The brain holds sensory information in a shared network, then accesses it when it becomes relevant.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Updates Global Workspace theory to include a temporally flexible “playground” before full conscious access.

claims.title: Retro-Perception Insight
claims.text: Attention after a stimulus can trigger delayed awareness of that earlier event.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Consciousness may not reflect real-time input but instead a flexible, context-sensitive timeline of relevance.

theories.name: W. Freeman's Intentional Neurodynamics
theories.summary: Walter Freeman’s neurodynamics holds that phenomenal consciousness is a sequence of brief, globally coherent cortical states—cinematographic-like frames formed by phase transitions emerging from the collective, interacting activity of neural populations—and arises within an action-perception cycle initiated by the limbic system. Perceptual meaning is constructed through learned, goal-directed engagement with the environment. Awareness comes late: it is a macroscopic order parameter that constrains self-organizing neural activity, neither epiphenomenon nor initiating agent, that works via circular causality, helping defer premature action while alternatives are evaluated. Later work explored quantum-field descriptions of their physical organization. His account links meaningful awareness to multiscale neurodynamics, but does not explain why these dynamics are felt.

theories.name: Ward's Thalamic Dynamic Core and Min's Thalamic Reticular Gate
theories.summary: Ward and Min independently propose that phenomenal consciousness arises from recurrent, synchronized interactions between the thalamus and cortex, with the thalamus functioning as an active organizer rather than a passive sensory relay. Together, the models propose that the cortex supplies highly differentiated representational content, while thalamic dynamics help determine whether that content forms a unified conscious field. The two mechanisms differ in their neurophysiological algorithms.

theorists.name: Byoung-Kyong Min
theorists.role: Cognitive neuroscientist and medical physiological psychologist

theories.name: Bayne’s Unified, Multidimensional Consciousness: Structure Before Mechanism
theories.summary: Bayne’s approach to consciousness is best understood not as a proposed neural mechanism or metaphysical solution to the hard problem, but as an attempt to identify structural constraints that any adequate theory of phenomenal consciousness must satisfy. His central claim is the Unity Thesis: necessarily, for any conscious subject at any time, the simultaneous conscious states that subject has are subsumed by a single total conscious state.

theories.name: Emergence
theories.summary: Emergence is the claim that qualitatively new, even radically novel properties in biological systems and psychological states arise from physical properties governed entirely by the laws of physics.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: New properties like consciousness arise from physical systems but are not reducible to them.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Complex interactions among physical parts give rise to behaviors the parts alone don’t explain.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Higher-level phenomena may need new laws; they can’t always be explained bottom-up.

claims.title: Weak vs. Strong
claims.text: Weak emergence is surprising but explainable; strong emergence defies reduction in principle.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: If consciousness is strongly emergent, physics may be incomplete—new fundamental laws may be needed.

theories.name: Epiphenomenalism (Materialism)
theories.summary: In epiphenomenalism, consciousness is entirely physical, solely the product of biological brains, but mental states cannot be entirely reduced to physical states (brains or otherwise), and mental states have no causal powers.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness is real and physical but has no power to cause anything—it’s causally inert.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Brain activity causes mental states, but mental states never cause brain or bodily actions.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Consciousness is like “foam on a wave”: always present, but never driving the wave itself.

theories.name: Flanagan’s Constructive Naturalism
theories.summary: To philosopher Owen Flanagan, “consciousness is neither miraculous nor terminally mysterious,” and he argues that “it is possible to understand human consciousness in a way that gives its subjective, phenomenal aspects their full due, while at the same time taking into account the neural bases of subjectivity.”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness is fully natural and brain-based, yet retains meaningful subjective and causal power.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Consciousness emerges from complex brain processes and must be studied across multiple levels.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Rejects both reductionism and epiphenomenalism; consciousness is real and causally effective.

claims.title: Subjective vs. Objective
claims.text: The mind and brain are the same thing seen from first-person and third-person views.

claims.title: Open Question
claims.text: How can we find meaning in a purely material world shaped by neuroscience and evolution?

theories.name: Functionalism
theories.summary: Functionalism in philosophy of mind is the theory that functions are dispositive—activities, roles, results, outputs—mediums are not.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Mental states are defined by what they do, not by what they're made of.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: If something functions like a mind—regardless of its material—it is a mind.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Consciousness depends on causal roles and patterns, not on brain tissue or biology.

claims.title: Challenges & Tensions
claims.text: Critics argue that function alone may not explain subjective experience or qualia.

theories.name: Goldstein’s Mind-Body Problem
theories.summary: Philosopher-novelist Rebecca Newberger Goldstein centers the mind-body problem around the nature of the person, with two distinct kinds of descriptions: our physical bodies and brains, which science can, in principle, analyze completely, and our inner thoughts, perceptions, emotions, dreams, which science can never access completely.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: We are fully physical, but inner experience can’t be fully captured by brain science.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Consciousness arises from the brain, yet remains partly inaccessible from the outside.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Science explains bodies; novels capture minds—both views are essential.

theories.name: Hardcastle’s Argument Against Materialism Skeptics
theories.summary: Philosopher Valerie Gray Hardcastle argues that the points of division between materialists and materialism-skeptics “are quite deep and turn on basic differences in understanding the scientific enterprise.”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness is physical and explainable; mystery arises from mindset, not metaphysics.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Materialists trust science to eventually explain consciousness like it has other complex phenomena.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Disagreement with skeptics stems from differing views on what counts as a valid explanation.

claims.title: Challenges & Tensions
claims.text: Identity claims may seem brute or unintelligible—but all theories stop somewhere.

claims.title: Philosophical Standoff
claims.text: If you reject the scientific framework, materialist explanations will never satisfy.

theories.name: Hobbes’s Mechanical Phantasms and the Material Mind
theories.summary: Hobbes’s theory is a remarkably early attempt to naturalize phenomenal awareness, positing that sensation, imagination, memory, thought, emotion, and deliberation are all activities of an embodied organism and ultimately explicable through matter and motion, without an immaterial soul. Sensory consciousness begins when motions originating in external bodies propagate through the sense organs inward to the brain and heart, producing a counter-motion, or “endeavor,” whose subjective manifestation is this phantasm.

theories.name: Hume’s Bundle Theory of Perceptions
theories.summary: A radically empiricist, non-substantialist account in which phenomenal consciousness consists entirely of “bundles” of transient “perceptions”—“lively" impressions and fainter ideas—organized by associative principles, affective valence, memory, custom, and imagination, with no further discoverable self, soul, mental substance, necessary connection, or mind-independent object given within experience. In other words, the mind is nothing more than the stream of these perceptions.

theories.name: Kim’s Supervenience
theories.summary: Supervenience theory of consciousness seeks to reconcile mental causation with a physicalist ontology. Supervenience is a way of thinking that defines how mental states relate to physical states, especially in the context of reductionism and the causal closure of the physical domain. According to Jaegwon Kim, “mental properties supervene on physical properties” means that “no mental difference without a physical difference.”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Mental states depend on physical states; no mental change occurs without a physical change.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Mental properties “supervene” on physical ones: same brain state, same mental state—no exceptions.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Supervenience explains dependency, not causation; it maps correlation, not mechanism.

claims.title: Causal Dilemma
claims.text: If mental states aren’t reducible, they risk being epiphenomenal—causally excluded by physical laws.

claims.title: Evolving View
claims.text: Kim shifted from non-reductive to reductive physicalism, then toward property dualism with naturalist roots.

theories.name: Locke’s Reflexive Consciousness and the Making of the Person
theories.summary: Locke defines consciousness as an immediate, self-intimating awareness internal to every perception, rather than a distinct faculty, substance, or second-order act. Phenomenal consciousness begins with passively received simple ideas, such as color or pain. He argues that personal identity consists in sameness of consciousness rather than in the identity of body or soul, making the person a forensic unit capable of moral accountability; whether that sameness reduces to memory is contested among interpreters. Crucially, Locke remains agnostic about whether the substance underlying consciousness is material or immaterial. He thereby established the modern psychological conception of the self while highlighting the mystery of how any physical arrangement could generate subjective experience.

theories.name: Materialism/Philosophical—Overview
theories.summary: Materialism is the claim that consciousness is entirely physical, solely the product of biological brains, and all mental states can be fully “reduced” to, or wholly explained by, physical states—which, at their deepest levels, are the fields and particles of fundamental physics. In short, materialism, in its many forms and flavors, gives a completely physicalist account of phenomenal consciousness. The Philosophical subcategory both presents theories that are central tenets of Materialism and houses methodological positions in the naturalistic orbit.

claims.title: Core Concepts
claims.text: Consciousness is wholly physical, fully explainable in terms of the brain’s biological and physical processes, with no irreducible mental realm.

claims.title: Scientific Context
claims.text: Dominant among scientists and many philosophers; supported by strong neuroscientific evidence but debated over the nature and reality of qualia.

claims.title: Why Meaningful
claims.text: Provides a comprehensive, naturalistic framework for consciousness, promising integration with established science and potential solutions to the hard problem.

claims.title: Major Challenges
claims.text: Critics cite an explanatory gap for subjective experience; unresolved questions remain on whether physical accounts can fully capture phenomenality.

theories.name: Mitchell’s 15 Questions
theories.summary: Kevin Mitchell offers 15 questions that an explanatory, integrated theory of consciousness should encompass, and he posits that if we had a theory accommodating all these elements and providing some coherent framework in which they related to each other, that would be a theory of consciousness.

theories.name: Ney’s Physicalism, Not Scientism
theories.summary: Philosopher Alyssa Ney argues that consciousness can and should be understood within a physicalist framework, but physicalism should be informed by fundamental physics rather than by outdated or folk notions of “the physical.”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness is physical but not fundamental; it emerges from the physical world described by physics.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Materialists trust science to eventually explain consciousness like it has other complex phenomena.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Disagreement with skeptics stems from differing views on what counts as a valid explanation.

claims.title: Challenges & Tensions
claims.text: dentity claims may seem brute or unintelligible—but all theories stop somewhere.

claims.title: Philosophical Standoff
claims.text: If you reject the scientific framework, materialist explanations will never satisfy.

theories.name: Philosophical History of Materialism
theories.summary: The philosophical history of materialism began in ancient Greece and India and has developed over the millennia, often in response to religious, idealist, or dualist traditions. It was accelerated by the scientific revolution, especially, in recent decades, by the cognitive and neurosciences.

claims.title: Historical Development
claims.text: Traces from ancient Greek and Indian atomism and naturalism, through Epicureanism, Enlightenment mechanistic models, and 19th-century scientific advances.

claims.title: Key Turning Points
claims.text: Marx and Engels’ dialectical materialism, rise of logical positivism and behaviorism, identity theory, and modern neuroscience-driven physicalism.

claims.title: Why Meaningful
claims.text: Grounds mind and consciousness in physical processes, shaping science, secular philosophy, and debates on the nature of reality.

claims.title: Current Status
claims.text: Dominant in science and analytic philosophy, evolving through emergentism, enactivism, AI research, and updated non-reductive physicalist models.

theories.name: Stoljar’s Epistemic View and Non-Standard Physicalism
theories.summary: Philosopher Daniel Stoljar has long focused on physicalism, its interpretation, truth, and philosophical significance; his views are nuanced and largely deflationary.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness is physical, but our ignorance of certain physical facts explains the appearance of a gap.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: We falsely assume we know all physical facts; this mistake drives arguments against physicalism.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Physicalism can be true even if we can't yet explain consciousness—missing knowledge is key.

claims.title: Epistemic View
claims.text: Consciousness seems mysterious because we lack access to some relevant physical properties.

claims.title: Modest Science
claims.text: If you reject the scientific framework, materialist explanations will never satisfy.

theories.name: Weisberg’s Explanatory Optimism via Automated Compression Theory
theories.summary: A physicalist explanation of phenomenal consciousness remains a plausible and positive path. The hard problem looks hard because first-person appearances are systematically misleading. The key step is an empirical model of first-person access: Automated Compression Theory (ACT), which holds that first-person access to consciousness is accomplished by automated accessing of compressed sensory information. Because of the distorting nature of this compressed access, it seems to subjects that consciousness possesses ‘exceptional’ properties—properties leading to the hard problem—even though no such properties are present.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness appears mysterious because first-person access is distorted by automated compression of sensory data.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Automaticity and compression make experiences seem direct, simple, indescribable, and contingently connected (DISC properties).

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Automated Compression Theory offers an empirical, physicalist model debunking the “hard problem” appearances of consciousness.

claims.title: Why Meaningful
claims.text: Shifts the burden: physicalist explanations remain viable once misleading first-person appearances are explained away.

theories.name: Andrews's Consciousness Without Complex Brains
theories.summary: Philosopher Kristin Andrews, an expert on animal minds, argues that progress in consciousness studies has been hampered by prevailing conventional wisdom that for an organism to be conscious, a complex brain is required.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness doesn’t require a complex brain; simpler animals may also be conscious.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Shifts focus from neural structures to behaviors like learning, avoidance, and reproduction.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Studying diverse animal minds breaks the “N = 1” bias in consciousness research.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Consciousness may be more widespread—and differently evolved—than current models assume.

theories.name: Birch’s Comparative Sentience: Consciousness Profiles Across Diverse Minds
theories.summary: Birch develops a theory-light, multidimensional framework for studying phenomenal consciousness, especially across nonhuman animals and nonbiological intelligences. It is methodological rather than ontological: conscious experience can be investigated empirically and acted upon ethically, without first settling what consciousness is. He treats sentience as the capacity for phenomenal experience, particularly valenced states such as pain and pleasure. He proposes that conscious perception enables clusters of flexible cognitive capacities that unconscious processing does not. He rejects one-dimensional scales of “more” or “less” consciousness, favoring profiles across perceptual richness, evaluative richness, unity, temporal integration, and self-consciousness. His theory-light approach rests on a minimal facilitation hypothesis compatible with most competing metaphysical theories, and his sentience-candidate framework prescribes proportionate precaution where the evidence leaves the question open.

theories.name: Cabral-Calderin, Hechavarria, and Melloni’s Neuroethological Approach
theories.summary: A Neuroethological Approach to Consciousness is a cross-species, developmental framework that expands the scope of consciousness research from traditional human-centric, report-dependent methods to a broader comparative strategy that accounts for the ecological, evolutionary, developmental, and neural diversity of conscious phenomena.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness should be studied across species and lifespans, not just in adult humans.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Uses Tinbergen’s four questions to explore neural, functional, developmental, and evolutionary aspects of consciousness.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Shifts the burden of proof away from nonhumans needing human traits to count as conscious.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Supports a graded, biologically grounded view of consciousness shaped by ecological and evolutionary context.

claims.title: Open Issue
claims.text: Can common neural principles explain consciousness across such diverse species and developmental stages?

theories.name: Cleeremans and Tallon-Baudry’s Functional Value
theories.summary: Cleeremans and Tallon-Baudry propose that “subject-level experience—‘What it feels like’—is endowed with intrinsic value, and it is precisely the value agents associate with their experiences that explains why they do certain things and avoid others.”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Conscious experiences have intrinsic value that guides behavior and decision-making.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: We act based on how experiences feel; consciousness serves as a kind of “mental currency.”

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Consciousness evolved because it adds value-based flexibility to behavior, not just information processing.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Ties the hard problem to function: if experiences drive action, they aren’t just byproducts.

theories.name: Dennett’s Evolution of Minds
theories.summary: Daniel Dennett delights us with the wondrous and sometimes counterintuitive power of evolution in the development of consciousness (or, more generally, “minds”), notably in his psychohistory journey, From Bacteria to Bach and Back: The Evolution of Minds.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Minds, including consciousness, evolved through natural selection without invoking any mysterious processes.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Evolution produced increasingly complex organisms that built “thinking tools,” enabling self-reflective minds.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Consciousness is not a starting point but a product of cultural and biological evolution over time.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Human minds can now understand their own origins—something no other species can do.

claims.title: Raises the Question
claims.text: If minds evolved gradually, when did self-awareness truly begin?

theories.name: Feinberg and Mallatt’s Ancient Origins of Consciousness
theories.summary: Neurologist/psychiatrist Todd Feinberg and evolutionary biologist Jon Mallatt propose that consciousness appeared much earlier in evolutionary history than is commonly assumed, and therefore all vertebrates and perhaps even some invertebrates are conscious.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness emerged over 500 million years ago with the first complex brains.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Sensory processing, internal signaling, and self–non-self distinction evolved into subjective experience.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: All vertebrates—and some invertebrates—may possess consciousness due to shared neural features.

claims.title: Evolutionary Scope
claims.text: Consciousness evolved gradually, not suddenly, tracing back to early life forms.

claims.title: Challenges & Tensions
claims.text: Critics question whether basic stimulus-response behavior qualifies as genuine consciousness.

theories.name: Ginsburg and Jablonka’s Associative Learning During Evolution
theories.summary: Neurobiologist Simona Ginsburg and evolutionary theorist Eva Jablonka propose that learning during evolution has been “the driving force” in the transition to basic or minimal consciousness.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness emerged from the evolution of advanced associative learning abilities.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: “Unlimited associative learning” lets organisms assign meaning to complex, novel stimuli.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Learning, not reflex or instinct, drove the rise of minimal consciousness across species.

theories.name: Godfrey-Smith’s Naturalist, Gradualist, Diversified Evolution of Consciousness
theories.summary: A theory of consciousness that is biologically naturalist and evolutionary gradualist, treating it as an evolved form of subjectivity that developed in diverse ways across animal life. Subjective experience is not an all-or-nothing trait but a graded phenomenon that emerged gradually over deep geological time. Consciousness arose from the basic biological need for an organism to sense its environment and coordinate a response, making it a feature of life that is likely far more widespread and far more varied than commonly assumed.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness evolved gradually across species as a biological adaptation, not as an all-or-nothing trait.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Subjectivity emerged through evolutionary processes linking sensing, acting, and reafferent self-monitoring in animals.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Consciousness isn’t a binary property or on a single scale, but a multidimensional, diversified phenomenon.

claims.title: Scientific Framing
claims.text: Compares nervous systems across species (especially cephalopods) to show divergent evolutionary paths to experience.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Rejects sharp mind/matter and conscious/unconscious divides; supports embodied, enactive, non-panpsychist accounts of mind.

theories.name: Halligan and Oakley’s Species-Enhancing Epiphenomenalism
theories.summary: Psychologists Peter Halligan and David Oakley propose that consciousness is an epiphenomenon—inner feelings without causal powers—that evolved from underlying brain physiology. They argue that much of the mind’s cognitive architecture evolved to service sociality (the tendency of groups and people as persons to develop social links and live in communities), a key survival strategy for human growth, well-being, and species reproduction.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness is a byproduct of brain activity with no causal influence on behavior.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Unconscious brain systems produce thoughts and actions; consciousness narrates them after the fact.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Consciousness evolved to enhance social communication and to guide individual behavior

claims.title: Challenges & Tensions
claims.text: Intuitive beliefs in free will and agency resist this view, but science may demand their revision.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Consciousness feels powerful but is more like a broadcast for social coordination than a control center.

theories.name: Holmgren’s Grainy, Atomic Feels
theories.summary: Human conscious experiences are ‘grainy,’ and they are built of discrete ‘atomic feels’ that emerge as microprocesses in our brains out of the continuous universe. Ultimately, large numbers of atomic feels ordered in rich spectra of qualities (qualia) are all there is to build knowledge from. A Multi-Aspect Monism, where reality is understood through multiple interrelated perspectives, emphasizes that consciousness cannot be reduced to a single scientific domain and must be studied through interdisciplinary lenses.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness is built from rapid, discrete ‘atomic feels’ emerging from continuous brain processes.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Microprocesses in the brain produce brief, localized feels that combine into rich spectra of qualia.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Knowledge and concepts arise by clustering atomic feels into memory engrams, bridging sensation and abstraction.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Consciousness reflects both evolutionary adaptation and a Multi-Aspect Monism view that resists reduction to one science.

theories.name: LeDoux’s Deep Roots of Consciousness
theories.summary: Neuroscientist Joseph LeDoux argues that the key to understanding human consciousness and behavior lies in viewing evolution through the prism of the first living organisms.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness emerged from survival mechanisms rooted in the earliest forms of life.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Nervous systems evolved to detect threats and support survival, later giving rise to conscious states.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Fear is not ancient—it's a modern cognitive layer atop primal defensive circuits.

theories.name: McGinn’s Living Consciousness
theories.summary: Elementary consciousness does not exist in all things, but it does exist in all organic things. The mind is confined to animate things. There are traces of it in all living tissue, but none in anything else. The mind is pan-biological but not pan-physical. Organic tissue is prone to developing mentality, but the same is not true of inorganic objects. Being organic is a precondition of consciousness; it disposes things to having minds in the full sense.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness exists only in living, organic matter—not in all physical things—making it pan-biological, not pan-physical.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Organic tissue uniquely gives rise to mentality, with varying degrees across the body; inanimate matter lacks this capacity.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Rejects panpsychism’s universality and proposes a “consciousness hierarchy” within the living body itself.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Suggests that blood flow, tissue type, and organic complexity may influence how much consciousness a body part expresses.

theories.name: Nichols’s Primal Eye
theories.summary: Primal Eye theory, also termed Median Vision Theory (MVT), holds that phenomenal consciousness, REM dreaming, abstract thought, and self-volitional modeling emerged from the evolutionary atrophy of the ancestral median, parietal, or “primal” eye during the transition from cold- to warm-blooded vertebrate physiology.

theories.name: No Hard Problem in William James’s Psychology
theories.summary: Writer Tracy Witham argues that William James flipped the paradigm in which the hard problem arises because James viewed consciousness through a problem he believed it solves by selecting for adaptive responses to specific environmental situations.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness evolved to solve the “selection problem” by favoring adaptive behaviors in complex environments.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Reflective experience helps organisms identify and retain behaviors that lead to better outcomes.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Consciousness isn’t mysterious—it’s a practical tool for sorting options in decision-making.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: By tying consciousness to adaptive action, James sidesteps the “hard problem” as a misframed puzzle.

theories.name: Phylogenetic/Evolutionary Additional Theories
theories.summary: Phylogenetic/Evolutionary Additional Theories

theories.name: Phylogenetic/Evolutionary—Overview
theories.summary: The phylogenetic evolution of consciousness, at first blush, is not a specific theory of consciousness per se. Rather, it is recruited as the mechanistic process for many (but not all) of the theories on the Landscape. Yet, is there a sense in which phylogenetic evolution can become a prime explanation of consciousness in its own right?

claims.title: Core Concepts
claims.text: Investigates consciousness through evolutionary processes, assessing its gradual development, adaptive roles, and species-specific manifestations.

claims.title: Scientific Context
claims.text: Draws on neuroscience, philosophy, and evolutionary biology, from gradualist models to critiques of consciousness as an adaptive trait.

claims.title: Why Meaningful
claims.text: Illuminates possible origins and purposes of consciousness, framing debates over its biological function and evolutionary uniqueness.

claims.title: Major Challenges
claims.text: Determining which species are conscious, how consciousness emerged, and whether it confers measurable survival advantages.

theories.name: Reber’s Cellular Basis of Consciousness
theories.summary: Cognitive psychologist Arthur Reber dubs his theory of the origins of mind and consciousness the Cellular Basis of Consciousness (CBC), arguing that “sentience emerged with life itself.”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness began with life; even single-celled organisms have primitive minds.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Basic sentience arises from cellular structures that sense, respond, and adapt to environments.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Consciousness isn’t brain-based but biologically embedded in all living cells.

claims.title: Hard Problem Reframed
claims.text: Consciousness isn’t added by brains—it’s layered from simpler, older organic functions.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: AI can’t be conscious, since minds depend on specific biological substrates, not computation.

theories.name: Sreedharan’s Affective Survival Theory
theories.summary: Affective Survival Theory (AST) is a Darwinian framework for the evolution of conscious experience. According to AST, consciousness evolved not as an incidental byproduct of brain complexity but as an adaptive system of affective prioritization selected for its contribution to behavioral flexibility, memory encoding, and social cooperation.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness evolved as an emotional system that boosts survival, not as a byproduct of brain complexity.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Felt emotions tag experiences with urgency and meaning, guiding memory, attention, and adaptive behavior.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: AST reframes the "hard problem" as a "hard advantage"—feeling itself is evolution’s useful feature.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Emotion, not intellect, lies at the root of consciousness—across species and throughout evolution.

claims.title: Open Issue
claims.text: How much affective complexity is needed before consciousness arises in simpler organisms?

theories.name: A. Clark and Chalmers’s Extended Mind
theories.summary: The extended mind, according to philosopher Andy Clark, features an “active externalism,” based on the participatory role of the environment in driving cognitive processes. He asserts that when the human organism is linked with an external entity in a two-way interaction, a “coupled system” is created that can be conceptualized as a cognitive system in its own right (independent of the two components).

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Cognition can extend beyond the brain into tools, environments, and social systems.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: When brain and external tools interact seamlessly, they form a single “coupled” cognitive system.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Rejects brain-bound thinking; treats mind as spread across brain, body, and world.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Redefines what counts as thinking, suggesting notebooks or smartphones can be part of the mind.

theories.name: Cooke’s Nondual Naturalism and Living Mirror Theory
theories.summary: A dual framework for understanding the place of consciousness in reality: Nondual Naturalism, which serves as a metaphysical and epistemological worldview, and the Living Mirror Theory, which situates consciousness within the very dynamics of life.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness exists not as a substance or neural computation, but as the relational, epistemic dynamics of life itself, embedded in a wider reality that is entirely relational.

claims.title: Worldview
claims.text: Nondual Naturalism holds that reality is not made of independent substances but of interdependent processes.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: The Living Mirror Theory proposes that organisms persist by minimizing entropy through predictive modeling of their environment—this process gives rise to the epistemic interface we call consciousness.

claims.title: Distinguishing Ideas
claims.text: Reality is fundamentally relational, and all living things possess experiential awareness.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Humans are part of the web of life, not separate from or superior to it. The mistaken belief in real separation underlies ecological breakdown and the climate crisis.

theories.name: Fish’s Naïve Realism
theories.summary: William Fish’s theory of consciousness is grounded in naïve realism, also known as relationalism. This perspective posits that conscious experiences are direct relations to external, mind-independent objects and their properties, rather than internal representations or constructions. Fish asserts that in veridical perception—when our sensory experiences accurately reflect the external world—the phenomenal character of experience is constituted by the external objects themselves.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Conscious experiences are direct relations to real, external objects—not internal mental representations.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Perception reveals the world itself; the apple’s redness is the redness experienced.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Uses disjunctivism: veridical perception connects to real objects; hallucinations do not.

claims.title: Extends to Memory
claims.text: Memory experiences may inherit their feel from past direct perceptions, not recreate them.

claims.title: Bridges the Gap
claims.text: Relational properties help explain consciousness without invoking mysterious inner qualities.

theories.name: Harman’s Object-Oriented Ontology
theories.summary: Harman argues that objects exist and interact independently of human consciousness, that human consciousness is just one way that objects relate to other objects, and that it should not be privileged ontologically.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness is just one kind of object relation, not ontologically special or foundational.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Objects interact through partial, indirect relations; consciousness is one such relation among many.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Objects withdraw from all encounters, including consciousness, which never accesses them fully.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Shifts philosophy’s focus away from mind or subjectivity to a flat ontology where all objects are equal.

claims.title: Raises the Question
claims.text: If no object can fully access another, how do meaningful relations—including conscious ones—occur at all?

theories.name: Hofstadter’s Strange Loops
theories.summary: Douglas Hofstadter posits “strange loops” as the foundation of consciousness and of its derivatives, especially the self and free will, describing strange loops as “a special kind of abstract feedback loop inhabiting our brains.” He calls “I” the most central and complex symbol in our brains, and his book, I Am a Strange Loop, makes the case that, “In the end, we are self-perceiving, self-inventing, locked-in mirages that embody small miracles of self-reference.” He describes the mind as a “near-infinitely extendable, self-referential loop of symbols.”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness emerges from self-referential “strange loops” in the brain’s symbol-processing system.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: The brain creates abstract feedback loops that represent and reflect on themselves recursively.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: The self is a dynamic, self-inventing pattern—not a substance but a looping illusion with causal power.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Challenges both dualism and reductionism by treating the “I” as real and causally potent despite being emergent.

claims.title: Open Issue
claims.text: Can abstract feedback alone explain the richness of subjective experience and agency?

theorists.name: Douglas Hofstadter
theorists.role: Professor of Cognitive and Computer Science

theories.name: J. Campbell’s Attention-Empowered Relationalism
theories.summary: Philosopher John Campbell's relational theory of consciousness emphasizes the integral role of conscious attention in our ability to refer to and think about objects in the world. Conscious attention is the basis for reference such that our capacity to refer to objects—especially through demonstratives like “that tree” or “this cup”—depends fundamentally on conscious visual attention. He posits that to refer to an object, one must not only perceive it but also consciously attend to it, distinguishing it from its surroundings. This conscious attention enables the formation of thoughts about specific objects.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Conscious attention is necessary to refer to and think about specific objects in the world.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Conscious visual attention binds features into coherent objects, enabling demonstrative thought like “that tree.”

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Reference depends on relational awareness, not internal representations or descriptive content.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Consciousness has causal power in cognition, directly shaping thought and language.

claims.title: Raises the Question
claims.text: Can reference or thought about objects occur without conscious attention—or at all in unconscious minds?

theories.name: Jaworski’s Hylomorphism
theories.summary: Philosopher William Jaworski argues that the hard problem of consciousness arises only if hylomorphism is false. Hylomorphism is the claim that structure is a basic ontological and explanatory principle and is responsible for individuals being the kinds of things they are and having the powers or capacities they have.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness is a structured activity; its nature is explained by the form or organization of the body.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Mental states arise from how physical parts are organized and coordinated, not just from the parts themselves.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Structure itself is a basic feature of reality, not reducible to matter or function.

claims.title: Hard Problem Reframed
claims.text: The mystery of consciousness only seems hard if we ignore structure as a fundamental principle.

claims.title: Challenges & Tensions
claims.text: Treating all structure as equally explanatory may oversimplify what makes consciousness distinct.

theories.name: Kojdić’s Interface Ontology of Consciousness
theories.summary: Consciousness is the capacity by which finite agents stabilize and render intelligible an empirical world that exists only as a boundary (interface) between a non-empirical ground and cognitive limitation. Drawing on Kant’s transcendental idealism, the theory treats empirical reality not as a self-standing domain of objects, but as an interface: a structured boundary at which a deeper, non-empirical ground becomes partially available to finite knowers.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness is a structural capacity by which finite agents stabilize and render intelligible an empirical world that exists only as an interface between a non-empirical ground and cognitive limitation.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Consciousness operates by locking onto, sustaining, and integrating lawlike patterns at the interface, thereby making a unified, coherent world present to a subject rather than merely registering isolated sensory inputs.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Consciousness is not an emergent add-on within a pre-given physical world, but a condition for the world’s intelligibility as a world; without conscious stabilization, empirical reality would lack unity, lawfulness, and experiential coherence.

claims.title: Scientific Framing
claims.text: The theory is compatible with empirical neuroscience and cognitive science but is meta-theoretical: it clarifies the structural role consciousness must play in any adequate world-model, while leaving open empirical questions about which biological or artificial systems instantiate this capacity.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Rejects both reductive eliminativism and panpsychism; explains why multiple consciousness theories capture partial truths; and links consciousness to normativity by treating ethical and social norms as conditions for maintaining a legible, shared empirical interface.

theories.name: Lahav’s Relativistic Theory
theories.summary: Physicist Nir Lahav characterizes consciousness as a physical phenomenon that is relative to the measurements of a “cognitive frame of reference.”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness is a physical phenomenon, but its appearance depends on the observer’s cognitive frame of reference.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Like motion in physics, consciousness manifests differently depending on whether you're inside or outside the system.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: First-person and third-person views aren’t opposites—they’re different measurements of the same underlying process.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Zombies are impossible, and consciousness could emerge in AI if the right relational structure exists.

claims.title: Bridges the Gap
claims.text: Translates subjective experience into third-person science via cognitive frame transformations.

theories.name: Loorits’s Structural Realism
theories.summary: Philosopher Kristjan Loorits's Structural Realism posits that “conscious experiences are fully structural phenomena that reside in our brains in the form of complex higher-order patterns in neural activity.”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Conscious experiences are structural patterns in the brain’s neural activity, not nonphysical or ineffable.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Qualia are complex, composed structures shaped by vast networks of unconscious associations.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: The brain misrepresents structural properties as simple, monadic qualities—creating the illusion of qualia.

claims.title: Solves the Hard Problem
claims.text: Consciousness becomes explainable in fully physical and structural terms, dissolving its apparent mystery.

claims.title: Challenges & Tensions
claims.text: Even if qualia are structural “behind the scenes,” they still feel intrinsic, leaving some mystery intact.

theories.name: Manzotti’s Mind-Object Identity ("Spread Mind")
theories.summary: Mind-Object Identity theory is the physicalist thesis that one's phenomenal experience of an object is identical to the external object itself, rather than to any brain-based processes. Its radical realism claim is that phenomenal consciousness is not an emergent brain property, but, by being identical with the physical object itself, the body and brain are causal-enabling conditions for experience, whereas the experienced object is the experience itself.

theories.name: McGinn’s Brain Perception
theories.summary: Consciousness is perceiving your own brain. This isn’t because all consciousness is a brain state; it’s because all consciousness is brain perception. Consciousness is brain awareness—awareness of the brain. All consciousness is consciousness-of… the brain. This can be stated as an identity theory: mental states are identical to perceptual states of brain awareness.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness is a perceptual relation to the brain: all mental states are perceptions of one’s own brain states.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Mental states are de re (not de dicto) awareness of brain activity—one perceives the brain without recognizing it as the brain.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Consciousness has double intentionality: it points outward to the world and inward to the brain.

claims.title: Justification
claims.text: Perception is defined as sensitivity to stimuli; the mind “tracks” the brain in the same way vision tracks the external world.

claims.title: Implication
claims.text: This reframes introspection and experience as a kind of inner neuroscience, where consciousness encodes brain states in subjective terms.

theories.name: Mitchell and Jennings’s Consciousness Needs a Subject
theories.summary: To be conscious is to be an experiencing subject. A subject is a living being with interests, and subjects with interests are conceptually (and evolutionarily) prior to consciousness. Thus, consciousness is intimately tied up with being an experiencing subject. Not just having a point of view at any moment, but being an integrated self with continuity and extension through time.

theories.name: Tsuchiya’s Relational Approach to Qualia
theories.summary: Neuroscientist Naotsugu ('Nao') Tsuchiya's relational and structural approach to consciousness—more specifically, to qualia—is not so much a theory of consciousness per se but more a fresh methodology, which he calls 'the Qualia Structure Paradigm.' It is “an alternative approach to characterize, and eventually define, consciousness through exhaustive descriptions of consciousness's relationships to all other consciousnesses.”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness can be characterized by the structure of how experiences relate to each other across minds.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Uses math from category theory to map qualia as relational structures rather than isolated properties.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Shifts focus from internal qualia to intersubjective patterns and structural similarities in experience.

claims.title: Methodological Innovation
claims.text: Introduces large-scale psychophysics and computational tools to empirically compare qualia.

claims.title: Open Issue
claims.text: Can mapping qualia relations clarify or replace the concept of qualia itself in explaining consciousness?

theories.name: Atmanspacher’s Dual-Aspect Monism
theories.summary: Physicist-philosopher Harald Atmanspacher presents mind and matter, mental and material domains of reality, as manifestations, or aspects, of one underlying, fundamental reality in which mind and matter are inseparable. He distinguishes between the epistemic discernment of both the separate domains and the underlying reality, and the ontic existence of the “psychophysically neutral domain.”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Mind and matter are inseparable aspects of a deeper, psychophysically neutral reality.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Mental and physical states emerge by breaking the symmetry of an underlying holistic domain.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Uses quantum holism and Bohm’s implicate/explicate order to explain mind–matter correlations.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Offers a scientifically framed alternative to physicalism, dualism, and idealism.

theories.name: Davidson’s Anomalous Monism
theories.summary: Anomalous Monism, developed by philosopher Donald Davidson, holds that mental properties and events must have a physical ontology but that psychology cannot be reduced to physics. As such, Anomalous Monism is a form of property dualism and shares features with Non-Reductive Physicalism.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Mental events are identical to physical events, but mental concepts can’t be reduced to physical laws.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Combines three claims: mental events cause physical events, causation requires laws, yet no psychophysical laws exist.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Rejects type-identity between mind and body while affirming token-identity through the impossibility of strict psychophysical laws.

theories.name: James’s Radical Empiricism of Monistic Pure Experience
theories.summary: James’s radical empiricism is a pluralistic neutral-monist theory in which phenomenal consciousness and physical reality are not two substances, but two functional organizations of a more primitive field of “pure experience.” In other words, mind and matter are both aspects or structures formed from a more fundamental pure experience, which is neither mental nor physical.

theories.name: Leibniz's Monads
theories.summary: Leibniz’s theory of consciousness is a monad-based, panexperiential account in which phenomenal consciousness is the apperceived or more distinct form of perception within simple, immaterial perceiving substances, while all reality consists of these non-spatial monads whose internal perceptual states express the whole universe from unique perspectives and unfold by “appetition” (i.e., the internal drive or activity of a simple substance), under a pre-established divine harmony.

theories.name: Leslie’s Consciousness Inside an Infinite Mind
theories.summary: Philosopher John Leslie suggests that ethical requirements, when not overruled by stronger ethical requirements, are creatively effective. The cosmos they create is a collection of infinitely many minds, each infinite mind eternally conscious of all that's worth contemplating. Our universe is a structure inside one such mind, its reality consisting simply in its being contemplated.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Our universe exists as a thought within an infinite mind, sustained by its contemplation.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Infinitely many divine-like minds create realities through ethical necessity, each holding countless possible worlds.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Conscious beings within these minds may be unaware they exist inside a greater consciousness.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Reality’s foundation is mental and ethical, not physical, with limitless alternative universes possible.

theories.name: Neutral Monism Additional Theories
theories.summary: Theorists offer their theories that are (or seem to be) neutral monisms.

theories.name: Neutral Monism—Overview
theories.summary: Monism is the theory that all of reality consists of exactly one concrete object or thing, and everything that exists is, in some sense, that one concrete object or thing. Monism also names a family of doctrines about one fundamental kind rather than one object, and it is in that sense that materialism, idealism, and neutral monism are all monisms. Neutral monism is a different claim. It is the theory that the fundamental nature of reality is neither mental nor physical but neutral between them, with mind and matter alike arising as constructions, aspects, or organizations of that common base. It is monist in holding that everything basic is of one kind of stuff, agreeing that far with materialism and idealism, and distinguished from them by its claim about what that one kind of stuff intrinsically is. It is neither mental nor physical, but that from which both are constructed.

claims.title: Core Concepts
claims.text: Reality is one unified entity; all mental and physical aspects are part of this single whole.

claims.title: Scientific Context
claims.text: Related to panpsychism but distinct; includes philosophical and metaphysical frameworks integrating mind and matter.

claims.title: Why Meaningful
claims.text: Offers parsimony, avoiding dualism’s split and materialism’s limits by uniting consciousness and reality in one substance.

claims.title: Major Challenges
claims.text: Boundaries with panpsychism blur; defining the “one thing” precisely remains philosophically and scientifically difficult.

theories.name: Pauli’s One World, Two Aspects: Psychophysical Complementarity
theories.summary: Pauli's speculative psychophysical ontology, developed through his long dialogue with Carl Jung, treats conscious experience as one aspect of a deeper, neutral, archetypally ordered reality in which psyche and matter are complementary manifestations rather than separate substances. Phenomenal consciousness is therefore not reduced to brain process, nor elevated into idealist world-foundation; it is the subjective pole of a broader order in which symbolic, mathematical, affective, and physical structures may share common roots.

theories.name: Pereira’s Triple-Aspect Monism
theories.summary: Philosopher of science Alfredo Pereira, Jr., has developed a “triple-aspect monism,” the physiological, mental unconscious, and conscious aspects of brain activity, positing that consciousness is a co-emergent property that arises from these three inseparable aspects of brain and mind, all grounded in a single substance with three aspects.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness co-emerges from three inseparable aspects—physiological, mental-unconscious, and mental-conscious—of a single substance.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Neuronal, glial-astrocyte, and electromagnetic processes interact to generate feelings that shape cognition and behavior.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Adds a distinct “mental-unconscious” aspect, bridging physical processes and conscious awareness.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Frames the Self as a dynamic “Feeling Self,” consistent with Buddhist ideas of co-origination and interdependence.

theories.name: Pluralist and Relational Metaphysics—Additional Theories
theories.summary: Some theories of phenomenal consciousness resist classification within Landscape’s standard categories because they locate consciousness neither in a single kind of fundamental substance nor straightforwardly on one side of the mental–physical divide. Instead, they propose that phenomenal consciousness arises through, consists in, or is mediated by relations among multiple ontologically significant principles, domains, poles, fields, subjects and objects, or processes. What is fundamental may therefore be not consciousness alone, matter alone, or even one neutral substrate, but a structured plurality whose relations make phenomenal consciousness possible. These theories are grouped here within the Neutral Monisms category as the closest available ontological neighborhood, but they should not thereby be understood as neutral monisms in the strict sense. Neutral Monism is their taxonomic home primarily by proximity rather than by identity.

theories.name: Polkinghorne’s Dual-Aspect Monism
theories.summary: To mathematical physicist and Anglican priest John Polkinghorne, the psychosomatic nature of human persons is best understood in terms of a “dual-aspect monism,” in which matter and mind are complementary aspects of a unitary being.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Mind and matter are complementary aspects of one unified reality, avoiding both dualism and reductionism.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Uses complexity theory to explain top–down causality, with consciousness as an irreducible aspect of embodied beings.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Reconceives the soul as an “information-bearing pattern” preserved by God for resurrection.

claims.title: Challenges & Tensions
claims.text: Critics argue that pattern identity alone cannot guarantee personal continuity in an afterlife scenario.

theories.name: QRI’s State-Space, Qualia Formalism, Valence Realism
theories.summary: The Qualia Research Institute (QRI), a not-for-profit pursuing unique approaches to the science of consciousness, stresses “Qualia Formalism,” the hypothesis that the internal structure of our subjective experience can be represented precisely by mathematics, and “Valence Realism,” the central importance of emotion/affect, that is, valence (how good or bad an experience feels) as a real and well-defined property of conscious states (Qualia Research Institute).

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Conscious experiences have precise mathematical structure, and their emotional valence is a real, measurable property.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Each experience maps to a unique point in a vast “state-space” whose geometry encodes similarities and valence.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Symmetry in the state-space correlates with pleasantness; asymmetry correlates with unpleasantness.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Treating valence as a natural kind could guide mental health, AI consciousness, and altered-state research.

theories.name: Ramachandran’s New Physics and Neuroscience
theories.summary: Neuroscientist V. S. Ramachandran states that the question of consciousness cannot be answered “in any obvious terms.” Most neuroscientists don't think about the question of consciousness, as it doesn't typically arise in neuroscience or in physics. But, he says, the ancient Vedic texts of India do address the problem of consciousness, the problem of qualia.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness is a real part of reality that physics alone cannot fully explain.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: A new hybrid discipline of physics and neuroscience must integrate first-person experience with physical laws.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Draws on both modern science and ancient Vedic thought to confront the problem of qualia.

theories.name: Russellian Monism
theories.summary: Russellian Monism, based on the insights of philosopher Bertrand Russell, is a view that phenomenal consciousness and the physical world are deeply intertwined.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: The physical world has hidden intrinsic features—phenomenal or proto-phenomenal—that ground consciousness.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Physics describes structure and relations, while consciousness arises from matter’s intrinsic, non-structural properties.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Bridges materialism and dualism by making consciousness part of fundamental reality without invoking non-physical causation.

theories.name: Spinoza’s One Reality: Embodied Mind and Graded Consciousness
theories.summary: Spinoza's theory of consciousness follows from his substance monism, God or Nature, of whose infinite attributes we know two—thought and extension—and a human mind simply is the idea, under the attribute of thought, whose object is an actually existing human body. Because a mode of extension and the idea of that mode are one and the same thing expressed in two ways, mind and body neither interact nor merely correlate but are a single item under two descriptions, which dissolves the Cartesian interaction problem at the price of making the mental exactly as pervasive as the physical.

theories.name: Strawson’s Realistic Monism and Real Materialism
theories.summary: In defining an all-pervading materialism, encompassing all mental as well as all physical properties and objects, philosopher Galen Strawson espouses his kind of monism, “Realistic Monism,” as he calls it. “I'm attracted to the thing-monist view,” he says, “according to which the universe is a single thing in some non-trivial sense.”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: True materialism requires acknowledging consciousness as a real, physical, and fundamental feature of the universe.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Rejects “radical emergence,” viewing all energy—and thus all physical reality—as inherently experience-involving.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Redefines physicalism so that experiential phenomena just are physical, revealing more to matter than physics describes.

theories.name: Tegmark’s State of Matter
theories.summary: Physicist Max Tegmark speculates that “the subjective experience that we call consciousness is the way information feels when being processed in certain complex ways,” and he comes to this strong physicalist view because his starting point is, “It's all physics.”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness is a physical state of matter, arising from specific patterns of information processing.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Distinctive “information, integration, independence, and dynamics” principles separate conscious matter from non-conscious matter.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Treats consciousness as “perceptronium,” extending ideas from solid/liquid/gas states to mind itself.

theorists.name: Max Tegmark
theorists.role: Professor of Physics, Cosmologist & AI Researcher

theories.name: Teilhard de Chardin’s Evolving Consciousness
theories.summary: The Jesuit philosopher/theologian and paleontologist Pierre Teilhard de Chardin envisioned the evolution of consciousness as axial in a grand cosmic system of continuing complexification where consciousness becomes planetized and even “God” is an emergent in a process of “theogenesis.”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Evolution is fundamentally the rise of consciousness, culminating in a unified, planetized mind.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Increasing complexity in matter generates greater interior consciousness, driven by a unifying energy of love.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: God and the world co-evolve toward the Omega Point, a personal and cosmic culmination of consciousness.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Humanity’s self-awareness marks evolution reflecting on itself, shaping the next phase of cosmic development.

theories.name: Velmans’s Reflexive Monism
theories.summary: Psychologist Max Velmans describes Reflexive Monism as “a dual-aspect theory” (in the tradition of Spinoza), which argues that the one basic stuff of which the universe is composed has the potential to manifest both in physical forms and as conscious experience.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: The universe is one fundamental “stuff” that manifests both physically and as conscious experience.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Conscious beings are the universe becoming aware of itself, with mind and brain as two perspectives on the same process.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Experiences occur roughly where they seem to occur, placing consciousness partly in the external phenomenal world.

theories.name: Whitehead's Experience is Fundamental, Consciousness is Not
theories.summary: Whitehead's theory of consciousness follows from his process metaphysics rather than standing alone: the final real things are momentary “actual occasions” of experience, not enduring substances. These drops of experience are constituted by prehension, the feeling and inheriting of antecedent occasions and unrealized possibilities. Experience is therefore coextensive with actuality, while consciousness is rare, late, and derivative, but metaphysically continuous with more primitive forms of experience. Whitehead’s panexperientialism reframes the hard problem by denying that consciousness must emerge from wholly nonexperiential matter. Panexperientialism is a neutral monism of dipolar events, not a panpsychism attributing psyches to electrons. The theory offers no precise mechanism, operational criterion, or clear account of how unified phenomenal consciousness arises from underlying experiential processes.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Reality is made of momentary occasions of experience; feeling is universal, consciousness rare

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Consciousness is the subjective form of a late-phase feeling that contrasts what is given with what might have been.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Panexperientialism, not panpsychism: experience goes all the way down, but only to genuine individuals, and consciousness almost never comes with it.

claims.title: Hard Problem Reframed
claims.text: There is no gap to cross, because there are no insentient ultimates; the question becomes why awareness is so rare.

claims.title: Open Issue
claims.text: Does integration by a "dominant occasion" solve the combination problem or merely relocate it?

theories.name: Azarian’s Self-Modeling Strange Loop Theory
theories.summary: Azarian's Self-Modeling Strange Loop Theory holds that consciousness arises when a predictive world model, built to resist entropy, recursively models itself as the agent doing the modeling and thus establishes a subject. The framework synthesizes existing approaches. The self-referential loop generates a first-person perspective; integrated and differentiated information is necessary but not sufficient. Qualia are positions occupied within a relational information geometry, their valence set by distance from the organism's equilibrium. His multilevel monism treats consciousness as an irreducible, causally effective natural process, potentially realizable in different materials. The self is a strongly emergent level with causal power. Zombies are impossible, and conscious machines require recurrent physical substrates, not simulation on conventional hardware.

theories.name: Cai and Cai’s Canxian
theories.summary: Canxian is a non-reductive physicalist, monist ontology that reframes the fundamental mind-body distinction not as a dualism of substance but as an opposition between the strict locality of the physical world and the intrinsic non-locality of the conscious realm, which emerges as a real, causally efficacious level of reality constructed from countless “Cognitive Canxians.” This theory posits that consciousness is a genuine organizational structure born from physical processes, possessing unique principles and the capacity for downward causation, thereby offering a solution that avoids both eliminativism and substance dualism.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness emerges from physical processes but forms its own real, causally powerful level of reality.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Minds “canxianize” spacetime by editing and grouping events into meaningful cognitive units called Cognitive Canxians.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Consciousness isn’t a substance but a non-local structure built from shared, transferable concepts across minds.

claims.title: Redefining Causality
claims.text: Intelligent minds re-engineer causality by building efficient, goal-directed psychological pathways beyond raw physics.

claims.title: Origin of Self
claims.text: The first Canxian is the Self, rooted in life’s physical boundary between “me” and “not me,” grounding subjective experience.

theories.name: Ellis’s Strong Emergence and Top-Down Causation
theories.summary: Mathematical physicist George Ellis approaches consciousness by combining non-reductionist strong emergence and top-down causation in the context of “possibility spaces.”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness arises from strong emergence, where higher-level properties have irreducible causal powers.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Top-down causation lets higher system levels shape lower ones, actualizing possibilities like thoughts and qualia.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: “Possibility spaces” define all potential conscious states, realized through brain-enabled emergence.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: If true, most purely reductionist materialist theories cannot fully explain consciousness.

theories.name: Herath's State-Space Selection and the Sentience Factor
theories.summary: A conscious episode is the stabilization of one configuration within a structured state-space; its felt "overlay" belongs to a separate, non-structural constituent, the Sentience Factor, that unites with structure only when the system responds to a configuration.

theories.name: Maxwell’s Unique-Matching Theory
theories.summary: Maxwell’s Unique-Matching Theory integrates multiple modes of understanding—scientific, personalistic, and metaphysical—without collapsing them into a single paradigm. It posits a one-to-one, structure-preserving isomorphism between a multidimensional space of all possible sensations and a corresponding space of functionally described brain processes. This structural necessity accounts for specific correlations without requiring reductive explanation.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness and brain processes align through a unique, structure-preserving mapping between sensation space and brain-process space.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: A multidimensional “space” of all possible sensations matches isomorphically with a corresponding space of functional brain states.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: The mapping is structurally necessary, preserving continuity and unity without reducing mind to matter.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Offers a non-reductive explanation of brain–mind correlation that integrates scientific, personalistic, and metaphysical perspectives.

theories.name: Montero’s Incomplete Post-Physicalism
theories.summary: It is time to come to terms with the difficulty of understanding what it means to be physical and start thinking about the mind–body problem from a new perspective. Instead of construing it as the problem of finding a place for mentality in a fundamentally physical world, we should think of it as the problem of finding a place for mentality in a fundamentally nonmental world, a world that is at its most fundamental level entirely nonmental.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness is physical, but our concept of the physical is incomplete.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Reframes the mind–body problem as fitting mentality into a fundamentally nonmental world.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Shifts focus from “physical vs. nonphysical” to “mental vs. nonmental” for clearer debate.

claims.title: Implications
