claims.text: Opens physicalism to revision while preserving realism about conscious experience’s causal role.

theories.name: Murphy’s Non-Reductive Physicalism
theories.summary: Christian philosopher Nancey Murphy, reflecting increasing Christian scholarship calling for acceptance of physicalism, argues that the theological workability of physicalism depends on the success of an argument against reductionism. She takes Non-Reductive Physicalism, a common term in philosophy of mind, to “signal opposition to anthropological dualisms of body and either mind or soul, as well as to physicalist accounts that reduce humans to nothing but complex animals.”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Humans are wholly physical beings, yet mental life cannot be reduced to biology alone.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Complex systems allow for “downward causation,” where higher-level wholes influence their physical parts.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Rejects both dualism and reductive materialism, grounding personhood in whole-organism dynamics.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Offers a biblically and scientifically compatible view of humanity, reframing “soul” as the whole living person.

theories.name: Nagasawa’s Nontheoretical Physicalism
theories.summary: Philosopher Yujin Nagasawa interrelates central debates in philosophy of mind (phenomenal consciousness) and philosophy of religion (existence of God) to construct a unique metaphysical thesis, which he calls “nontheoretical physicalism,” by which he claims that although this world is entirely physical, there are physical facts that cannot be captured even by complete theories of the physical sciences.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: The world is wholly physical, yet some physical facts elude complete physical theories.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Shifts physicalism from theory-based to entity-based, leaving room for untheorizable facts.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Links philosophy of mind and religion via parallels in knowledge-limit arguments.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Preserves physicalism while admitting the irreducibility of certain experiential realities.

theories.name: Non-Reductive Physicalism—Overview
theories.summary: Non-Reductive Physicalism takes consciousness to be entirely physical, solely the product of biological brains, but mental states or properties are irreducibly distinct from physical states or properties such that they cannot be entirely explained by physical laws, principles, or discoveries (in brains or otherwise).

claims.title: Core Concepts
claims.text: Consciousness is fully physical yet irreducible to physical explanations, emerging from but distinct from lower-level brain processes.

claims.title: Scientific Context
claims.text: Responds to early identity theory problems, using emergence and supervenience while countering reductionist physicalism and dualism.

claims.title: Why Meaningful
claims.text: Offers a framework for mental causation, integrating scientific naturalism with philosophical and sometimes theological perspectives.

claims.title: Major Challenges
claims.text: Reconciling mental causal power with physical causal closure; avoiding collapse into reductive materialism or property dualism.

theories.name: Northoff’s Non-Reductive Neurophilosophy
theories.summary: Northoff frames his views on consciousness as “non-reductive neurophilosophy,” which, he says, is “primarily a methodological approach,” a particular strategy that takes into account “certain phenomena which otherwise would remain outside our scope [consciousness studies].”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness research needs a systematic, non-reductive method linking philosophy and neuroscience.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Connects conceptual brain–mind models with empirical brain data without reducing one to the other.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Treats theory–data integration as a methodological tool usable in both philosophy and neuroscience.

theories.name: Poznanski’s Processual Relational Geometry: Self-Intending Transscale Consciousness
theories.summary: Poznanski’s Processual Relational Geometry (PRG) holds that phenomenal consciousness is the intrinsic realization of a physically embodied, transscale continuity of relational organization. Consciousness is not generated by computation, neural integration, biological complexity, or quantum activity considered separately; it occurs when physical realization and constitutive realization become reciprocally realized manifestations of one ontophysical continuity, stabilized through self-intending projective closure. Phenomenality is the intrinsically realized manifestation of this conscious actuality, while perception, cognition, memory, affect, and bodily regulation are downstream dispositional expressions rather than its constitutive source.

theories.name: Sanfey’s Abstract Realism
theories.summary: Abstract Realism claims to bridge the mind-matter explanatory gap by demonstrating that consciousness has a precisely definable physical function. The Temporal Uncertainty Principle (TUP) defines consciousness as the integration of two contradictory, temporal perspectives, diachronic and simultaneous, whose interaction manages the same fundamental problem that mystifies the integration of quantum and classical mathematics. Consciousness evolves as a physical mechanism that enables temporally extended information to operate at point-equivalent instants without computational paralysis.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness arises from a complementarity between first- and third-person perspectives, each with an equivalent observer function.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Phenomenal simultaneity grants conscious presence causal power through two interacting, complex information systems in the brain.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Consciousness is unobservable in principle yet equivalent in effect to strong emergence without requiring new physics.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Integrates consciousness into Non-Reductive Physicalism while avoiding reductive, panpsychist, or idealist accounts.

theories.name: Sperry’s Mentalist Paradigm
theories.summary: Neuropsychologist/neurobiologist Roger Sperry, who was awarded the Nobel Prize for hemispheric lateralization in split-brain patients, proposes a “mentalist paradigm” in which consciousness is a causal emergent in brain function. “Emergent determinism,” he says, “is the basic key concept behind this paradigm shift.”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness is a causal, emergent property of brain function with genuine top-down control.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Higher-level brain systems govern lower-level neural processes, legitimizing mental causation.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Rejects both dualism and reductionism, framing “Mentalist Monism” as a new causal framework.

claims.title: Challenges & Tensions
claims.text: Clashes with traditional micro-deterministic science that excludes subjective experience.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Repositions consciousness as a legitimate scientific factor, bridging neuroscience and humanistic values.

theories.name: Van Inwagen’s Christian Materialism and Resurrection of the Dead
theories.summary: Christian philosopher/metaphysician Peter van Inwagen combines a wholly materialist ontology of the human person with a committed belief in the resurrection of the dead as the Christian hope of eternal life.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Humans are wholly material beings, yet can be resurrected without invoking an immortal soul.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: God preserves a “bare kernel” of one’s current material being to ensure continuity after death.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Rejects dualism as a Greek import into Christianity, grounding resurrection in materialist ontology.

claims.title: Challenges & Tensions
claims.text: Continuous atomic turnover raises the problem of reassembly without producing mere duplicates.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Redefines Christian afterlife hope in purely physical terms while remaining biblically and philosophically consistent.

theories.name: A. Harris’s Panpsychism as Fundamental Field
theories.summary: Neuroscience/consciousness writer Annaka Harris posits that “consciousness isn't self-centered” and that we should “think of consciousness like spacetime—a fundamental field that's everywhere.”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness may be a fundamental field, like spacetime, present throughout reality.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Consciousness is intrinsic to matter; complex arrangements yield subjective points of view.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Removes the “self” from the combination problem, seeing no literal merging of consciousnesses.

theories.name: Chalmers’s Panpsychism
theories.summary: Panpsychism's renaissance can be attributed, at least in part, to philosopher David Chalmers, who has long entertained panpsychism as a possibly viable theory of consciousness.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness may be a fundamental feature of physical reality, embedded in its most basic entities.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Expands physical ontology to include phenomenal or protophenomenal properties at the fundamental level.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Frames panpsychism as a synthesis between materialism and dualism, contingent on solving the combination problem.

theories.name: Coleman’s Panqualityism
theories.summary: A panprotopsychist form of Russellian monism in which the fundamental basis of the physical world is intrinsically qualitative but not intrinsically conscious, so that phenomenal consciousness arises only when organized qualities are made subjectively available by an awareness-conferring structure such as higher-order representation, thereby recognizing qualia without positing ubiquitous micro-subjects.

theories.name: Cosmopsychism
theories.summary: Cosmopsychism reverses the standard explanatory ontology that facts about big things are grounded in facts about small things. It posits that facts about little things are grounded in facts about big things.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: The universe as a whole is conscious, and smaller facts derive from this cosmic mind.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: A top-down ontology grounds micro-level realities in macro-level cosmic consciousness.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Avoids panpsychism’s combination problem by starting with one unified, conscious cosmos.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Offers a parsimonious alternative to theism and multiverse for explaining fine-tuning.

theories.name: Goff’s Panpsychism
theories.summary: Philosopher Philip Goff starts from the premise “one thing that science could never show is that consciousness does not exist” and he mounts a vigorous, rigorous case for panpsychism, the staggering idea (at least initially) that “consciousness is a fundamental and ubiquitous feature of the physical world.”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness is a fundamental and ubiquitous feature of the physical world, beyond materialism’s reach.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Expands science’s scope by reintegrating consciousness into its foundations, countering purely quantitative limits.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Defends a hybrid panpsychism where experiences emerge weakly, but subjects emerge strongly, leaning toward cosmopsychism.

theories.name: Kadić's Monadic Panpsychism
theories.summary: “Monadic panpsychism” is a relational explanation of how simple subjects could constitute complex experiences, without them having to combine in virtue of their subjectivity.” The claim is that monadic panpsychism overcomes the notorious main obstacle for panpsychism: “the difficulty of explaining how simple subjects could combine to form complex subjects." This version of panpsychism "avoids talk of combination” by recruiting "microphenomenal structuralism," which views phenomenal qualities as relational, at the level of fundamental simples, though it admits of the basic consciousness of microsubjects-in-isolation as well.

theorists.name: Nino Kadić
theorists.role: Senior Assistant at the Institute of Philosophy in Zagreb

theories.name: Micropsychism
theories.summary: Proponents position panpsychism as a solution to the vexing problems of both materialism and dualism: replacing materialism's apparent impotence to account for consciousness and avoiding dualism's sharply bifurcated reality.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness exists at the microphysical level, forming the basis for all macro-level experiences.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Macroexperience arises from microexperience, either constitutively or through strong emergence.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Positions panpsychism as a middle path between materialism’s limits and dualism’s split reality.

claims.title: Key Challenge
claims.text: Faces the “combination problem” of explaining how microexperiences unite into complex consciousness.

theories.name: Mørch's Phenomenal-Causal Powers Panpsychism
theories.summary: Philosopher Hedda Hassel Mørch advocates a version of panpsychism that integrates insights from both philosophy and neuroscience. It is inspired by Bertrand Russell's concept of a neutral monism, where consciousness is a fundamental and ubiquitous feature of the physical world, meaning that even basic particles possess rudimentary forms of consciousness. In her “Phenomenal Powers” view, Mørch proposes that phenomenal properties—our inner felt awareness (i.e., consciousness)—are not just passive experiences but have active, real-world, causal efficacy.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness is a fundamental, ubiquitous feature of the physical world with real causal powers.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Phenomenal qualities are identical to causal powers, grounding how matter behaves physically.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Links panpsychism with IIT and proposes consciousness as the intrinsic “hardware” of reality’s structure.

theories.name: Panprotopsychism
theories.summary: Panprotopsychism is distinguished from panpsychism in that the most basic protophenomenal properties are not themselves forms of consciousness but rather must combine to generate forms of consciousness.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Basic protophenomenal properties aren’t conscious but combine to produce consciousness.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Emergence occurs when unexperienced qualities transform into experienced ones.

claims.title: Key Challenge
claims.text: Explaining how non-conscious qualities become conscious experience (“phenomenal magic”).

theories.name: Panpsychism Additional Theories
theories.summary: Additional panpsychism theories, often from less well-known individuals, that offer original ideas and perspectives.

theories.name: Panpsychisms—Overview
theories.summary: Panpsychism is the theory that phenomenal consciousness exists because physical ultimates, fundamental physics, have phenomenal or proto-phenomenal properties. This means that the essence of mentality, awareness, experience is a primitive, non-reducible feature of each and every part or aspect of physical reality, similar to the fundamental fields and particles in physics. Everywhere there is energy-matter, perhaps everywhere there is even spacetime, panpsychism says there is also something of consciousness. Everything that exists has a kind of inherent consciousness or “proto-consciousness,” which, in certain aggregates and under certain conditions, can generate inner awareness and experience. Panpsychism has multiple forms, nuances, and variants, as one would expect.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness is a basic feature of physical reality, present even at the smallest scales of matter and energy.

claims.title: How it Works
claims.text: All entities have proto-consciousness; under the right conditions, these combine into richer minds via resonance or structure.

claims.title: Diverse Expressions
claims.text: From ancient traditions to modern theories like General Resonance Theory, panpsychism spans cultures, philosophies, and sciences.

claims.title: Major Challenges
claims.text: Faces questions about testability, coherence, and how micro-conscious elements combine into unified conscious experience.

theories.name: Qualia Force
theories.summary: In the theory of Qualia Force, consciousness is a deep feature of physical reality that emerges from the fields and particles of fundamental physics, perhaps in the strong emergence sense that it cannot be explained by fundamental physics, even with knowledge beyond the current, even in principle.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness is a fundamental yet emergent feature of physical reality, arising beyond physics’ full explanation.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Differs from panpsychism by making consciousness derivative from—but not reducible to—physical laws.

theories.name: Qualia Space
theories.summary: In the theory of Qualia Space, consciousness is an independent, non-reducible feature of reality that exists in addition to the deepest laws of fundamental physics (i.e., the four forces, spacetime, mass-energy).

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness is a non-reducible, independent feature of reality alongside fundamental physical laws.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Posits a distinct “qualia space” dimension or structure where phenomenal properties are organized.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Exemplified by IIT’s conceptual structures, but not necessarily universal or classic panpsychist.

theories.name: Schneider and Bailey’s Entangled Superpsychism
theories.summary: A new version of panpsychism, called “Superpsychism,” where the fundamental level of physics has a more advanced form of consciousness than spacetime occupants do.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: The deepest level of reality hosts a “superconscious” state—more coherent and integrated than any spacetime mind.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Spacetime emerges from a timeless “prototime” dimension; quantum entanglement in prototime yields unified, maximal-coherence consciousness.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Unlike cosmopsychism, the highest consciousness isn’t the whole universe but a non-spatiotemporal entangled megaobject.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Could unify quantum puzzles and consciousness theory, reframing both as emerging from the same non-spatiotemporal base.

theorists.name: Susan Schneider
theorists.role: Director, Center for Future Mind, Florida Atl. Un.

theorists.name: Mark Bailey
theorists.role: Chair, Cyber Intel. & Data Sci., Nat. Intel. Un.

theories.name: Sheldrake’s Self-Organizing Systems at All Levels of Complexity
theories.summary: Iconoclastic biologist Rupert Sheldrake's radical views on the nature of reality inform theories of consciousness in two ways. One, covered here, envisions self-organizing systems at all levels of complexity as a robust form of panpsychism.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness exists at every level of nature, from atoms to the entire universe.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Self-organizing systems with open possibilities use mind-like processes, mediated by electrical fields.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Nonbiological minds (e.g., stars, galaxies) have distinct forms of consciousness unlike human awareness.

theories.name: Starrett’s Radical Panpsychism
theories.summary: Radical Panpsychism is a mathematically grounded philosophical framework for understanding consciousness, which proposes that experience is a fundamental and ubiquitous aspect of reality, not limited to complex organisms but present in all entities.

claims.title: Core Concepts
claims.text: Reality is one unified entity; all mental and physical aspects are part of this single whole.

claims.title: Scientific Context
claims.text: Related to panpsychism but distinct; includes philosophical and metaphysical frameworks integrating mind and matter.

claims.title: Why Meaningful
claims.text: Offers parsimony, avoiding dualism’s split and materialism’s limits by uniting consciousness and reality in one substance.

claims.title: Major Challenges
claims.text: Boundaries with panpsychism blur; defining the “one thing” precisely remains philosophically and scientifically difficult.

theories.name: Strawson’s Panpsychism
theories.summary: Philosopher Galen Strawson calls panpsychism “the most parsimonious, plausible and indeed ‘hard-nosed’ position that any physicalist who is remotely realistic about the nature of reality can take up in the present state of our knowledge.”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness is a fundamental feature of matter, making panpsychism the most realistic physicalist stance.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Reframes panpsychism as “real materialism,” expanding physicalism to include experiential properties.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Treats panpsychism not as anti-materialist, but as the only consistent form of true physicalism.

theories.name: Tye’s Irreducible Consciousness*
theories.summary: Philosopher Michael Tye has come to support a nuanced version of panpsychism, because he now holds that there are no borderline cases of phenomenal consciousness: it’s an on/off matter. Phenomenal consciousness is irreducible, and at the most fundamental level, there is what Tye labels ‘consciousness*,’ which others would call ‘protoconsciousness.’

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Phenomenal consciousness is irreducible and exists as fundamental “consciousness*” or protoconsciousness.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Consciousness resides in basic entities and transfers to complex systems meeting specific functional and representational conditions.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Retains representationalism but solves panpsychism’s combination problem by making consciousness strictly on/off.

theories.name: Wallace’s Panpsychism Inside Physics
theories.summary: To philosopher of physics David Wallace, one way to motivate panpsychism is as a kind of synthesis of materialism (consciousness is just reducible to the physical) and dualism (consciousness is separate from the physical). Each, he says, has major advantages and major disadvantages.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Panpsychism unites materialism’s causal closure with dualism’s recognition of consciousness as fundamental.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Consciousness is the intrinsic nature of physical entities, giving causal power within physics’ laws.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: No extra forces are needed; physics’ equations describe conscious reality “from the inside.”

theories.name: Whitehead’s Process Theory (Panpsychism)
theories.summary: Although Whitehead's Process Theory is already classified comprehensively under Neutral Monism, it is also discussed here under Panpsychism—even though most scholars conclude he is not a panpsychist. The motivation is process philosopher Matthew Segall's bringing Whitehead's Philosophy of Organism “into conversation with the recent panpsychist turn in analytic philosophy of mind.”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Reality’s basic units are “drops of experience,” making experience universal but consciousness rare and emergent.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Actual entities are processual events with primitive experiential subjectivity, combining past facts with future potentials.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Reframes the combination problem as “concrescence,” a creative synthesis rather than additive assembly of parts.

theories.name: Bitbol’s Radical Neurophenomenology
theories.summary: Philosopher of science and phenomenologist Michel Bitbol promotes a “radical neurophenomenology” in which a “tangled dialectic of body and consciousness” is the “metaphysical counterpart” and whose goal is to advance Varela's neurophenomenology project of criticizing and dissolving the “hard problem” of consciousness.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness can't be explained objectively because it is the condition for all explanation.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Dissolves the “hard problem” by shifting focus from explanation to transformation of lived experience.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Consciousness and objectivity co-emerge; neither has metaphysical priority over the other.

claims.title: Challenges & Tensions
claims.text: Demands researchers abandon neutrality and engage in existential self-inquiry.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Reframes science as rooted in experience, aligning neurophenomenology with quantum participatory realism.

theories.name: Brentano’s Intentionality and Self-Awareness
theories.summary: Brentano’s theory of phenomenal consciousness is a structured field of mental acts intrinsically directed toward objects and simultaneously aware of themselves. His decisive thesis is that intentionality—being of, about, or directed toward something—is the mark of the mental; every conscious episode presents an object—it is about something. Brentano thereby created the immediate prehistory of Husserlian phenomenology.

theories.name: D.W. Smith’s Three-Facet Ontological Phenomenology
theories.summary: D.W. Smith’s theory of consciousness is an ontological phenomenology in which phenomenal consciousness is understood through three inseparable but distinguishable facets: intentional form, phenomenal appearance, and natural substrate. Consciousness is not reducible to neural or computational mechanisms, yet neither is it beyond nature; it is a structured phenomenon whose subjectivity, intentionality, qualitative appearance, embodiment, and basis in biological-cultural life require an ontology broad enough to hold them together

theories.name: Dennett’s Heterophenomenology
theories.summary: Heterophenomenology is not a phenomenology at all, but a deliberate opposition to the entire phenomenology enterprise—a third-person method for studying what subjects say, believe, judge, remember, and report about their conscious lives, giving the third-person study greater veridical value than first-person reports. Phenomenal consciousness should not be approached through allegedly incorrigible first-person access, but through the same disciplined evidential stance used in the sciences: subjects’ reports are indispensable data, but not privileged revelations of inner qualitative reality.

theories.name: Derrida’s Deconstruction of Self-Presence
theories.summary: Derrida offers a sustained argument against the assumption underlying most Western theories of consciousness, a sustained deconstruction of the assumption that consciousness is a primal, foundational, self-present, and self-transparent immediacy in which the subject coincides with itself and its experience is given "in person."

theories.name: Gallagher’s Embodied Self and Interactive Consciousness
theories.summary: Phenomenal consciousness is an embodied and enactive account that is not a process occurring inside the brain, but an activity of the whole embodied organism engaged with its environment, and on which the structure of that experience is best disclosed by subjecting phenomenological distinctions to empirical scrutiny. The central contribution is two distinctions—between body image and body schema, and between the minimal self and the narrative self.

theories.name: Gurwitsch’s Structured Field of Experience
theories.summary: Phenomenal consciousness is never a bare succession of contents but always a structured field with this invariant tripartite structure: a theme occupying focal awareness, a thematic field of contents experienced as materially relevant to the theme, and a margin of co-present but irrelevant data. Thus, phenomenal consciousness is a dynamically organized totality rather than a succession of isolated sensations or a narrow attentional spotlight.

theories.name: Heidegger’s Dasein (Being-In-The-World) Without Qualia
theories.summary: Heidegger’s theory of consciousness is best understood not as a theory of inner mental activities, qualia, or subject-object representation, but as an anti-Cartesian phenomenological ontology in which what we call phenomenal consciousness is a derivative of Dasein’s more basic being-in-the-world: an affectively attuned, practically absorbed, temporally structured, socially normed disclosure of beings as meaningful. Heidegger displaces “consciousness” from the foundational role, arguing that the primary phenomenon is not an inner subject inspecting contents, but a finite being already involved with tools, others, tasks, moods, possibilities, and mortality,

theories.name: Henry’s Auto-Affective Self-Revelation of Life
theories.summary: Michel Henry’s theory of phenomenal consciousness is a radical phenomenology of Life: consciousness in its most original sense is not intentional awareness of objects in a world, not ecstatic, and not directed toward a world, but is life feeling itself—an immediate self-affection with no distance, no gap, and no otherness internal to it but Life’s immediate, invisible, affective self-revelation in radical immanence.

theories.name: Husserl’s Transcendental Phenomenology
theories.summary: Husserl’s theory of consciousness is a transcendental phenomenology: a rigorous descriptive inquiry into how anything can appear as meaningful, objective, temporal, embodied, and intersubjectively available within lived experience. Phenomenal consciousness is therefore not adequately captured by neural correlation, behavioral report, functional access, or introspective inventory alone; it is the field in which objects, worlds, others, selves, meanings, and evidences are constituted as appearing.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness is intentional, structured, temporal, embodied, and world-disclosing experience; it must be described as lived and given before being explained causally.

claims.title: Method of Epoché
claims.text: The epoché suspends the unexamined “natural attitude” toward the world in order to investigate how world, objectivity, self, and others are constituted in experience.

claims.title: Noesis–Noema Correlation
claims.text: Every intentional act has an act-character—perceiving, judging, imagining, remembering, doubting—and an object-as-meant, the noematic sense through which the object is given.

claims.title: Time and Self-Awareness
claims.text: The living present is structured by primal impression, retention, and protention, making possible continuity, melody, memory, anticipation, and the minimal self-presence of experience.

claims.title: Embodiment and Intersubjectivity
claims.text: The lived body, kinesthetic movement, empathy, and shared horizons of verification ground the experience of an objective world common to many subjects.

claims.title: Lifeworld Grounding
claims.text: Scientific objectivity is an achievement abstracted from, and dependent on, the pretheoretical lifeworld of ordinary practical, perceptual, embodied, and social experience.

theories.name: James’s Stream of Thought/Consciousness
theories.summary: James’s phenomenological theory of consciousness is his account of the “stream of thought”: a continuous, personal, changing, selective, object-directed flow in which the fringe, transitions, relations, bodily feelings, attention, emotion, and will are as integral as focal contents. His theory is proto-phenomenological because it analyzes consciousness as lived, dynamic, perspectival, temporal, and interest-laden.

theories.name: Meinong's Self-Presenting Experience
theories.summary: Meinong’s account of consciousness crafts Brentano’s intentionality into a systematic theory of how experience can be directed toward anything—existent, possible, fictional, incomplete, or impossible. Phenomenal consciousness comprises differentiated acts and psychological contents that disclose objects without creating them or requiring that they possess being/existence.

theories.name: Merleau-Ponty's Embodied Perception and the Lived Body
theories.summary: Merleau-Ponty locates consciousness not in an interior theater of mental states but in the lived body (le corps propre), whose pre-reflective, motor engagement with a world is the condition of there being any phenomenal field at all. Phenomenal consciousness is fundamentally perceptual, embodied, motoric, affective, spatial, temporal, and intersubjective: the world shows up not first as neutral information but as a field of solicitations, possibilities, obstacles, meanings, and bodily powers.

theories.name: Peirce’s Phaneroscopic Semiotics
theories.summary: Peirce reconstructs consciousness "phaneroscopically," as the observational study of whatever appears to mind, analyzed through three irreducible categories—Firstness (qualitative feeling), Secondness (brute reaction), and Thirdness (mediation, habit, signification). Phenomenal consciousness falls under Firstness, a simple quality "veiled from introspection." Rejecting introspection and intuition, Peirce makes experience continuous with semiosis and, cosmologically, with an idealist universe where matter is "effete mind." Recent scholarship positions him as phenomenology's independent precursor—chronologically prior to Husserl, outside his lineage.

theories.name: Petitmengin’s Micro-Phenomenology
theories.summary: Petitmengin’s theory of consciousness is best understood methodologically as micro-phenomenology: a disciplined first-person and second-person method for making the fine-grained, normally unnoticed structure of lived experience available to description, analysis, and scientific use.

theories.name: Phenomenology—Overview
theories.summary: Phenomenology is the disciplined philosophical investigation of consciousness as it is lived, undergone, and disclosed from the first-person point of view. This systematic structuring of experience is independent of any theory about its physical basis, metaphysical presuppositions, or ultimate nature. As a theory-space for phenomenal consciousness, phenomenology seeks to clarify the forms of appearance without prematurely translating them into causal mechanisms.

theories.name: Sartre’s Pre-reflective Consciousness as For-Itself
theories.summary: Consciousness is not a thing, a container of contents, or a self behind experience, but a wholly intentional, self-transcending activity—always consciousness of some transcendent object—that is at the same time implicitly and in a non-objectifying way aware of itself in a non-positional or pre-reflective mode.

theories.name: Shanon's Cartography and Structured Spectrum
theories.summary: Shanon’s Psychological Theory of Consciousness presents phenomenal consciousness as a differentiated but coherent system spanning elementary sentience, ordinary mental awareness, reflective metamentation, and non-ordinary or self-transcendent states. The theory maps the types, parameters, regions, and dynamic transformations of experience itself. Its central claim is that ordinary consciousness cannot be adequately characterized without comparing it with dreams, hallucinations, psychedelic visions, and mystical states.

theorists.name: Benny Shanon
theorists.role: Cognitive psychologist and philosopher of psychology

theories.name: Thompson's Phenomenology: Waking, Dreaming, Sleeping, Pure Awareness
theories.summary: Phenomenal consciousness must be studied as lived, embodied, temporally structured, intentionally world-disclosing experience, using disciplined first-person, second-person, contemplative, and neurobiological methods in reciprocal constraint. It is best understood as an embodied, naturalized, neurophenomenological account of phenomenal consciousness

theories.name: Varela’s Neurophenomenology
theories.summary: Neuroscientist and philosopher Francisco Varela proposes what he calls “neurophenomenology,” which seeks to articulate mutual constraints between phenomena present in experience, inspired by the style of inquiry of phenomenology and the correlative field of phenomena established by the cognitive sciences.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness must be studied through both lived experience and neuroscience, equally and together.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Links first-person experience with brain science to uncover mutual patterns and constraints.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Experience is not a byproduct but a valid, rigorous domain for scientific investigation.

claims.title: Challenges & Tensions
claims.text: First-person data is hard to collect and interpret reliably, yet essential to the project.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Reframes the “hard problem” as a collaborative, ongoing dialogue between subjectivity and science.

theories.name: Winkelman's Integrative Mode of Neurognostic Structures
theories.summary: Consciousness is best understood via neurophenomenology—through the reciprocal constraint of first-person phenomenology and third-person neurobiology, mind and brain alike being manifestations of the inherent structures of the human organism. Humans possess several biologically based modes of consciousness—waking, deep sleep, dreaming, and a fourth "integrative mode" underlying altered states. Phenomenal consciousness is the organism's cognized model of the world, built from "neurognostic" structures: innate, genetically predisposed forms of knowing.

theories.name: Zahavi’s Pre-Reflective For-Me-Ness
theories.summary: A phenomenological account of phenomenal consciousness as intrinsically first-personal, self-manifesting, and pre-reflectively self-conscious. An experience is not first a neutral mental event that subsequently becomes “mine”; rather, its very appearing involves “for-me-ness,” or first-personal givenness. This minimal selfhood is not an introspected object, substantial soul, or social construction, but the subjective character without which phenomenal consciousness would not be experience at all.

theories.name: Beck-Eccles’s Quantum Processes in the Synapse
theories.summary: Sir John Eccles, Nobel laureate for his seminal work on the synapse, the small space between neurons across which neurochemicals flow to excite or inhibit contiguous neurons, was a pioneer in early efforts to construct a “quantum neurobiological” theory of consciousness.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Conscious intentions can influence brain activity by biasing quantum events at neuronal synapses.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Mental volition alters the probability of neurotransmitter release via quantum state reduction during exocytosis.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Links free will to quantum uncertainty in calcium ion dynamics at synaptic trigger sites.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Suggests consciousness can directly shape neural activity, challenging strictly mechanistic brain models.

theories.name: Bohm’s Implicate-Explicate Order
theories.summary: Quantum physicist David Bohm, colleague of Einstein, famously introduced the idea of “implicate order” and “explicate order” as ontological implications of quantum theory to explain two radically opposed perspectives of the same phenomenon—something seems to be needed to account for the bizarrely divergent ways of conceiving reality, quantum and classical, both of which seemed undeniably correct.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Reality has two intertwined orders: the visible explicate order and the hidden implicate order.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: The implicate order enfolds all reality; the explicate order unfolds it into everyday experience.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Mind and matter share a common higher-dimensional ground beyond either’s independent existence.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Suggests a unified, dynamic wholeness linking consciousness and matter in continuous transformation.

claims.title: Challenges & Tensions
claims.text: Critics question how to test or formalize implicate order within conventional science.

theories.name: Carr’s Higher Dimensions and Mental Space
theories.summary: Mathematician-astronomer Bernard Carr speculates that a higher dimension, or “mental space,” an unknown aspect of reality, may be the ultimate foundation of consciousness. “Even if you believe that consciousness collapses the wave function,” he says, “that doesn't really accommodate consciousness within physics.”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness is a fundamental aspect of reality requiring a higher-dimensional “mental space” beyond spacetime.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: The brain limits experience, while mind operates within an expanded space linking minds and matter.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Marries matter and mind from the universe’s beginning, not as one emerging from the other.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Could explain paranormal and transpersonal experiences, demanding physics expand to include consciousness.

theories.name: Cavelier's Entangled Spins at the NMDA Receptor
theories.summary: Conscious experience could be registered in the brain by being embedded in entangled radical-pair spin states associated with N-methyl-D-aspartate receptors, and the information so embedded is transferred into the spike-frequency and timing codes of the associated neural circuits. The framework describes electronic wavefunctions across successive scales—photons and spins, molecular conformation, ion channel gating, circuit oscillation, and finally the spiking patterns from which qualia are held to emerge.

theorists.name: German Cavelier
theorists.role: Biomedical research administrator and molecular biophysicist

theories.name: Chalmers and McQueen’s Quantum Collapse
theories.summary: Chalmers and McQueen draw parallels between our understanding of quantum mechanics and consciousness. On the one hand, “One of the hardest philosophical problems arising from contemporary science is the problem of quantum reality. What is going on in the physical reality underlying the predictions of quantum mechanics?” On the other hand, “Another of the hardest philosophical problems arising from contemporary science is the mind-body problem. What is the relation between mind and body, or more specifically, between consciousness and physical processes?”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness may trigger quantum wave function collapse, bridging gaps in physics and mind-body theory.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Combines Integrated Information Theory with quantum collapse dynamics to link conscious states to collapse events.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Positions wave function collapse as a “causal gap” where consciousness could exert physical influence.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Offers a testable research program uniting quantum mechanics and consciousness without committing to strict dualism.

claims.title: Challenges & Tensions
claims.text: Faces skepticism from physicists and philosophers over causal closure and dualist implications.

theories.name: Faggin’s Quantum Information-Based Panpsychism
theories.summary: Physicist/inventor Federico Faggin’s “Quantum Information-based Panpsychism” (QIP) states that consciousness isn’t an emergent byproduct of matter, but rather an irreducible property of nature. He leverages quantum properties—uncertainty, entanglement, superposition—to show that classical reductionism fails and that reality includes an “inner” experiential dimension. He proposes that “the holistic Whole contains not only the seeds of the inanimate universe but also those of free will, consciousness, and life.”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness is an irreducible property of nature, intrinsic to quantum systems in pure states.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Pure quantum states mirror conscious experience through their definiteness, privacy, and integration of qualia.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: “Seities,” fundamental quantum-conscious agents, predate spacetime and generate both physical laws and lived experience.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Suggests free will, creativity, and consciousness arise from quantum reality, beyond algorithmic or mechanistic replication.

claims.title: Raises the Question
claims.text: If consciousness is intrinsic to quantum systems, could it persist beyond bodily death?

theories.name: Fisher’s Quantum Cognition
theories.summary: Condensed matter physicist Matthew Fisher proposes that quantum processing with nuclear spins might be operative in the brain and key to its functioning. He identifies “phosphorus as the unique biological element with a nuclear spin that can serve as a qubit for such putative quantum processing—a neural qubit—while the phosphate ion is the only possible qubit-transporter.”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness may involve quantum computation in the brain using phosphorus nuclear spins as neural qubits.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Phosphorus atoms in “Posner molecules” preserve entanglement, influencing neuron firing via calcium release.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Identifies a concrete biological structure (Posner molecule) as a long-lived quantum memory in the brain.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Points to a possible bridge between quantum biology and neuroscience, sparking a new “quantum neuroscience” field.

claims.title: Open Issue
claims.text: Experimental proof of Posner molecule quantum effects in living brains is still lacking.

theories.name: Gambini and Pullin’s Quantum Panprotopsychism
theories.summary: The Quantum Panprotopsychism theory of consciousness proposes that an ontology of quantum mechanics in terms of states and events with internal phenomenal aspects, that is, a form of panprotopsychism, is well suited to explaining consciousness.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness arises from quantum events with intrinsic phenomenal aspects, a form of panprotopsychism.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Quantum states and events carry internal phenomenal qualities; entanglement generates emergent properties beyond classical physics.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Solves the subject-summing “combination problem” by appealing to quantum indeterminacy and causal efficacy of consciousness.

claims.title: Why Meaningful
claims.text: Offers a physics-grounded ontology where consciousness is neither epiphenomenal nor reducible, linking quantum processes to selfhood.

theories.name: Globus’s Quantum Thermofield Brain Dynamics
theories.summary: Psychiatrist-philosopher Gordon Globus seeks to link two seemingly independent discourses: an application of quantum field theory to brain functioning, which he calls “quantum brain dynamics,” and the continental postphenomenological tradition, especially the work of Martin Heidegger and Jacques Derrida.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: The brain discloses the phenomenal world through dissipative quantum thermofield dynamics, not via perceptual consciousness.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Brain states (“brain-p” phenomenal, “brain-q” quantum) are triply tuned by senses, memory, and self-adjustment to create reality.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Merges quantum brain theory with Heideggerian and Derridean philosophy into a non-Cartesian, disclosure-based ontology.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Reframes the hard problem and quantum measurement problem as issues of disclosure, bypassing standard consciousness models.

claims.title: Open Issue
claims.text: Highly abstract; lacks empirical pathways to test the philosophical-quantum synthesis it proposes.

theories.name: Hameroff’s Consciousness Came Before Life
theories.summary: Consciousness is an intrinsic, fundamental feature of the universe rather than an emergent property of biological complexity. Based on the Penrose-Hameroff quantum theory of consciousness, the theory holds that consciousness may have enabled evolution and life in the first place. Consciousness came before life.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness is a process of quantum self-collapses called Penrose ‘objective reductions’ (‘OR’) connected to Planck scale spacetime geometry, the fundamental level of the universe. Such events select classical states and proto-conscious qualia with ‘hedonic valence’, including pleasure.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Organic aromatic ring hydrocarbons with pi electron resonance orbitals are produced by stars, prevalent in interstellar dust and throughout the universe, the basis for life on earth, and conducive to quantum optical processes in non-polar, water-excluding regions in living systems. Penrose OR proto-conscious ‘qualia’ would have been present in the early universe before life began. In a ‘primordial soup on early Earth, aromatic ring molecules (e.g., dopamine-like) could have coupled by quantum van der Waals forces, oscillated in terahertz, and potentially reached the threshold for Penrose OR to have proto-conscious moments. Some would be pleasurable, and provide a feedback function for aromatic rings to arrange to optimize pleasure, and thus spark the origin and evolution of life

claims.title: Reverses Evolutionary Order
claims.text: Consciousness didn’t emerge from life; life evolved to amplify and organize pre-existing conscious processes.

claims.title: Biological Candidates
claims.text: Polyaromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) produced by stars are prevalent in the universe, the basis for organic chemistry and life on Earth. In biological systems, they form quantum-friendly regions in helical oscillators, including RNA and microtubules. As helical organic oscillators evolved and grew larger to optimize pleasure by OR, self-similar global oscillations occurred at slower frequencies – a time crystal. RNA world and then microtubules developed to process information and manifest purposeful behavior to optimize pleasure.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Consciousness is tied to spacetime geometry, and may have existed there prior to life, and perhaps will exist there afterwards, remaining entangled and persisting in spacetime as a “quantum soul.”

theories.name: Kauffman’s Mind Mediating Possibles to Actuals
theories.summary: Theoretical biologist Stuart Kauffman posits the following: (i) Quantum measurement converts Res potentia—ontologically real Possibles—into Res extensa - ontologically real Actuals. (ii) Brain/mind/consciousness cannot be purely classical physics because no classical system can be an analog computer whose dynamic behavior can be isomorphic to “possible uses”, and therefore, brain/mind/consciousness must be partly quantum.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness helps convert quantum “Possibles” (Res potentia) into actual events (Res extensa).

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Mind, partly quantum, collapses the wave function, turning potential states into experienced realities.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Adopts Heisenberg’s “potentia” as ontologically real, avoiding both materialism and substance dualism.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Suggests mind is nonlocal and plays an active causal role in the physical world.

theories.name: Keppler’s Zero-Point Field
theories.summary: Physicist Joachim Keppler posits that consciousness is an intrinsic feature of the universe embedded in the quantum vacuum, specifically the zero-point field (ZPF) from quantum field theory, and that the brain acts as a resonant, dynamical interface that modulates and orchestrates specific modes of the ZPF, allowing access to certain conscious states.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness is a fundamental feature of the universe, rooted in the quantum vacuum’s zero-point field.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: The brain resonates with specific ZPF modes, selectively amplifying them to produce conscious states.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Treats the ZPF as a universal “palette” of qualia, with brain activity acting like a resonant filter.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Suggests neurotransmitter control of ZPF coupling could explain shifts in awareness and guide new research.

theories.name: King’s Symbiotic Existential Cosmology
theories.summary: ‘Symbiotic Existential Cosmology’ is a biogenic, psycho-physical cosmology of conscious life in the universe. Subjective consciousness and the physical universe have an irreducible, asymmetric, complementary interactive relationship in which life is a biospherically symbiotic climax phenomenon in the mature universe. Interactivity is key to cosmology, affirming the ability of subjective consciousness to participate in causal intent and acausal anticipation through coupled, physically indeterminate phase transition states, which are seen as key to why subjective consciousness has been preserved by biological evolution over computational biology.

claims.title: Core Thesis
claims.text: Subjective consciousness forms an irreducible, interactive complement to the physical universe, enabled by critical phase transition states in both brain dynamics and cosmology.

claims.title: Protection of Evolving Life
claims.text: The climactic unfolding of Earth's biosphere is cosmologically sacrosanct—a privileged, protected outcome of universal evolution.

claims.title: Paradigm Disruption
claims.text: This paradigm-shifting theory challenges scientific zeitgeist, asserting that subjective conscious agency provides a uniquely privileged window into the universe.

claims.title: Key Principles
claims.text: Biocosmology: Conscious life is is a climax condition of cosmology, shaped by symmetry-breaking and the fractal, nonlinear dynamics of molecular interaction. Existence: The cosmos comprises subjective consciousness and the physical universe as complements—our only access to physical reality is through consciousness. Symbiosis: Despite individual selection, evolution is symbiotically cumulative; predators and parasites play essential roles in biospheric stability.

theories.name: Morrison’s Position Selecting Interactionism
theories.summary: Colin Morrison posits that the direct physical correlate of our subjective experience is the wavefunction of a single rare particle (no doubt of a complex, compound nature), confined within a very small region of the brain (most likely a single neuron) that he calls ‘the cavity.’

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness correlates with the wavefunction of a single rare particle confined within a neuron’s “cavity.”

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Particle position-measurements, influenced by sensory inputs, memories, and emotion, direct shifts in attention.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Subjective images form when sensory systems modulate the particle’s wavefunction amplitude in distinct ways for different qualia.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Explains attention’s randomness, the “spotlight” effect, and how qualia bind into unified perceptual scenes.

claims.title: Challenges & Tensions
claims.text: Requires a yet-unidentified rare particle and mechanisms that ensure that only one particle of this type is present in a neuron-sized cavity.

theories.name: Neven's Quantum Superposition Formation
theories.summary: The physical substrate of consciousness is a single, precisely specified quantum-mechanical event: the formation of a superposition. The theory proposes that conscious experience is generated not by classical computation and neural information processing alone, nor by the collapse of a quantum state, but by the creation of a quantum superposition itself: “Conscious experience arises whenever a quantum mechanical superposition forms.”

theorists.name: Hartmut Neven
theorists.role: Founder/manager, Quantum Artificial Intelligence Lab, Google

theories.name: Pacheco’s Science of Unity
theories.summary: The “Science of Unity” model posits matter and consciousness as deeply intertwined, following a fractal-like hierarchical arrangement from fundamental forms to macro-structures. Reality unfolds across higher frequential dimensions, where different Standard Models coexist within the same space but experience distinct physical properties.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Matter and consciousness form a single fractal continuum, differing only in density and vibrational state.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Consciousness filters through layered densities in an inverted fractal pattern, shaped by structural and perceptual shifts.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Introduces a “non-causal dimension” of mathematical indeterminacy, enabling genuine free will beyond determinism.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Bridges science and spirituality, unifying material and immaterial concepts into one structured reality.

claims.title: Open Issue
claims.text: The coexistence of multiple Standard Models in parallel frequency realities remains speculative and untested.

theories.name: Penrose-Hameroff’s Orchestrated Objective Reduction
theories.summary: Penrose-Hameroff's quantum consciousness, which they call Orchestrated Objective Reduction (OrchOR), is the claim that consciousness arises in the fundamental gap between the quantum and classical worlds.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness emerges from quantum state collapses in neuronal microtubules, linking brain activity to spacetime geometry.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Orchestrated quantum reductions in microtubules avoid decoherence, enabling non-computational processing and unified conscious moments.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Bridges quantum mechanics and classical physics, making consciousness a product of quantum gravity effects.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Suggests consciousness predates life, explains binding and causation, and potentially accounts for anomalous experiences.

claims.title: Challenges & Tensions
claims.text: Faces skepticism over sustaining quantum coherence in the brain and lack of direct experimental confirmation.

theories.name: Poznanski’s Dynamic Organicity Theory
theories.summary: The Dynamic Organicity theory of consciousness is a materialist framework grounded in an ontology of quasi-strong emergence. Quasi-strong emergence serves as a conceptual bridge between Polanyian emergence and nonreductive physicalism, offering an account of consciousness as a self-intending projection of intrinsically agential dynamics arising from embodied, quantum-delocalized information systems.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness emerges from quantum-delocalized, self-referential information systems in living brains, grounded in quasi-strong emergence.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Multiscale, holarchical brain dynamics integrate quantum-level effects with changing boundary conditions to create intentional agency.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Replaces “emergence” with a self-reference principle, focusing on functional pathways over structural descriptions.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Challenges panpsychism and pure functionalism, framing experience as embodied, enacted, and tied to negentropic brain states.

claims.title: Open Issue
claims.text: The FMultiComplexity > FMaxComplexity threshold is conceptually bold but awaits empirical verification in biological systems.

theories.name: Pylkkänen’s Quantum Potential Energy and Active Information
theories.summary: Philosopher Paavo Pylkkänen proposes a view in which “the mechanistic framework of classical physics and neuroscience is complemented by a more holistic underlying framework in which conscious experience finds its place more naturally.” Recognizing that it is “very likely that some radically new ideas are required if we are to make any progress” on the hard problem, he turns to quantum theory “to understand the place of mind and conscious experience in nature.”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness fits more naturally in a Bohm-inspired quantum framework where matter contains “active information.”

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Quantum reality includes a new kind of potential energy that guides systems holistically, influencing mind–matter links.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Rejects purely mechanical physics, proposing non-mechanical, organic concepts to bridge neurophysiology and consciousness.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Opens the door for genuine mental causation without violating physics, challenging epiphenomenalism.

theories.name: QBism’s Primitive, Participatory Experience: Quantum Agency and the First-Person World
theories.summary: QBism (Quantum Bayesianism) is not itself a theory of consciousness, but its interpretation of quantum mechanics has unusually strong implications for phenomenal consciousness because experience is already primitive in its formulation and it places the individual agent’s personal experience at the conceptual foundation of quantum theory. To be explicit: Qbism is an interpretation of quantum mechanics with implications for consciousness, rather than a quantum-neural mechanism that generates consciousness.

theories.name: Quantum & Dimensions—Overview
theories.summary: Quantum theories of consciousness take seriously the idea that quantum mechanics plays a necessary, if not sufficient, role in the specific generation of phenomenal consciousness in certain physical entities like brains—beyond the general application of quantum mechanics in all physical entities. The kinds of quantum theories or models on offer differ radically.

claims.title: Core Concepts
claims.text: Proposes quantum mechanics plays a direct, possibly necessary role in generating phenomenal consciousness in brains.

claims.title: Scientific Context
claims.text: Includes diverse approaches, from quantum brain processes to quantum-inspired cognitive models, often with experimental implications.

claims.title: Why Meaningful
claims.text: Challenges classical-only neuroscience by linking two deep mysteries—quantum reality and conscious experience—in potentially unifying ways.

claims.title: Major Challenges
claims.text: Lacks consensus, clear mechanisms, and sustained empirical support; many scientists remain skeptical of quantum–mind connections.

theories.name: Quantum/Dimensional Additional Theories
theories.summary: The following theories of consciousness are not quantum theories per se in that they do not have quantum mechanics as the essence or generator of consciousness. Rather, each reflects how quantum mechanics could facilitate or interact with other theories of consciousness. All are highly speculative.

theories.name: Rourk’s Catecholaminergic Neuron Electron Transport Theory
theories.summary: The Catecholaminergic Neuron Electron Transport (CNET) theory sits among quantum theories, but with an important qualifier: it is best understood as a quantum-biological neural-correlate theory rather than a general quantum-metaphysical account of consciousness. Its central explanatory target is phenomenal consciousness as integrated, selected, salient, and action-guiding experience. Its proposed contribution is to identify a possible physical binding and selection mechanism linking GNW-style global availability, GPR-style action selection, prefrontal organization, catecholaminergic modulation, and ferritin/neuromelanin electron transport

theories.name: Rovelli’s Relational Physics
theories.summary: Physicist Carlo Rovelli focuses on “the profoundly relational aspect of physics, manifest in general relativity, but especially in quantum mechanics.” 20th-century physics, he says, “is not about how individual entities are by themselves. It is about how entities manifest themselves to one another. It is about relations.”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Physics describes relations between systems, not intrinsic properties, making reality inherently perspectival.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Entities manifest only through interactions, with all descriptions relative to specific physical systems.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Relationalism reduces the gap between mental and physical by reframing both as perspective-dependent.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: May offer a mild form of panpsychism while deflating the “hard problem” of consciousness.

claims.title: Challenges & Tensions
claims.text: Subjective experience still seems more private than physics’ relational descriptions allow.

theories.name: Shiah’s Cryptochrome Theory
theories.summary: Cryptochrome Theory proposes that cryptochrome—a flavoprotein found in all living systems—functions as a biological "transducer" that translates consciousness-driven information into physical manifestations of psi (psychic) phenomena through quantum-mechanical radical-pair reactions.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness can directly influence the physical world through quantum processes mediated by the protein cryptochrome.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Cryptochromes act as biological transducers, converting consciousness-driven information into physical effects via radical-pair quantum reactions.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Identifies a specific molecule and quantum mechanism linking mind, biology, and reported psi phenomena.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Suggests consciousness is a non-local force, with potential applications in biology, medicine, and future communication technologies.

theories.name: Smolin’s Causal Theory of Views
theories.summary: Physicist Lee Smolin approaches the question of how qualia fit into the physical world in the context of his “relational and realist completion of quantum theory, called the causal theory of views.”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness arises from rare, novel “views” of events within a relational universe of causal perspectives.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Each event has a “view” from its causal past; unprecedented, unique views correlate with conscious moments.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Restricts panpsychism to a small set of rare, non-duplicated event views, tying qualia to physical novelty.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Offers a realist, physics-based selection principle linking qualia to the structure and history of the universe.

theories.name: Stapp’s Collapsing the Wave Function via Asking “Questions”
theories.summary: Mathematical physicist Henry Stapp argues for the quantum nature of consciousness by relying on a traditional interpretation of quantum mechanics, where quantum wave functions collapse only when they interact with consciousness in an act of measurement.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness collapses quantum wave functions by posing “questions,” making mind fundamental to physical reality.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Observer choices trigger quantum state collapses in the brain, linking mental events to physical outcomes.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: The choice of quantum questions is undetermined by physics, allowing genuine causal power for consciousness.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Positions consciousness as an active agent, overturning classical materialism’s view of mind as inert or illusory.

claims.title: Challenges & Tensions
claims.text: Critics question coherence with neuroscience and risk of reintroducing dualism in modern quantum theory.

theories.name: Strømme’s Universal Consciousness as Foundational Field
theories.summary: Maria Strømme proposes that consciousness is not an emergent property of neural processes, but is a fundamental field of reality from which space–time, matter, and individual minds emerge. It is a non-reductive, non-dual, cosmological theory, where solving the mind–brain problem requires reframing the ultimate, deep structural relation among consciousness, physics, individuality, and reality as a whole. The result is a non-dual metaphysics, where individual subjects of experience are not separate centers of consciousness in the deepest ontological sense; they are localized differentiations of a single field

theories.name: Torday’s Cellular and Cosmic Consciousness
theories.summary: Developmental physiologist John Torday offers an original cellular-based explanation of consciousness that embeds quantum mechanics. He describes consciousness as a two-tiered system, derivative from physiology, having been “constructed” from the environment via factors in the environment that have been assimilated via symbiogenesis and integrated as cell physiology—the cell semi-permeable membrane being the first tier, and the compartmentation and integration of cell physiologic data as cell-cell communication as the second tier.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness emerges from cellular physiology, linking quantum processes in cells to cosmic-scale awareness.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Symbiogenesis and quantum entanglement connect local cellular memories with non-local cosmic consciousness.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: The cell acts like a Möbius strip, seamlessly uniting “inside” biology with the wider cosmos.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Suggests consciousness is continuous from physiology to universal mind, challenging strict materialism.

claims.title: Open Issue
claims.text: How physiological quantum entanglement translates into subjective experience remains speculative.

theories.name: Tozzi’s Multidimensional Brain
theories.summary: Arturo Tozzi offers a topological and computational framework for neuroscience by challenging the view that neural activity is confined to three spatial dimensions plus time. Leveraging advances in big data, computational modeling, and topological mathematics, he posits that brain functions, ranging from perception and cognition to emotion and consciousness, are best understood within high-dimensional phase spaces exceeding conventional spatial representation.

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Brain activity unfolds in high-dimensional spaces beyond the familiar three spatial dimensions plus time.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Topological data analysis and manifold modeling reveal hidden geometries linking distant brain regions.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Higher dimensions may be real anatomical/functional properties, not just abstract mathematical tools.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Multidimensional mapping could improve understanding of cognition, consciousness, and brain disorders.

claims.title: Challenges & Tensions
claims.text: Uncertainty remains over whether extra dimensions are ontological realities or modeling conveniences.

theories.name: Van Dusen’s Hyperspatial Dimension Theory
theories.summary: Van Dusen’s dimensional theory of consciousness proposes that mind is not contained within ordinary four-dimensional physical space-time, but is identical with operations in real higher-dimensional spaces. Phenomenal consciousness, on this view, is not produced by the brain; it is the differentiated “line of awareness” running through these levels, with the brain serving as its lower physical anchor.

theories.name: Wigner–von Neumann’s Consciousness-Collapse: Experience at the Quantum Cut
theories.summary: Wigner–von Neumann consciousness-collapse theory originates in von Neumann’s distinction between continuous unitary quantum evolution and discontinuous measurement, together with a measurement chain extendable from apparatus through brain to an observer. Von Neumann did not clearly claim that consciousness causes collapse; Wigner drew the explicit conclusion that consciousness causes collapse, arguing from the premise that experience is invariably determinate and never superposed, and from a principle of reciprocal action requiring that what acts on consciousness must be acted upon by it. Wigner proposed that conscious experience may induce nonunitary physical change, giving phenomenal consciousness causal efficacy. The theory does not explain why consciousness exists or has qualitative character; it presupposes phenomenality while assigning it a fundamental dynamical role. Wigner later retreated from the proposal, although modern mathematically explicit consciousness-collapse models remain empirically open.

theories.name: Wolfram’s Consciousness in the Ruliad
theories.summary: Physicist and computer scientist Stephen Wolfram seeks “to formalize issues about consciousness, and to turn questions about consciousness into what amounts to concrete questions about mathematics, computation, logic or whatever that can be formally and rigorously explored.” He begins by embedding consciousness in what he calls the “ruliad” (neologism from “rules”), which he defines as “the entangled limit of everything that is computationally possible: the result of following all possible computational rules in all possible ways.”

claims.title: Core Claim
claims.text: Consciousness is our coherent, sequential experience formed by sampling the “ruliad,” the space of all possible computations.

claims.title: How It Works
claims.text: Our minds extract simplified, bounded-computation descriptions from the ruliad to create definite, coherent thoughts.

claims.title: Distinguishing Idea
claims.text: Consciousness is not maximal computation but a “step down” enabling coherent perception of a branching universe.

claims.title: Implications
claims.text: Links consciousness to the fundamental structure of physical law and to our position in “rulial space.”

claims.title: Raises the Question
claims.text: Could different consciousnesses meet by moving through both physical and rulial space?
